full_text_sections.discussion: DISCUSSIONThe placenta is a critical immunological gatekeeper during pregnancy, balancing its essential roles in nutrient and oxygen exchange with the need to protect the fetus from invading pathogens. Our data suggest that placental IAV exposure induces a cascade of immune defenses, including a robust placental type I IFN response (IFN-β). These responses are characteristic of a rapid antiviral defense state, in which the placenta prioritizes pathogen restriction over immune quiescence to protect and nourish the fetus. This placental antiviral response occurred independently of maternal lung disease severity, supporting the concept that the placenta transitions into a defensive immune state in response to maternal infection, effectively shielding the fetus from infection at the potential cost of immune injury to the placenta and fetus, and stillbirth.To our knowledge, this study provides the first demonstration that maternal IAV infection can broadly perturb the fetal immune landscape in a manner linked to maternal metrics of immunity and disease in an NHP model. As vertical transmission was not detected in our experiments, the data suggest that immunologic, rather than virologic, signals are responsible for the profound changes in the fetal immune landscape observed after in utero exposure to maternal IAV infection. Notably, fetuses in the FLU cohort exhibited significantly higher frequencies of multiple T cell populations and reduced frequencies of monocytes compared with CTRLs, with these changes evident across multiple organs and fluid compartments and correlated with key metrics of maternal IAV disease. Although the mechanisms by which host-pathogen interactions shape fetal immune development and long-term health remain incompletely understood, maternal disease severity represents a potentially modifiable determinant of these outcomes. We also note that several articles in rodent models have previously shown a link between maternal IAV infection and perturbations in fetal thymic transcriptome (24), hematopoietic development (45), and lymphoid organ compartmentalization (46).Altered fetal immunity has previously been described following in utero exposure to maternal HIV infection, even in the absence of maternal–fetal viral transmission. Perinatally HIV-exposed but uninfected infants have been shown to have a lower frequency of naïve CD4+ and CD8+ T cells, among other abnormalities in immune activation, compared to perinatally HIV-unexposed infants (47–50). Similar findings of a perturbed fetal immune landscape have been reported in cases of maternal severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) infection. Perturbed monocyte cell populations with increased NK cell and regulatory T cell frequencies were reported in uninfected neonates exposed to maternal SARS-CoV-2 (41, 44). These changes in fetal immunity may represent an intermediate biological state that accompanies pathways leading to abnormal neurodevelopment, as described in many cohorts of adults exposed to maternal influenza and other infections during fetal life (15, 16, 21, 22, 51, 52).Stillbirth occurred in two animals in the FLU cohort, an outcome that was unexpected based on the CTRL cohort and historical colony experience. The placental antiviral program triggered by IAV H1N1 is known to promote inflammation and tissue injury during acute viral infections and has been directly implicated in the pathogenesis of stillbirth in mouse models of congenital Zika virus infection (53–56). Whether a viral-associated ISR may have also contributed to stillbirth through translational repression and maladaptive stress signaling is unknown. We are cautious to causally attribute these stillbirths solely to the placental type I IFN or ISR response for several reasons. A spectrum of placental pathology was observed in FLU animals, with similar lesions (i.e., infarction and necrotizing villitis) also present in several CTRL placentas from clinically healthy animals. Background placental pathology in macaques is known to be relatively high, with prior studies documenting marginal infarctions and villitis as common findings even in uncomplicated pregnancies (37–39). Moreover, unlike human stillbirth evaluations, which routinely involve extensive histopathologic sampling across the entire placental disc, the placental tissue in this study was allocated to multiple downstream immunologic and transcriptomic analyses, thereby limiting a comprehensive histopathologic examination. Together, these factors limit our ability to assign a specific pathological mechanism to the two stillbirths, underscoring the need for cautious interpretation while highlighting a biologically plausible link between antiviral placental immune activation and adverse perinatal outcomes.The primary strength of our study lies in the translational nature of the NHP model, which closely recapitulates human pregnancy, enabling modeling of an IAV infection in the context of pregnancy. NHPs are highly similar to humans in their genetics, anatomy, physiology, immune responses, and pregnancies (29). Macaques have a long gestational period and a placental architecture similar to that of humans. Another strength of the pregnant NHP model of IAV infection is the ability to study antiviral immune responses at a defined time after infection onset, which is not possible during human pregnancy. Further, this study was deliberately conducted in the third trimester of pregnancy, a time when pregnant women experience the greatest maternal morbidity and mortality (57, 58). NHP studies excel at identifying integrated physiologic outcomes that cannot be replicated in other models, providing an essential translational context for human pregnancy. Defining molecular mechanisms in NHP models is constrained by biology and ethics, in contrast to in vitro or mice models, which offer considerably greater experimental manipulation. These features of the pregnant NHP model of IAV infection demonstrate the translational relevance of this model and the marked impact of our findings, while also providing possible mechanistic insights for future studies.This study has several limitations, primarily related to ethical constraints involved with NHP studies and the modest sample size. We did not study end points earlier or later than 5 days postinfection, preventing assessment of the trajectory of the antiviral response in the maternal lungs and placenta. We used multiple routes of viral inoculation to ensure productive disease; experiments using lower inocula delivered via aerosol would more closely recapitulate IAV transmission in humans. Examining multiple end points was not feasible with our limited sample size, but future studies could investigate alterations in fetal immune regulation after maternal IAV disease resolution and the potential for development of an ISR in the placenta. While the stillbirths are notable cases, the study’s conclusions are drawn from patterns across the entire infected cohort. Our CTRL cohort consisted of historical uninfected controls used in prior studies. While housing conditions, sample collection, and experimental protocol remained consistent across all animals, the use of historical controls provides challenges in accurately controlling confounding variables, such as the gestational age at the inoculation and necropsy time points. After performing analyses using a subset of the CTRL cohort to account for these variations in gestational age, we found that most of our conclusions remained significant, even with reduced statistical power.Together, these findings position the placenta as an active and autonomous organ that mounts a robust type I IFN defense against IAV, which may partly explain the rarity of vertical transmission. In contrast, fetal immunity appears to be sensitive to maternal disease severity, with perturbations in fetal T cells and monocytes across multiple fetal compartments occurring in a coordinat…
full_text_sections.other: INTRODUCTIONInfluenza A virus (IAV) infections remain a global public health threat, which is especially pronounced in immunologically vulnerable populations such as pregnant women (1, 2). IAV is a negative-sense, single-stranded RNA virus composed of eight segments. Pandemics occur when reassortment of viral segments produces new combinations of its surface glycoproteins, hemagglutinin (HA) and neuraminidase. Epidemiologic evidence from several IAV pandemics (e.g., 1918, 1957, 1968, and 2009) indicates that IAV infections in pregnancy impart a greater risk of maternal mortality and adverse pregnancy outcomes, such as stillbirth (3–14). There may also be a long-term risk of neuropsychiatric disease in the children born to pregnant women infected with IAV or other infectious diseases, which has been reported in multiple populations (15–22).The effects of placental and fetal exposure to maternal IAV have been studied primarily in murine models. Experimental IAV infection in pregnant mice and rats (e.g., H1N1 and H3N2) has been associated with a range of adverse outcomes, including preterm birth, low birth weight, and stillbirth (resorptions) (23–27). These models demonstrate robust activation of innate and adaptive immunity in the maternal compartment, with increased monocytes, neutrophils, and T cells detected in the lung, placenta, and gut-associated lymphoid tissue. In mice, IAV can disrupt progesterone and prostaglandin signaling in the placenta, which was associated with adverse perinatal outcomes and placental remodeling (26, 28). Severe maternal IAV-associated vascular inflammation has been associated with placental growth restriction and fetal brain hypoxia (23). In contrast, relatively few studies have examined fetal immune perturbations following in utero exposure to maternal IAV, with reports describing only altered fetal thymic transcription and reduced neutralizing antibody responses to IAV (24, 25). Thus, the extent to which systemic maternal disease coordinates immune changes across the placenta and fetus, whether these responses scale with disease severity, and how they ultimately influence fetal development remain unclear.The objective of our study was to determine the immunologic impact of a maternal infection with an IAV H1N1 2009 pandemic strain on the placenta and fetus in a pigtail macaque (Macaca nemestrina) model, with a focus on whether severity of maternal lung disease influenced these changes. While some of these molecular mechanisms have been identified in mice and rats, these animal models differ from human pregnancy in many respects, including a short gestation (3 to 5 weeks). Humans have a gestational period that is 8 to 10 times longer than these species, allowing for extended fetal brain development in utero. However, this long gestational period also increases placental and fetal exposure to seasonal waves of IAV infection. Nonhuman primates (NHPs) share many similarities with human pregnancy, including longer gestation, placental structure, and labor physiology (29, 30). NHPs are also frequently used in IAV disease modeling due to their similarities in human clinical and pathological features (31, 32). A few studies using pregnant NHPs have modeled IAV infection but were performed to specifically understand complement activation and infant brain development in African green monkeys and rhesus macaques, respectively (33, 34). Thus, our central goal was to broadly characterize how IAV infection during pregnancy affects placental and fetal immunity in a pigtail macaque model, a highly translational model to human pregnancy. title_original: Influenza A virus infection induces immune dysregulation in the placenta and fetus without vertical transmission in nonhuman primates

analysis.research_question_and_background: This study aimed to investigate the effects of influenza A virus infection on placental and fetal immune responses in nonhuman primates, addressing the gap in understanding how maternal influenza infection might impact fetal immunity without direct vertical transmission.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study involved pregnant pigtail macaques inoculated with IAV [A/California/07/2009 (H1N1)] and uninfected controls. A total of 11 infected and 16 uninfected pregnant animals were included, with delivery and fetal necropsy performed 5 days postinfection.
analysis.methods: IAV H1N1 virus was cultivated and quantified using a TCID50 assay. RNA was isolated from tissue samples and analyzed using RT-qPCR with a WHO-approved primer/probe set. RNA sequencing was performed on the NovaSeq 6000 system, and differential expression analysis was conducted on placental samples.
analysis.main_results: Vertical transmission was not observed, but low levels of viral RNA were detected in two placentas. Maternal infection was associated with a type I interferon response in the placenta and altered immune cell populations in the fetus.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpreted that maternal influenza infection induces immune dysregulation in the placenta and fetus, highlighting the potential for indirect effects on fetal immunity despite the absence of vertical transmission.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings suggest that influenza A virus infection during pregnancy may have implications for fetal immune development and could inform strategies for monitoring and managing maternal influenza in human populations.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study used historical controls, which may introduce potential confounding variables, and the tissue quality was a limitation for fetal sample collection. The evidence is moderate due to these factors.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigated the effects of influenza A virus (IAV) infection on placental and fetal immune responses in nonhuman primates. Pregnant pigtail macaques were inoculated with IAV [A/California/07/2009 (H1N1)] and compared to uninfected controls. The results showed that vertical transmission was not observed, but low levels of viral RNA were detected in two placentas. Maternal infection was linked to a type I interferon response in the placenta and changes in immune cell populations in the fetus. The authors interpreted these findings as evidence of immune dysregulation in the placenta and fetus without direct transmission. The study's use of historical controls and issues with fetal tissue quality limit the confidence in the results, making the evidence moderate. These findings could inform understanding of maternal influenza's impact on fetal immunity and guide surveillance and management strategies in human populations.

title: Distinct influenza interfaces in cattle: repeated spillovers of highly pathogenic avian influenza A(H5N1) from wild birds and enzootic circulation of influenza D virus

source_records.title: Distinct influenza interfaces in cattle: repeated spillovers of highly pathogenic avian influenza A(H5N1) from wild birds and enzootic circulation of influenza D virus

full_text: AbstractCattle now occupy two epidemiologically distinct influenza interfaces. This Mini Review comparatively synthesizes epidemiological, pathological, experimental-transmission, genomic, and surveillance evidence for highly pathogenic avian influenza A(H5N1) and influenza D virus (IDV), asking how source ecology, tissue tropism, shedding, transmission, persistence, and zoonotic evidence differ between the two viruses. Genetically distinct H5N1 viruses have spilled over repeatedly from wild birds into United States dairy cattle. In lactating cows, infection is prominent in mammary alveolar epithelium and produces high titers of infectious virus in raw milk; inter-herd cattle movements have disseminated genotype B3.13 through dairy production networks. On affected farms, viral RNA has been detected in milk and respiratory specimens; infectious virus is recovered consistently from raw milk and mammary tissues but only sporadically from respiratory or environmental samples such as milking-parlour air and wastewater. These findings identify exposure settings but do not resolve the dominant natural cow-to-cow transmission route or how the virus reaches the mammary gland. Occupational infections have occurred, but sustained cattle adaptation or long-term reservoir status has not been demonstrated. In contrast, IDV is a cattle-adapted respiratory virus maintained through direct contact and short-range airborne transmission, with interlineage reassortment among IDV genome segments and frequent association with bovine respiratory disease complex (BRDC), although an independent causal role in BRDC remains unproven. Human seroreactivity and efficient replication in human airway models indicate exposure and biological compatibility, but not confirmed productive human infection or onward transmission. These contrasts support event-triggered, milk-centered investigation for H5N1 and longitudinal respiratory and genomic surveillance for IDV, built on shared One Health diagnostic, sequencing, epidemiological, and occupational-health infrastructure.Keywords: bovine respiratory disease complex, cattle, cross-species transmission, highly pathogenic avian influenza a(H5N1), influenza D virus, mammary tropism, one health surveillance 6.DiscussionAlthough both viruses infect cattle, their assessment requires different risk frameworks. Epidemiological consequences depend on the principal replication site and its relationship to production. In H5N1-infected dairy cows, mammary infection links viral shedding to milk production and milking practices. High-titer shedding in milk creates a direct exposure pathway; animal movements facilitate dissemination, while occupational contact creates opportunities for human exposure. IDV lacks this production-linked route; instead, it is maintained by respiratory transmission and interacts with other pathogens within the polymicrobial setting of BRDC. The most informative samples, genomic priorities, and response thresholds therefore differ.The principal uncertainties differ between the two viruses. For H5N1, the natural portal of entry, the relative contributions of milking-associated, respiratory, and environmental transmission, and whether cattle constitute a long-term reservoir remain unresolved. For IDV, respiratory replication and cattle-to-cattle transmission are established, but its independent contribution to naturally occurring BRDC remains uncertain, as does the clinical significance of human exposure signals. Resolving these questions will require studies that integrate viral kinetics with tissue lesions, co-pathogen dynamics, animal-movement histories, clinical outcomes, and transmission phenotypes.The supporting evidence is asymmetric in scope and design. H5N1 evidence derives mainly from intensively investigated outbreaks in lactating United States dairy cattle and a few experiments; extrapolation to non-lactating cattle, beef cattle, calves, and other production systems remains uncertain. IDV studies span more regions and years but often use cross-sectional PCR or serology, heterogeneous sampling, and incomplete genomic data. These differences preclude simple comparisons of prevalence, transmission efficiency, pathogenicity, or zoonotic risk. Preparedness should therefore reflect virus-specific replication sites and production systems rather than host species alone. 1.IntroductionInfluenza A virus ecology is commonly framed around wild aquatic birds as the principal natural reservoir, with poultry, swine, and humans occupying different host roles in amplification, reassortment, adaptation, and disease emergence (Krammer et al., 2018). Cattle received little attention because sustained influenza A virus circulation had not been documented in bovine populations. In 2024, clade 2.3.4.4b highly pathogenic avian influenza A(H5N1) [HPAI A(H5N1)] was confirmed in United States dairy cattle (Caserta et al., 2024), and genomic analysis traced spread through interconnected dairy production networks (Nguyen et al., 2025). A joint assessment by the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO), World Health Organization (WHO), and World Organization for Animal Health (WOAH), based on data available through 1 March 2026, documented several independent spillovers from wild birds into cattle, demonstrating that multiple viral genotypes can infect this host (Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations et al., 2026).The emergence of H5N1 in dairy cattle established a production-linked influenza interface centered on lactation, milking, and cattle movement. Field and experimental studies documented mammary infection, high virus titers in milk, mastitis, abnormal milk, and production loss (Caserta et al., 2024; Baker et al., 2025; Peña-Mosca et al., 2025). Movement of infected cattle facilitated long-distance dissemination (Nguyen et al., 2025), whereas genetically distinct spillovers from wild birds created new points of entry (Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations et al., 2026). Thus, raw milk and milking procedures are central exposure settings, cattle movement links herds, and contaminated equipment, aerosols, wastewater, cross-species contact, and occupational contact define additional exposure pathways whose contributions to natural transmission remain unresolved.Influenza D virus (IDV) follows a different ecological pattern. First isolated from a pig with respiratory disease (Hause et al., 2013), it was later established as a distinct orthomyxovirus with cattle as its principal maintenance host (Hause et al., 2014). Experimental studies in calves demonstrated direct-contact (Ferguson et al., 2016) and short-range airborne transmission (Salem et al., 2019). Case-control (Ng et al., 2015) and cohort (Nissly et al., 2020) studies associate IDV with bovine respiratory disease complex (BRDC) without establishing independent or dominant causation. Whole-genome studies document diversification and geographic structure (Limaye et al., 2024), interlineage reassortment among IDV genome segments (Collin et al., 2015), and regional persistence (Li H. et al., 2026), favoring longitudinal surveillance over outbreak-limited investigation.The two viruses differ most clearly in their principal replication sites. Mammary replication links H5N1 to milk and dairy production networks, whereas respiratory replication links IDV to enzootic circulation and BRDC. We therefore compare shedding, transmission, disease context, evolutionary dynamics, and surveillance across these compartments, while distinguishing occupational exposure signals from evidence of productive human infection or onward transmission. 2.Highly pathogenic avian influenza A(H5N1) in dairy cattle: emergence, mammary infection, and unresolved transmission routesThe United States cattle epizootic was initially dominated by genotype B3.13. Phylogenetic and epidemiological analysis support a single wild-bird-to-bovine spillover followed by extensive cattle-associated, movement-linked spread (Nguyen et al., 2025). Genotype D1.1 detections in Nevada and Arizona represented two additional independent spillovers from wild birds, each with limited cattle transmission (Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations et al., 2026). Repeated entry and sustained circulation are therefore separate processes. Unresolved questions are how often wild-bird-derived H5N1 crosses into cattle, which changes arise after spillover, and which routes sustain transmission. Extensive cattle-associated spread alone does not establish long-term reservoir status.After introduction, the distinctive pathological feature in lactating cows is mammary infection. Field investigations detected abundant viral RNA and infectious virus in milk, epithelial necrosis, and H5N1 antigen by immunohistochemistry in mammary alveolar epithelial cells (Caserta et al., 2024). Intramammary inoculation reproduced severe mastitis, abnormal milk, reduced production, and high-titer milk shedding (Baker et al., 2025). In contrast, oronasal inoculation of calves produced moderate upper-respiratory replication and nasal shedding, without detected transmission to sentinels (Halwe et al., 2025). Because these experiments differed in age, lactation status, target tissue, and inoculation route, they establish mammary tropism but do not identify the natural entry route.Transmission evidence remains less definitive. Low-dose intramammary challenge caused robust infection and high-titer shedding in milk, but transmission to sentinel cows was not detected despite repeated exposure to contaminated milking equipment and close contact. Respiratory and oral exposures were also less efficient than intramammary inoculation at establishing productive infection under the tested conditions (Lee et al., 2026). Across 14 California dairy farms, infectious virus was recovered from milking-parlour air on three farms and from wastewater on one farm; viral RNA was also detected in exhaled breath and milk from cows without overt clinical signs (Campbell et al., 2026). The persistent, spatially heterogeneous distribution of positive udder quarters suggested that shared milking equipment was unlikely to be the sole route. Collectively, these observations identify plausible exposure settings but do not resolve the natural portal of entry or the route by which the virus reaches the mammary gland.Mechanistic studies have examined why mammary tissue is permissive. Plant lectins and haemagglutinin probes identified glycans compatible with contemporary avian H5 binding, but gave discordant signals for putative human-type receptors; lectin staining cannot establish functional receptor use (Kristensen et al., 2024; Rios Carrasco et al., 2024). Glycan binding also cannot explain route-specific infection or farm transmission. A bovine clade 2.3.4.4b isolate replicated in mammary and airway organoids without demonstrating respiratory transmission in vivo (Li C. et al., 2026). Intramammary challenge elicited compartmentalized cytokine responses, systemic myeloid remodeling, lymphocyte activation, and increased H5- and N1-specific antibody titers (Singh et al., 2026). Protease availability, local innate immunity, tissue physiology, dose, and lactation stage may also contribute.The consequences of mammary infection extend from production loss to cross-species exposure. In one affected herd, about one fifth of adult cows developed clinical disease, and average milk production per affected cow was estimated to be 901 kg lower than expected during the 60 days after diagnosis (Peña-Mosca et al., 2025). Because this estimate comes from a single herd, it should not be extrapolated across management systems. Raw milk or colostrum from infected cows can also expose other species: farm cats fed these products developed fatal systemic and neurological disease, and closely related viruses were found in cattle and cats on the same premises (Burrough et al., 2024).For people, the clearest evidence is occupational spillover. The first recognized infection involved a Texas dairy worker who developed conjunctivitis after exposure to affected cattle (Uyeki et al., 2024). Additional infections were later identified among dairy workers, who usually presented with conjunctivitis or mild respiratory illness (Garg et al., 2025). These cases do not demonstrate sustained human-to-human transmission. The May 2026 FAO/WHO/WOAH assessment rated the global risk to the general population as low and the risk to occupationally or frequently exposed people as low to moderate, depending on local epidemiology and protective measures (Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations et al., 2026). A WHO update covering reports available through 7 July 2026 likewise found no sustained human-to-human transmission of A(H5) viruses (World Health Organization, 2026). Validated commercial pasteurization conditions effectively inactivate H5N1, whereas raw milk from infected cattle may expose people and animals to infectious virus (United States Food and Drug Administration, 2026).At the viral level, replication in cattle creates a new selective environment for H5N1. Early in the outbreak, polymerase substitutions including PB2 M631L and PA K497R became enriched among cattle-associated viruses and were shown to increase polymerase activity in bovine cells and enhance viral replication in mammary tissue models (Dholakia et al., 2026). However, these substitutions have not been shown to confer efficient bovine respiratory or airborne transmission, and their detection alone is insufficient to infer pandemic potential (Dholakia et al., 2026; Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations et al., 2026). Substitutions that recur or increase in frequency should be evaluated phenotypically in relevant bovine and other mammalian models. 3.Influenza D virus in cattle: enzootic respiratory circulation, BRDC, and evolutionIDV was first isolated in 2011 from a pig with respiratory disease and described as influenza C-like (Hause et al., 2013). Subsequent work established IDV as a distinct orthomyxovirus and identified cattle as its principal maintenance host, based partly on substantially higher seroprevalence in cattle than in swine (Hause et al., 2014). Surveillance has since documented broad but uneven circulation in bovine populations (Collin et al., 2015; Limaye et al., 2024; Li H. et al., 2026).In experimentally infected cattle, IDV replicates in the upper and lower airways, causes mild clinical signs and tracheal lesions, and transmits to direct-contact animals (Ferguson et al., 2016). In another experiment, sentinel calves housed 3 m from aerosol-inoculated animals became infected despite the absence of direct or fomite contact, supporting short-range airborne transmission (Salem et al., 2019). Together, these experiments support direct-contact and short-range airborne transmission. Prospective studies should relate viral kinetics to airway lesions, bacterial colonization of the lower respiratory tract, host responses, and clinical outcomes.Enzootic circulation provides repeated opportunities for diversification. full_text_sections.abstract: AbstractCattle now occupy two epidemiologically distinct influenza interfaces. This Mini Review comparatively synthesizes epidemiological, pathological, experimental-transmission, genomic, and surveillance evidence for highly pathogenic avian influenza A(H5N1) and influenza D virus (IDV), asking how source ecology, tissue tropism, shedding, transmission, persistence, and zoonotic evidence differ between the two viruses. Genetically distinct H5N1 viruses have spilled over repeatedly from wild birds into United States dairy cattle. In lactating cows, infection is prominent in mammary alveolar epithelium and produces high titers of infectious virus in raw milk; inter-herd cattle movements have disseminated genotype B3.13 through dairy production networks. On affected farms, viral RNA has been detected in milk and respiratory specimens; infectious virus is recovered consistently from raw milk and mammary tissues but only sporadically from respiratory or environmental samples such as milking-parlour air and wastewater. These findings identify exposure settings but do not resolve the dominant natural cow-to-cow transmission route or how the virus reaches the mammary gland. Occupational infections have occurred, but sustained cattle adaptation or long-term reservoir status has not been demonstrated. In contrast, IDV is a cattle-adapted respiratory virus maintained through direct contact and short-range airborne transmission, with interlineage reassortment among IDV genome segments and frequent association with bovine respiratory disease complex (BRDC), although an independent causal role in BRDC remains unproven. Human seroreactivity and efficient replication in human airway models indicate exposure and biological compatibility, but not confirmed productive human infection or onward transmission. These contrasts support event-triggered, milk-centered investigation for H5N1 and longitudinal respiratory and genomic surveillance for IDV, built on shared One Health diagnostic, sequencing, epidemiological, and occupational-health infrastructure.Keywords: bovine respiratory disease complex, cattle, cross-species transmission, highly pathogenic avian influenza a(H5N1), influenza D virus, mammary tropism, one health surveillance
full_text_sections.discussion: 6.DiscussionAlthough both viruses infect cattle, their assessment requires different risk frameworks. Epidemiological consequences depend on the principal replication site and its relationship to production. In H5N1-infected dairy cows, mammary infection links viral shedding to milk production and milking practices. High-titer shedding in milk creates a direct exposure pathway; animal movements facilitate dissemination, while occupational contact creates opportunities for human exposure. IDV lacks this production-linked route; instead, it is maintained by respiratory transmission and interacts with other pathogens within the polymicrobial setting of BRDC. The most informative samples, genomic priorities, and response thresholds therefore differ.The principal uncertainties differ between the two viruses. For H5N1, the natural portal of entry, the relative contributions of milking-associated, respiratory, and environmental transmission, and whether cattle constitute a long-term reservoir remain unresolved. For IDV, respiratory replication and cattle-to-cattle transmission are established, but its independent contribution to naturally occurring BRDC remains uncertain, as does the clinical significance of human exposure signals. Resolving these questions will require studies that integrate viral kinetics with tissue lesions, co-pathogen dynamics, animal-movement histories, clinical outcomes, and transmission phenotypes.The supporting evidence is asymmetric in scope and design. H5N1 evidence derives mainly from intensively investigated outbreaks in lactating United States dairy cattle and a few experiments; extrapolation to non-lactating cattle, beef cattle, calves, and other production systems remains uncertain. IDV studies span more regions and years but often use cross-sectional PCR or serology, heterogeneous sampling, and incomplete genomic data. These differences preclude simple comparisons of prevalence, transmission efficiency, pathogenicity, or zoonotic risk. Preparedness should therefore reflect virus-specific replication sites and production systems rather than host species alone.
full_text_sections.other: 1.IntroductionInfluenza A virus ecology is commonly framed around wild aquatic birds as the principal natural reservoir, with poultry, swine, and humans occupying different host roles in amplification, reassortment, adaptation, and disease emergence (Krammer et al., 2018). Cattle received little attention because sustained influenza A virus circulation had not been documented in bovine populations. In 2024, clade 2.3.4.4b highly pathogenic avian influenza A(H5N1) [HPAI A(H5N1)] was confirmed in United States dairy cattle (Caserta et al., 2024), and genomic analysis traced spread through interconnected dairy production networks (Nguyen et al., 2025). A joint assessment by the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO), World Health Organization (WHO), and World Organization for Animal Health (WOAH), based on data available through 1 March 2026, documented several independent spillovers from wild birds into cattle, demonstrating that multiple viral genotypes can infect this host (Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations et al., 2026).The emergence of H5N1 in dairy cattle established a production-linked influenza interface centered on lactation, milking, and cattle movement. Field and experimental studies documented mammary infection, high virus titers in milk, mastitis, abnormal milk, and production loss (Caserta et al., 2024; Baker et al., 2025; Peña-Mosca et al., 2025). Movement of infected cattle facilitated long-distance dissemination (Nguyen et al., 2025), whereas genetically distinct spillovers from wild birds created new points of entry (Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations et al., 2026). Thus, raw milk and milking procedures are central exposure settings, cattle movement links herds, and contaminated equipment, aerosols, wastewater, cross-species contact, and occupational contact define additional exposure pathways whose contributions to natural transmission remain unresolved.Influenza D virus (IDV) follows a different ecological pattern. First isolated from a pig with respiratory disease (Hause et al., 2013), it was later established as a distinct orthomyxovirus with cattle as its principal maintenance host (Hause et al., 2014). Experimental studies in calves demonstrated direct-contact (Ferguson et al., 2016) and short-range airborne transmission (Salem et al., 2019). Case-control (Ng et al., 2015) and cohort (Nissly et al., 2020) studies associate IDV with bovine respiratory disease complex (BRDC) without establishing independent or dominant causation. Whole-genome studies document diversification and geographic structure (Limaye et al., 2024), interlineage reassortment among IDV genome segments (Collin et al., 2015), and regional persistence (Li H. et al., 2026), favoring longitudinal surveillance over outbreak-limited investigation.The two viruses differ most clearly in their principal replication sites. Mammary replication links H5N1 to milk and dairy production networks, whereas respiratory replication links IDV to enzootic circulation and BRDC. We therefore compare shedding, transmission, disease context, evolutionary dynamics, and surveillance across these compartments, while distinguishing occupational exposure signals from evidence of productive human infection or onward transmission. 2.Highly pathogenic avian influenza A(H5N1) in dairy cattle: emergence, mammary infection, and unresolved transmission routesThe United States cattle epizootic was initially dominated by genotype B3.13. Phylogenetic and epidemiological analysis support a single wild-bird-to-bovine spillover followed by extensive cattle-associated, movement-linked spread (Nguyen et al., 2025). Genotype D1.1 detections in Nevada and Arizona represented two additional independent spillovers from wild birds, each with limited cattle transmission (Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations et al., 2026). Repeated entry and sustained circulation are therefore separate processes. Unresolved questions are how often wild-bird-derived H5N1 crosses into cattle, which changes arise after spillover, and which routes sustain transmission. Extensive cattle-associated spread alone does not establish long-term reservoir status.After introduction, the distinctive pathological feature in lactating cows is mammary infection. Field investigations detected abundant viral RNA and infectious virus in milk, epithelial necrosis, and H5N1 antigen by immunohistochemistry in mammary alveolar epithelial cells (Caserta et al., 2024). Intramammary inoculation reproduced severe mastitis, abnormal milk, reduced production, and high-titer milk shedding (Baker et al., 2025). In contrast, oronasal inoculation of calves produced moderate upper-respiratory replication and nasal shedding, without detected transmission to sentinels (Halwe et al., 2025). Because these experiments differed in age, lactation status, target tissue, and inoculation route, they establish mammary tropism but do not identify the natural entry route.Transmission evidence remains less definitive. Low-dose intramammary challenge caused robust infection and high-titer shedding in milk, but transmission to sentinel cows was not detected despite repeated exposure to contaminated milking equipment and close contact. Respiratory and oral exposures were also less efficient than intramammary inoculation at establishing productive infection under the tested conditions (Lee et al., 2026). Across 14 California dairy farms, infectious virus was recovered from milking-parlour air on three farms and from wastewater on one farm; viral RNA was also detected in exhaled breath and milk from cows without overt clinical signs (Campbell et al., 2026). The persistent, spatially heterogeneous distribution of positive udder quarters suggested that shared milking equipment was unlikely to be the sole route. Collectively, these observations identify plausible exposure settings but do not resolve the natural portal of entry or the route by which the virus reaches the mammary gland.Mechanistic studies have examined why mammary tissue is permissive. Plant lectins and haemagglutinin probes identified glycans compatible with contemporary avian H5 binding, but gave discordant signals for putative human-type receptors; lectin staining cannot establish functional receptor use (Kristensen et al., 2024; Rios Carrasco et al., 2024). Glycan binding also cannot explain route-specific infection or farm transmission. A bovine clade 2.3.4.4b isolate replicated in mammary and airway organoids without demonstrating respiratory transmission in vivo (Li C. et al., 2026). Intramammary challenge elicited compartmentalized cytokine responses, systemic myeloid remodeling, lymphocyte activation, and increased H5- and N1-specific antibody titers (Singh et al., 2026). Protease availability, local innate immunity, tissue physiology, dose, and lactation stage may also contribute.The consequences of mammary infection extend from production loss to cross-species exposure. In one affected herd, about one fifth of adult cows developed clinical disease, and average milk production per affected cow was estimated to be 901 kg lower than expected during the 60 days after diagnosis (Peña-Mosca et al., 2025). Because this estimate comes from a single herd, it should not be extrapolated across management systems. Raw milk or colostrum from infected cows can also expose other species: farm cats fed these products developed fatal systemic and neurological disease, and closely related viruses were found in cattle and cats on the same premises (Burrough et al., 2024).For people, the clearest evidence is occupational spillover. The first recognized infection involved a Texas dairy worker who developed conjunctivitis after exposure to affected cattle (Uyeki et al., 2024). Additional infections were later identified among dairy workers, who usually presented with conjunctivitis or mild respiratory illness (Garg et al., 2025). These cases do…

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to understand how the ecology, tissue tropism, shedding, transmission, persistence, and zoonotic potential of highly pathogenic avian influenza A(H5N1) and influenza D virus (IDV) differ in cattle.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study analyzed epidemiological, pathological, experimental-transmission, genomic, and surveillance evidence from dairy cattle in the United States, focusing on H5N1 and IDV. It included case-control and cohort studies that associated IDV with bovine respiratory disease complex (BRDC) without confirming independent causation.
analysis.methods: The study used metagenomic sequencing, PCR, serology, and experimental models in calves to investigate shedding, transmission, and disease context. It also employed plant lectins and haemagglutinin probes to identify receptor compatibility.
analysis.main_results: Viral RNA was detected in milk and respiratory specimens of H5N1-infected cows, with infectious virus consistently recovered from raw milk and mammary tissues but only sporadically from respiratory or environmental samples. IDV was found to be maintained through respiratory transmission and interactions with other pathogens in BRDC.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpret that the principal replication sites and transmission routes differ significantly between H5N1 and IDV, with H5N1 linked to milk production and IDV to respiratory systems. This distinction highlights the need for tailored surveillance strategies.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings inform targeted surveillance and risk frameworks for H5N1 and IDV, emphasizing the importance of understanding their distinct replication sites and transmission dynamics for effective control and prevention.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The evidence is limited by the use of cross-sectional PCR or serology for IDV and the lack of confirmed productive human infection or onward transmission for H5N1, resulting in a moderate confidence assessment.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigates the differences in the ecology, tissue tropism, shedding, transmission, persistence, and zoonotic potential of highly pathogenic avian influenza A(H5N1) and influenza D virus (IDV) in cattle. It highlights that H5N1 is associated with mammary alveolar epithelium and produces high titers of infectious virus in raw milk, while IDV is a cattle-adapted respiratory virus maintained through direct contact and short-range airborne transmission. The study emphasizes the need for tailored surveillance strategies based on the distinct replication sites and transmission routes of these viruses. However, the evidence is limited by the use of cross-sectional methods for IDV and the absence of confirmed human infection for H5N1, resulting in a moderate confidence assessment.

elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 该研究分析了来自美国奶牛的流行病学、病理学、实验性、基因组和 监测 证据,重点关注 H5N1 和 IDV。它包括病例对照和 队列研究 研究,这些研究将 IDV 与牛呼吸道疾病综合征 (BRDC) 相关联,但未确认独立因果关系。
elements_zh.methods: 该研究使用宏基因组测序、PCR、传播 和小牛实验模型来研究脱落、传播 和疾病背景。它还使用植物凝集素和血凝素探针来识别受体相容性。
elements_zh.main_results: 在感染 H5N1 的奶牛的牛奶和呼吸道样本中检测到了病毒 RNA,感染性病毒始终从原料奶和乳腺组织中回收,但仅从呼吸道或环境样本中零星回收。发现 IDV 通过呼吸道 传播 以及与 BRDC 中其他病原体的相互作用来维持。
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 作者解释说,H5N1 和 IDV 之间的主要复制位点和 传播 途径存在显着差异,其中 H5N1 与产奶量有关,而 IDV 与呼吸系统有关。这种区别凸显了定制 监测 策略的必要性。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 研究结果为 H5N1 和 IDV 的针对性 监测 和风险框架提供了信息,强调了解其独特的复制位点和 传播 动态对于有效控制和预防的重要性。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 由于使用 IDV 横断面 PCR 或 血清学 以及缺乏已证实的有效人类感染或 H5N1 后续 传播,证据受到限制,导致可信度评估适中。

analysis_zh.research_question_and_background: 该研究旨在了解高致病性禽流感 A (H5N1) 和流感 D 病毒 (IDV) 在牛中的生态学、组织嗜性、脱落、传播、持久性和人畜共患潜力有何不同。
analysis_zh.study_design_and_population: 该研究分析了来自美国奶牛的流行病学、病理学、实验性、基因组和 监测 证据,重点关注 H5N1 和 IDV。它包括病例对照和 队列研究 研究,这些研究将 IDV 与牛呼吸道疾病综合征 (BRDC) 相关联,但未确认独立因果关系。
analysis_zh.methods: 该研究使用宏基因组测序、PCR、传播 和小牛实验模型来研究脱落、传播 和疾病背景。它还使用植物凝集素和血凝素探针来识别受体相容性。
analysis_zh.main_results: 在感染 H5N1 的奶牛的牛奶和呼吸道样本中检测到了病毒 RNA,感染性病毒始终从原料奶和乳腺组织中回收,但仅从呼吸道或环境样本中零星回收。发现 IDV 通过呼吸道 传播 以及与 BRDC 中其他病原体的相互作用来维持。
analysis_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 作者解释说,H5N1 和 IDV 之间的主要复制位点和 传播 途径存在显着差异,其中 H5N1 与产奶量有关,而 IDV 与呼吸系统有关。这种区别凸显了定制 监测 策略的必要性。
analysis_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 研究结果为 H5N1 和 IDV 的针对性 监测 和风险框架提供了信息,强调了解其独特的复制位点和 传播 动态对于有效控制和预防的重要性。
analysis_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 由于使用 IDV 横断面 PCR 或 血清学 以及缺乏已证实的有效人类感染或 H5N1 后续 传播,证据受到限制,导致可信度评估适中。

full_text: AbstractAfrican swine fever (ASF) and swine influenza (SI) are among the most consequential infectious threats to global swine production because they combine major economic burden with fundamentally different transmission ecology, tissue tropism, and immune-pathological behavior. ASF is a highly lethal systemic disease characterized by macrophage tropism, immune dysregulation, environmental persistence, and severe trade and production consequences, whereas SI is a highly transmissible respiratory infection associated with recurrent herd-level morbidity, viral evolution, and zoonotic significance. Although these diseases differ markedly in biology and field presentation, both highlight the limitations of isolated pathogen-centered control strategies when implemented without integrated herd-level resilience measures. This meta-review synthesizes the cited literature into an evidence-based framework encompassing epidemiology, pathogenesis, surveillance, vaccination, biosecurity, herd management, supportive care, nutritional and immune-supportive measures, and host-directed regenerative approaches. Across the reviewed literature, the strongest field-supported evidence remains centered on surveillance, vaccination where applicable, biosecurity, and production-system management. At the same time, regenerative and host-supportive biologic strategies, including mitochondria-targeted peptides, thymic and organ-derived peptides, extracellular vesicle-based approaches, and stem cell-related therapies, demonstrate growing translational and immunomodulatory relevance within the broader context of immune resilience and recovery support. Comparative analysis further demonstrates that intervention priorities must remain aligned with disease biology: ASF control depends primarily on preventing viral introduction and limiting outbreak dissemination, whereas SI management benefits from integrated vaccination strategies, environmental optimization, mitigation of secondary bacterial disease, and continual adaptation to antigenic evolution. Within this framework, immune resilience is best understood not as a replacement for conventional disease control, but as a layered outcome arising from reduced infection pressure, preserved immune competence, regulated inflammatory responses, tissue recovery capacity, and supportive production practices.Keywords: African swine fever, biosecurity, herd management, host-directed therapy, swine influenza, transboundary 12.DiscussionThe comparative framing of ASF and SI provides a useful perspective for understanding how differences in pathogen biology influence disease control. ASF depends heavily on exclusion, early detection, biosecurity, surveillance, movement control and rapid containment because of its high mortality and environmental or wildlife-associated persistence. In contrast, SI is generally managed as an endemic respiratory disease through vaccination, herd immunity, strain surveillance and transmission control, although antigenic drift, strain mismatch and maternal antibodies can reduce vaccine effectiveness (27, 29, 30).Vaccination further illustrates this contrast. SI vaccination is already established in commercial practice, whereas ASF vaccination remains less mature and is limited by concerns regarding safety, cross-protection, DIVA capability, viral diversity and field consistency (14, 22). Therefore, ASF vaccination should complement, rather than replace, biosecurity and outbreak-control measures.Despite these differences, host factors influence disease outcomes in both infections. Immune competence, inflammatory regulation, age, co-infections, metabolic status and environmental stress can affect disease severity (80). Immune resilience should therefore be viewed as the ability to mount an effective antiviral response while limiting excessive inflammation and preserving tissue function. In ASF, host-directed approaches are more relevant as complementary research strategies for immune dysregulation, disease tolerance and recovery, whereas in SI, improving mucosal immunity and controlling pulmonary inflammation may more directly reduce disease severity and production losses (46).Important gaps remain in the development of immune-resilience strategies for ASF and SI. ASF research requires clearer protective immune correlates across viral genotypes and vaccine platforms, as well as improved understanding of immune evasion and disease tolerance, while SI research must address antigenic evolution, reassortment and the need for broader, more durable mucosal immunity. Future studies should validate interventions under commercial production conditions using standardized characterization, dose–response studies, controlled challenge experiments and independent replication, particularly for host-directed and regenerative approaches such as MO, PSC and NOP, whose efficacy in pigs remains unconfirmed. These strategies should be evaluated as complements to vaccination, biosecurity and antiviral control using standardized virological, immunological, clinical and production-related outcomes. 13.ConclusionAfrican swine fever and swine influenza remain highly appropriate diseases for comparative review because they reveal two different but interconnected dimensions of vulnerability in global swine health. ASF is defined by lethality, environmental persistence, and the central importance of preventing introduction and limiting spread after incursion (22, 64). SI is defined by high transmissibility, recurrent productivity losses, zoonotic significance, and the challenge of maintaining vaccine effectiveness in the face of viral evolution (6, 43). These differences justify different operational priorities but also support a shared resilience framework.On current evidence, the core pillars of control remain surveillance, biosecurity, herd management, and vaccination where biologically and operationally feasible (11, 12). Supportive care, environmental optimization, and nutritional adequacy are meaningful adjuncts, especially for SI, but they do not replace pathogen-specific control (10, 63). Host-directed peptides, mitochondrial strategies, and regenerative biologics are emerging areas of investigation that may contribute to resilience-oriented approaches, although their role in large-scale production systems continues to evolve alongside the evidence base (69, 79, 81). 1.IntroductionPork remains one of the most widely consumed animal proteins worldwide, making swine health central to food security, farm income, and stability of international agricultural trade (1). In parallel with rising demand, pig production systems have become more intensified, more interconnected, and in many regions more vulnerable to infectious disease due to dense animal populations, movement networks, and uneven biosecurity infrastructure. Viral diseases are therefore no longer only clinical problems at farm level; they are increasingly structural threats to productivity, market access, and regional food systems (2, 3).Among these threats, African swine fever and swine influenza occupy particularly important positions because they represent two distinct but complementary stress tests of modern swine systems. ASF is caused by African swine fever virus (ASFV), a large double-stranded DNA virus. Its severity depends on the interplay between viral strain virulence and host immune responses, as reflected in variations in clinical signs and mortality across diverse regional epidemiological scenarios (4). In contrast, SI is caused primarily by influenza A viruses (IAVs), which are segmented RNA viruses characterized by substantial genetic diversity and zoonotic potential (5). Clinically, SI is a highly transmissible respiratory disease associated with high morbidity, depressed growth performance, risk of secondary bacterial infection, and ongoing productivity loss at herd level (6). ASF, by contrast, is a severe systemic viral disease with mortality that can approach 100% in susceptible populations and remains defined by the absence of widely deployable curative treatment, the importance of environmental persistence, and the necessity of strict outbreak control measures (7, 8).A side-by-side analysis of ASF and SI is analytically useful because these diseases reveal different points of fragility in swine production. SI illustrates the burden of endemic circulation, antigenic evolution, and repeated respiratory outbreaks, whereas ASF illustrates the catastrophic consequences of a high-fatality transboundary disease in which prevention of entry is more feasible than therapy after establishment (9). Accordingly, this review adopts a meta-analytic perspective, with stronger emphasis on evidence hierarchy, biological plausibility, practical readiness, and the distinction between established intervention pillars and emerging approaches. 2.Scope and meta-review approachA key challenge in the literature is that interventions supported by strong field evidence are often presented alongside emerging biologic or regenerative concepts with evidence bases at molecular level, and without sufficiently clear stratification by evidentiary strength or practical relevance specifically in pig. That concern is particularly important in veterinary infectious disease because the practical usefulness of an intervention depends not only on mechanistic plausibility but also on cost, scalability, route of administration, herd-level logistics, and compatibility with commercial production (1, 10).In this meta-review, the literature is interpreted through four evidence layers. The first includes established field interventions such as biosecurity, surveillance, herd management, and commercially used SI vaccines (6, 11, 12). The second includes validated but context-dependent tools, such as emerging ASF vaccines that demonstrate strong pig challenge data but still face deployment and regulatory considerations (13, 14). Despite advances in ASF vaccine development and the authorization of some vaccine candidates for use in parts of Asia, there is currently no licensed ASF vaccine in the European Union. The third includes biologically grounded approaches supported by experimental and translational pig studies, including β-defensin-related strategies and other immune-modulating interventions (15, 16). The fourth includes host-directed and regenerative approaches, encompassing peptide-based, cellular, and signaling-modulation strategies that aim to enhance immune competence, tissue repair, and overall resilience under infectious challenge (17–19).For the present analysis, immune resilience is defined as the capacity of pigs and herds to limit infection, reduce disease severity, preserve immune competence, maintain tissue integrity, and recover functional productivity under pathogen exposure (20, 21). This definition deliberately avoids vague notions of generalized immune stimulation and instead emphasizes an interaction among pathogen pressure, innate and adaptive immune quality, inflammatory regulation, environmental load, and management structure. Within this framework, resilience is not a single therapy but an emergent outcome of layered control. 3.Epidemiology and global disease burdenAfrican swine fever (ASF) and swine influenza (SI) are distinct infectious disease with markedly different epidemiological characteristics and represent major threats to the global porcine sector. ASFV and swine influenza A viruses differ profoundly in how they persist and spread across swine populations. ASFV persistence is shaped by environmental stability, contamination of fomites and pork products, wildlife reservoirs or interfaces, and human-mediated dissemination events, including long-distance jumps linked to transport and biosecurity breaches (22–25). In contrast, SI persists through endemic respiratory transmission, ongoing reassortment, antigenic drift, and repeated movement of viruses through swine populations interconnected by trade and production systems (26–29).These contrasting ecologies have practical consequences. ASF often behaves as a transboundary emergency in which the central question is whether the virus can be excluded or rapidly contained after entry (4, 30). SI behaves more like a constantly shifting endemic respiratory threat that repeatedly erodes production through cycles of infection, reinfection, and antigenic mismatch (6, 31). Both are damaging, but they operate on different temporal and epidemiological scales (Figure 1).Figure 1Comparative replication cycles of African swine fever virus (ASFV) and swine influenza virus (SIV). ASFV infects macrophages and replicates predominantly in the cytoplasm within perinuclear viral factories following endosomal escape and viral DNA release. Early and late gene expressions precede genome replication, virion assembly, maturation, and release via budding or cell lysis. In contrast, SIV infects respiratory epithelial cells and undergoes endocytosis followed by hemagglutinin-mediated membrane fusion and uncoating. Viral ribonucleoproteins are transported to the nucleus, where transcription and RNA replication occur, and progeny virions assemble at the plasma membrane and are released by neuraminidase-facilitated budding.Infographic compares African swine fever virus (ASFV) and swine influenza virus (SIV) replication cycles in pig cells. Steps for ASFV: attachment, endosome escape, DNA release, cytoplasmic replication, assembly, and release by budding and lysis. Steps for SIV: attachment, endosome escape and vRNP release, nuclear replication with RNA transcription, viral assembly, and release via budding and neuraminidase-mediated mechanisms. Both cycles are illustrated clearly with color-coded steps and labeled components.ASF spread since the emergence of the genotype II pandemic lineage has been characterized by persistent regional expansion, wildlife-associated maintenance, and episodic jump events across affected territories (4, 25, 32). However, ASFV exhibits substantial genetic diversity, with multiple genotypes circulating in Africa, while genotypes I and II have achieved broader geographical spread beyond the continent. Genotype I ASFVs were detected in domestic pigs in China in 2021, including low-virulence but efficiently transmissible strains associated with chronic infection (33). More recently, naturally occurring genotype I/II recombinant ASFVs have also been identified, including highly virulent and transmissible recombinant viruses detected in China (34). The co-circulation and recombination of genetically distinct ASFV lineages add further complexity to surveillance, disease control, and vaccine development. Consequently, this genetic diversity may impact vaccine efficacy, as cross-protection against heterologous ASFV strains and genotypes can be variable (35). Rathakrishnan et al. (36) demonstrated that a gene-modified genotype II live attenuated vaccine conferred complete homologous protection against genotype II ASFV, but only partial protection against genotype I and no protection against genotype IX, reflecting the need to consider circulating genotype diversity when evaluating the geographical applicability and breadth of ASF vaccines. In contrast, SI circulation is globally interconnected yet regionally structured, with North America and Europe acting as important source regions in long-term phylogeographic analyses, and live swine movement serving as a major driver of dissemination (5, 29, 37). The emergence of A(H1N1)pdm09 in 2009 illustrates the potential contribution of swine-origin influenza lineages to pandemic emergence. Following human-to-swine transmission, A(H1N1)pdm09 viruses can persist, evolve, and reassort with endemic swine influenza viruses, contributing to viral diversity and subsequent zoonotic risk (38). Markin et al. (39) and Zanella et al. (40) further demonstrated that continued circulation and evolution of these viruses in swine can increase genetic and antigenic diversity and maintain opportunities for subsequent zoonotic transmission. These patterns indicate that control strategies cannot simply transfer from one disease to the other; intervention design must reflect whether persistence is driven mainly by environmental durability and introduction events, or by respiratory circulation and viral evolution. For both diseases, current viral diversity emphasizes the importance of surveillance to detect newly emerging genotypes, reassortants, and variants that could alter transmission, vaccine efficacy, or zoonotic risk. 4.Transmission ecology and surveillance constraintsTransmission ecology sits at the interface between pathogen biology and farm practice. In ASF, circulation may involve domestic pigs, contaminated pork products, fomites, wild boar, and in some ecological context soft ticks (8, 22, 24). The importance of environmental survival means that virus introduction can occur even without direct pig-to-pig contact, which is why disinfection, feed safety, carcass management, and control of human and vehicle traffic are so important (11, 12, 23).In SI, by contrast, aerosol and direct-contact transmission dominate (41). High animal density, continuous flow systems, mixing of age groups, and repeated entry of new animals all favor persistence and spread (1, 37). Because influenza A viruses also reassort and accumulate antigenic changes, the epidemiological problem is not just the occurrence of outbreaks but the continual generation and circulation of immunologically variable viruses (26, 28).Surveillance limitations affect both diseases but in different ways. For ASF, variable reporting timeliness, inconsistent premise classification, and structural data gaps impede rapid detection and cross-country interpretation of outbreak patterns (32, 42). For SI, voluntary sampling systems, asymptomatic infections, and incomplete surveillance at the animal-human interface can underestimate prevalence and obscure zoonotic…

ASF, by contrast, is a severe systemic viral disease with mortality that can approach 100% in susceptible populations and remains defined by the absence of widely deployable curative treatment, the importance of environmental persistence, and the necessity of strict outbreak control measures (7, 8).A side-by-side analysis of ASF and SI is analytically useful because these diseases reveal different points of fragility in swine production. SI illustrates the burden of endemic circulation, antigenic evolution, and repeated respiratory outbreaks, whereas ASF illustrates the catastrophic consequences of a high-fatality transboundary disease in which prevention of entry is more feasible than therapy after establishment (9). Accordingly, this review adopts a meta-analytic perspective, with stronger emphasis on evidence hierarchy, biological plausibility, practical readiness, and the distinction between established intervention pillars and emerging approaches. 2.Scope and meta-review approachA key challenge in the literature is that interventions supported by strong field evidence are often presented alongside emerging biologic or regenerative concepts with evidence bases at molecular level, and without sufficiently clear stratification by evidentiary strength or practical relevance specifically in pig. That concern is particularly important in veterinary infectious disease because the practical usefulness of an intervention depends not only on mechanistic plausibility but also on cost, scalability, route of administration, herd-level logistics, and compatibility with commercial production (1, 10).In this meta-review, the literature is interpreted through four evidence layers. The first includes established field interventions such as biosecurity, surveillance, herd management, and commercially used SI vaccines (6, 11, 12). The second includes validated but context-dependent tools, such as emerging ASF vaccines that demonstrate strong pig challenge data but still face deployment and regulatory considerations (13, 14). Despite advances in ASF vaccine development and the authorization of some vaccine candidates for use in parts of Asia, there is currently no licensed ASF vaccine in the European Union. The third includes biologically grounded approaches supported by experimental and translational pig studies, including β-defensin-related strategies and other immune-modulating interventions (15, 16). The fourth includes host-directed and regenerative approaches, encompassing peptide-based, cellular, and signaling-modulation strategies that aim to enhance immune competence, tissue repair, and overall resilience under infectious challenge (17–19).For the present analysis, immune resilience is defined as the capacity of pigs and herds to limit infection, reduce disease severity, preserve immune competence, maintain tissue integrity, and recover functional productivity under pathogen exposure (20, 21). This definition deliberately avoids vague notions of generalized immune stimulation and instead emphasizes an interaction among pathogen pressure, innate and adaptive immune quality, inflammatory regulation, environmental load, and management structure. Within this framework, resilience is not a single therapy but an emergent outcome of layered control. 3.Epidemiology and global disease burdenAfrican swine fever (ASF) and swine influenza (SI) are distinct infectious disease with markedly different epidemiological characteristics and represent major threats to the global porcine sector. ASFV and swine influenza A viruses differ profoundly in how they persist and spread across swine populations. ASFV persistence is shaped by environmental stability, contamination of fomites and pork products, wildlife reservoirs or interfaces, and human-mediated dissemination events, including long-distance jumps linked to transport and biosecurity breaches (22–25). In contrast, SI persists through endemic respiratory transmission, ongoing reassortment, antigenic drift, and repeated movement of viruses through swine populations interconnected by trade and production systems (26–29).These contrasting ecologies have practical consequences. ASF often behaves as a transboundary emergency in which the central question is whether the virus can be excluded or rapidly contained after entry (4, 30). SI behaves more like a constantly shifting endemic respiratory threat that repeatedly erodes production through cycles of infection, reinfection, and antigenic mismatch (6, 31). Both are damaging, but they operate on different temporal and epidemiological scales (Figure 1).Figure 1Comparative replication cycles of African swine fever virus (ASFV) and swine influenza virus (SIV). ASFV infects macrophages and replicates predominantly in the cytoplasm within perinuclear viral factories following endosomal escape and viral DNA release. Early and late gene expressions precede genome replication, virion assembly, maturation, and release via budding or cell lysis. In contrast, SIV infects respiratory epithelial cells and undergoes endocytosis followed by hemagglutinin-mediated membrane fusion and uncoating. Viral ribonucleoproteins are transported to the nucleus, where transcription and RNA replication occur, and progeny virions assemble at the plasma membrane and are released by neuraminidase-facilitated budding.Infographic compares African swine fever virus (ASFV) and swine influenza virus (SIV) replication cycles in pig cells. Steps for ASFV: attachment, endosome escape, DNA release, cytoplasmic replication, assembly, and release by budding and lysis. Steps for SIV: attachment, endosome escape and vRNP release, nuclear replication with RNA transcription, viral assembly, and release via budding and neuraminidase-mediated mechanisms. Both cycles are illustrated clearly with color-coded steps and labeled components.ASF spread since the emergence of the genotype II pandemic lineage has been characterized by persistent regional expansion, wildlife-associated maintenance, and episodic jump events across affected territories (4, 25, 32). However, ASFV exhibits substantial genetic diversity, with multiple genotypes circulating in Africa, while genotypes I and II have achieved broader geographical spread beyond the continent. title_original: Enhancing immune resilience in swine: a comprehensive meta-review of preventive and host-directed strategies against African swine fever and swine influenza

analysis.scope_and_question: The review focuses on enhancing immune resilience in swine against African swine fever (ASF) and swine influenza (SI). The central question is how to integrate preventive and host-directed strategies to improve disease control and reduce economic and health impacts on swine populations.
analysis.evidence_base_and_review_method: The review is a meta-review that synthesizes the cited literature into an evidence-based framework. It includes studies on epidemiology, pathogenesis, surveillance, vaccination, biosecurity, herd management, supportive care, nutritional and immune-supportive measures, and host-directed regenerative approaches. The review explicitly mentions the use of standardized outcomes for evaluating interventions.
analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: The review concludes that surveillance, vaccination where applicable, biosecurity, and production-system management are the strongest field-supported evidence for controlling both ASF and SI. Immune resilience is emphasized as a layered outcome arising from reduced infection pressure, preserved immune competence, regulated inflammatory responses, tissue recovery capacity, and supportive production practices.
analysis.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: There are conflicting findings regarding the effectiveness of SI vaccination, particularly due to antigenic drift, strain mismatch, and maternal antibodies. Additionally, the review notes that ASF vaccination remains less mature and is limited by safety concerns, cross-protection, DIVA capability, viral diversity, and field consistency. These limitations highlight the need for further research and standardization of outcomes.
analysis.research_and_practice_implications: The review suggests that future research should evaluate regenerative and host-supportive biologic strategies as complements to vaccination, biosecurity, and antiviral control. It also emphasizes the importance of considering circulating genotype diversity when assessing the geographical applicability and breadth of ASF vaccines. Operational priorities should align with disease biology, with ASF requiring strict outbreak control and SI benefiting from integrated vaccination strategies and adaptation to antigenic evolution.

analysis.summary_en: This review examines strategies to enhance immune resilience in swine against African swine fever (ASF) and swine influenza (SI). It highlights the distinct biological and epidemiological characteristics of these diseases, emphasizing the need for integrated control measures. The review identifies surveillance, vaccination, biosecurity, and herd management as the most supported interventions. However, it also notes limitations in ASF vaccination due to safety, cross-protection, and viral diversity. The findings suggest that future research should focus on evaluating host-directed therapies and adapting strategies to the specific biology of each disease. The review underscores the importance of a shared resilience framework while acknowledging the need for tailored approaches based on disease-specific challenges.

elements_zh.scope_and_question: 该综述的重点是增强猪对非洲猪瘟(ASF)和猪流感(SI)的免疫能力。核心问题是如何将预防性策略和 宿主 导向策略结合起来,以改善疾病控制并减少对猪群的经济和健康影响。
elements_zh.evidence_base_and_review_method: 该综述是一种元综述,将引用的文献综合成一个基于证据的框架。它包括对 流行病学、发病机制、监测、疫苗接种、生物安全、牛群管理、支持性护理、营养和免疫支持措施以及 宿主 导向的再生方法的研究。该审查明确提到使用标准化结果来评估干预措施。
elements_zh.consensus_and_key_conclusions: 审查得出的结论是,监测、疫苗接种(如果适用)、生物安全和生产系统管理是控制 ASF 和 SI 的最有力的现场支持证据。免疫弹性被强调为由感染压力降低、免疫能力保留、炎症反应调节、组织恢复能力和支持性生产实践产生的分层结果。
elements_zh.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: 关于 SI 疫苗接种 的有效性存在相互矛盾的发现,特别是由于 抗原漂移、菌株不匹配和母源抗体。此外,审查还指出,ASF 疫苗接种 仍然不太成熟,并且受到安全问题、交叉保护、DIVA 能力、病毒多样性和现场一致性的限制。这些局限性凸显了进一步研究和结果标准化的必要性。
elements_zh.research_and_practice_implications: 该综述建议未来的研究应评估再生和 宿主 支持的生物策略,作为 疫苗接种、生物安全和 抗病毒药物 控制的补充。它还强调了在评估 ASF 疫苗 的地理适用性和广度时考虑流行基因型多样性的重要性。操作重点应与疾病生物学相一致,非洲猪瘟需要严格的 暴发 控制,SI 受益于综合 疫苗接种 策略和对抗原 进化 的适应。
