full_text: AbstractSeasonal epidemics, zoonotic spillover, antiviral resistance, and pandemic risk continue to make influenza a major challenge for respiratory preparedness. The recent spread of highly pathogenic avian influenza A(H5N1) in mammalian hosts has made it increasingly important to consider molecular adaptation, surveillance, treatment, and vaccination as connected parts of preparedness rather than as separate issues. This review focuses on four interconnected areas: host–virus interactions, surveillance technologies, antiviral management and resistance, and vaccine preparedness. Evidence on mammalian adaptation includes receptor specificity, viral polymerase–host factor compatibility, innate immune antagonism, ANP32 proteins, and aberrant viral RNA generation, while surveillance has expanded to multiplex and CRISPR-based assays, point-of-care platforms, genomic sequencing, artificial intelligence-assisted risk assessment, and environmental monitoring. These approaches differ in intended use and stage of validation. Antiviral benefit depends strongly on host risk and treatment timing. Resistance-associated substitutions, however, cannot be interpreted from sequence data alone and require phenotypic and epidemiological context. Vaccine development spans nanoparticle, mRNA, and intranasal platforms designed to broaden antigenic coverage, strengthen mucosal immunity, or improve protection in specific populations. Better analytical performance and stronger immune responses do not by themselves demonstrate reductions in severe disease, hospitalization, or mortality. Influenza preparedness ultimately depends on how effectively these four domains inform one another and how consistently emerging approaches are evaluated against clinically meaningful outcomes.Keywords: antiviral resistance, emerging respiratory threats, host–virus interactions, influenza virus, surveillance technologies, vaccine preparedness Graphical abstract The central figure represents the host/patient. The surrounding modules summarize viral threats, pathogenic mechanisms, diagnostic and surveillance approaches, epidemiology and risk stratification, clinical management and recovery, and vaccine development. Examples shown include H5N1 threats; M1, NS2, mvRNA, and RIG-I-related mechanisms; multiplex PCR and CRISPR-based diagnostics; AI-assisted and wastewater surveillance; smartwatch-based recovery assessment; and COBRA, nanoparticle, and mRNA vaccine platforms. The converging arrows indicate the translational focus of the review: using information from these domains to improve protection of human health.Conceptual diagram illustrating host-virus interaction at the center, surrounded by six labeled sections: vaccine development, viral threats, mechanisms and immunity, diagnostics and technologies, epidemiology and surveillance, and treatment, each with icons and relevant keywords summarizing advancements, challenges, and monitoring strategies in influenza research. 7.DiscussionThe evidence reviewed here points to a series of translational handoffs across the four domains. Molecular findings need confirmation in human-derived systems, and surveillance signals need enough standardization to support action. Antiviral susceptibility data require phenotypic and treatment context. Vaccine-induced immune responses must ultimately be assessed against clinically meaningful outcomes. Weakness at any transition can reduce the preparedness value of an otherwise promising approach.Mammalian adaptation shows the distance between mechanistic insight and practical risk assessment. Receptor usage, viral polymerase regulation, ANP32-family proteins, NS1/NS2 function, and aberrant viral RNA generation have refined current models of cross-species adaptation. Much of the evidence still derives from structural studies, cultured cells, or animal models. Human infection adds variables such as age, pre-existing immunity, immunosenescence, fever, and other physiological conditions that can alter viral replication and host responses. Molecular adaptation markers remain candidate risk indicators until supported by human-derived experimental systems, clinical cohorts, and epidemiological evidence.Surveillance signals vary in scale, source, and validation endpoint. Multiplex assays, CRISPR-based platforms, genomic sequencing, AI-assisted analysis, and wastewater monitoring cannot be judged by a single criterion. Sampling procedures, analytical thresholds, and reporting practices add further variation. Wastewater detection of A(H5N1) is especially difficult to interpret because viral material may reflect human shedding, infected animals, or animal waste. Environmental findings are most informative when combined with clinical testing, genomic characterization, epidemiological investigation, and veterinary surveillance within a One Health framework.Clinical management has a similar interpretive constraint. A resistance-associated sequence change is not synonymous with clinical resistance. Phenotypic susceptibility, antiviral exposure, viral subtype, fitness, and treatment outcome remain necessary for judging its significance. Host-directed and TCM-derived interventions are harder to compare because study design, intervention standardization, and quality control vary. Wearable monitoring may capture longitudinal recovery patterns, but useful clinical thresholds and incremental benefit over routine assessment have not been established. These adjunctive and monitoring approaches remain investigational.Vaccine studies make the gap between immune readouts and clinical benefit especially clear. COBRA antigens, nanoparticle vaccines, mRNA platforms, and intranasal approaches address antigenic mismatch, manufacturing speed, or weak mucosal immunity. Broader antibody responses or higher neutralizing titers do not necessarily mean fewer hospitalizations or less severe disease. In older or immunocompromised populations, immunosenescence and impaired cellular immunity can weaken the relationship between serological responses and protection. Evaluation should include humoral, cellular, and mucosal responses, durability, and clinically meaningful outcomes in the intended population.Influenza preparedness depends on how these links function in practice. Evidence of viral adaptation can inform surveillance and risk assessment, and surveillance can guide clinical and public-health responses. full_text_sections.abstract: AbstractSeasonal epidemics, zoonotic spillover, antiviral resistance, and pandemic risk continue to make influenza a major challenge for respiratory preparedness. The recent spread of highly pathogenic avian influenza A(H5N1) in mammalian hosts has made it increasingly important to consider molecular adaptation, surveillance, treatment, and vaccination as connected parts of preparedness rather than as separate issues. This review focuses on four interconnected areas: host–virus interactions, surveillance technologies, antiviral management and resistance, and vaccine preparedness. Evidence on mammalian adaptation includes receptor specificity, viral polymerase–host factor compatibility, innate immune antagonism, ANP32 proteins, and aberrant viral RNA generation, while surveillance has expanded to multiplex and CRISPR-based assays, point-of-care platforms, genomic sequencing, artificial intelligence-assisted risk assessment, and environmental monitoring. These approaches differ in intended use and stage of validation. Antiviral benefit depends strongly on host risk and treatment timing. Resistance-associated substitutions, however, cannot be interpreted from sequence data alone and require phenotypic and epidemiological context. Vaccine development spans nanoparticle, mRNA, and intranasal platforms designed to broaden antigenic coverage, strengthen mucosal immunity, or improve protection in specific populations. Better analytical performance and stronger immune responses do not by themselves demonstrate reductions in severe disease, hospitalization, or mortality. Influenza preparedness ultimately depends on how effectively these four domains inform one another and how consistently emerging approaches are evaluated against clinically meaningful outcomes.Keywords: antiviral resistance, emerging respiratory threats, host–virus interactions, influenza virus, surveillance technologies, vaccine preparedness Graphical abstract The central figure represents the host/patient. The surrounding modules summarize viral threats, pathogenic mechanisms, diagnostic and surveillance approaches, epidemiology and risk stratification, clinical management and recovery, and vaccine development. Examples shown include H5N1 threats; M1, NS2, mvRNA, and RIG-I-related mechanisms; multiplex PCR and CRISPR-based diagnostics; AI-assisted and wastewater surveillance; smartwatch-based recovery assessment; and COBRA, nanoparticle, and mRNA vaccine platforms. The converging arrows indicate the translational focus of the review: using information from these domains to improve protection of human health.Conceptual diagram illustrating host-virus interaction at the center, surrounded by six labeled sections: vaccine development, viral threats, mechanisms and immunity, diagnostics and technologies, epidemiology and surveillance, and treatment, each with icons and relevant keywords summarizing advancements, challenges, and monitoring strategies in influenza research.
full_text_sections.discussion: 7.DiscussionThe evidence reviewed here points to a series of translational handoffs across the four domains. Molecular findings need confirmation in human-derived systems, and surveillance signals need enough standardization to support action. Antiviral susceptibility data require phenotypic and treatment context. Vaccine-induced immune responses must ultimately be assessed against clinically meaningful outcomes. Weakness at any transition can reduce the preparedness value of an otherwise promising approach.Mammalian adaptation shows the distance between mechanistic insight and practical risk assessment. Receptor usage, viral polymerase regulation, ANP32-family proteins, NS1/NS2 function, and aberrant viral RNA generation have refined current models of cross-species adaptation. Much of the evidence still derives from structural studies, cultured cells, or animal models. Human infection adds variables such as age, pre-existing immunity, immunosenescence, fever, and other physiological conditions that can alter viral replication and host responses. Molecular adaptation markers remain candidate risk indicators until supported by human-derived experimental systems, clinical cohorts, and epidemiological evidence.Surveillance signals vary in scale, source, and validation endpoint. Multiplex assays, CRISPR-based platforms, genomic sequencing, AI-assisted analysis, and wastewater monitoring cannot be judged by a single criterion. Sampling procedures, analytical thresholds, and reporting practices add further variation. Wastewater detection of A(H5N1) is especially difficult to interpret because viral material may reflect human shedding, infected animals, or animal waste. Environmental findings are most informative when combined with clinical testing, genomic characterization, epidemiological investigation, and veterinary surveillance within a One Health framework.Clinical management has a similar interpretive constraint. A resistance-associated sequence change is not synonymous with clinical resistance. Phenotypic susceptibility, antiviral exposure, viral subtype, fitness, and treatment outcome remain necessary for judging its significance. Host-directed and TCM-derived interventions are harder to compare because study design, intervention standardization, and quality control vary. Wearable monitoring may capture longitudinal recovery patterns, but useful clinical thresholds and incremental benefit over routine assessment have not been established. These adjunctive and monitoring approaches remain investigational.Vaccine studies make the gap between immune readouts and clinical benefit especially clear. COBRA antigens, nanoparticle vaccines, mRNA platforms, and intranasal approaches address antigenic mismatch, manufacturing speed, or weak mucosal immunity. Broader antibody responses or higher neutralizing titers do not necessarily mean fewer hospitalizations or less severe disease. In older or immunocompromised populations, immunosenescence and impaired cellular immunity can weaken the relationship between serological responses and protection. Evaluation should include humoral, cellular, and mucosal responses, durability, and clinically meaningful outcomes in the intended population.Influenza preparedness depends on how these links function in practice. Antiviral use generates information relevant to resistance monitoring. Viral evolution and changing population immunity influence vaccine development and updating. Standardized validation, transparent evidence grading, interoperable data sharing, and evaluation in high-risk populations are needed throughout the pathway. During seasonal epidemics, zoonotic outbreaks, or pandemics, the reliability of these links may matter more than the performance of any single technology.

analysis.research_question_and_background: This review addresses the need to integrate molecular adaptation, surveillance, treatment, and vaccination strategies to enhance preparedness against seasonal influenza and emerging respiratory threats.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study is a comprehensive review of evidence from multiple domains, including host–virus interactions, surveillance technologies, antiviral management, and vaccine development, focusing on human influenza and its ecological and epidemiological contexts.
analysis.methods: The review synthesizes evidence on mammalian adaptation, such as receptor specificity and viral polymerase–host factor compatibility, alongside surveillance technologies like multiplex PCR, CRISPR-based assays, and AI-assisted risk assessment, and evaluates antiviral management and vaccine platforms including nanoparticle, mRNA, and intranasal designs.
analysis.main_results: The review highlights that recent A(H5N1) infections in humans, particularly in the United States, have been linked to exposure to infected dairy cattle or poultry, with one fatal case associated with backyard poultry exposure. It also notes the expanding mammalian host range of A(H5N1) as evidenced by its infection of cats in South Korea.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpret that the integration of findings across the four domains is critical for improving influenza preparedness, and that current evidence often relies on structural studies, cultured cells, or animal models, which may not fully capture human infection complexities.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings inform the need for standardized surveillance systems and better understanding of antiviral resistance and vaccine efficacy in relation to clinically meaningful outcomes, particularly for emerging threats like A(H5N1) in human populations.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The evidence is primarily derived from non-human models and structural studies, which may limit its direct applicability to human health. The review identifies weaknesses in translational handoffs between domains, suggesting moderate confidence in the conclusions.

analysis.summary_en: This review addresses the need to integrate molecular adaptation, surveillance, treatment, and vaccination strategies to enhance preparedness against seasonal influenza and emerging respiratory threats. It evaluates evidence on mammalian adaptation, surveillance technologies, and vaccine platforms, highlighting recent A(H5N1) infections in humans and the expanding host range of the virus. The authors emphasize the importance of connecting findings across domains to improve human health protection, noting that current evidence often relies on non-human models and structural studies. The review identifies limitations in the translational focus and the need for standardized surveillance and phenotypic context for antiviral resistance. These findings suggest that while the evidence is informative, its application to human health remains constrained by the reliance on animal models and the lack of direct clinical validation, resulting in moderate confidence in the conclusions.

It also notes the expanding mammalian host range of A(H5N1) as evidenced by its infection of cats in South Korea.
analysis_en.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpret that the integration of findings across the four domains is critical for improving influenza preparedness, and that current evidence often relies on structural studies, cultured cells, or animal models, which may not fully capture human infection complexities.
analysis_en.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings inform the need for standardized surveillance systems and better understanding of antiviral resistance and vaccine efficacy in relation to clinically meaningful outcomes, particularly for emerging threats like A(H5N1) in human populations.
analysis_en.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The evidence is primarily derived from non-human models and structural studies, which may limit its direct applicability to human health. The review identifies weaknesses in translational handoffs between domains, suggesting moderate confidence in the conclusions.

Molecular findings need confirmation in human-derived systems, and surveillance signals need enough standardization to support action. analysis_zh.research_question_and_background: 本综述解决了整合分子适应、监测、治疗 和 疫苗接种 策略的需要,以加强针对 季节性流感 和新出现的呼吸道威胁的准备。
analysis_zh.study_design_and_population: 该研究对来自多个领域的证据进行了全面审查,包括 宿主 与病毒相互作用、监测 技术、抗病毒药物 管理和 疫苗 开发,重点关注人类流感及其生态和流行病学背景。
analysis_zh.methods: 该综述综合了哺乳动物适应的证据,例如受体特异性和病毒聚合酶-宿主因子兼容性,以及多重PCR、基于CRISPR的检测和人工智能辅助风险评估等监测技术,并评估了抗病毒药物管理和疫苗平台,包括纳米颗粒、mRNA和鼻内设计。
analysis_zh.main_results: 该审查强调,最近发生的人类 A(H5N1) 感染,特别是在美国,与接触受感染的奶牛或家禽有关,其中一例死亡病例与接触后院家禽有关。它还注意到 A(H5N1) 哺乳动物 宿主 范围的扩大,韩国猫的感染就证明了这一点。
analysis_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 作者解释说,整合四个领域的研究结果对于改善流感防范至关重要,目前的证据通常依赖于结构研究、培养细胞或动物模型,而这些可能无法完全捕捉人类感染的复杂性。
analysis_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 这些发现表明需要标准化的 监测 系统,并更好地了解 抗病毒药物 耐药性和 疫苗 与临床有意义的结果相关的功效,特别是对于人群中出现的新威胁,如 A(H5N1)。
analysis_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 证据主要来自非人类模型和结构研究,这可能限制其对人类健康的直接适用性。该评论指出了领域之间翻译切换的弱点,表明对结论有一定的信心。

title: Knowledge of Avian Influenza Among Poultry Workers & Development of SIM on Prevention of Avian Influenza
abstract: Avian influenza is an important zoonotic disease of global concern, with poultry workers at particular risk because of their close and frequent contact with birds and contaminated environments.This study assessed the level of knowledge regarding avian influenza among poultry workers in selected poultry farms of Sangli and Miraj city, with a view to developing a self-instructional module on its prevention.A descriptive cross-sectional design was used, and 60 poultry workers were selected by simple random sampling from identified farms in the study area.Data were collected using a structured questionnaire consisting of demographic variables and 16 multiple-choice items covering transmission, clinical manifestations in humans and birds, diagnosis, vaccination, biosecurity measures, safe cooking practices, and use of personal protective equipment.Knowledge scores were categorized as bad, average, good, or excellent.The findings showed that 70% of poultry workers had average knowledge and 30% had good knowledge; none had bad or excellent knowledge.More than half of the workers reported no prior knowledge of avian influenza, and among those who had heard about it, the main sources were social media, newspapers, television, and health workers.Important gaps were observed in the understanding of human-to-human transmission, recommended personal protective equipment, appropriate cooking practices, reporting of sick or dead birds, and farm-level biosecurity.Chi-square analysis revealed no statistically significant association between knowledge level and selected demographic variables such as age, education, type of work, work experience, and previous knowledge.In response to the identified deficiencies, a self-instructional module was developed focusing on essential concepts and practical preventive measures.The study highlights the need for simple, locally appropriate educational interventions to strengthen knowledge and promote safer practices among poultry workers, thereby reducing the risk of avian influenza transmission at the human-poultry interface.

Email ID: baswant.dhudum@bharatividyapeeth.edu Abstract Avian influenza is an important zoonotic disease of global concern, with poultry workers at particular risk because of their close and frequent contact with birds and contaminated environments. This study assessed the level of knowledge regarding avian influenza among poultry workers in selected poultry farms of Sangli and Miraj city, with a view to developing a self‐instructional module on its prevention. A descriptive cross‐sectional design was used, and 60 poultry workers were selected by simple random sampling from identified farms in the study area. Data were collected using a structured questionnaire consisting of demographic variables and 16 multiple‐choice items covering transmission, clinical manifestations in humans and birds, diagnosis, vaccination, biosecurity measures, safe cooking practices, and use of personal protective equipment. Knowledge scores were categorized as bad, average, good, or excellent. The findings showed that 70% of poultry workers had average knowledge and 30% had good knowledge; none had bad or excellent knowledge. More than half of the workers reported no prior knowledge of avian influenza, and among those who had heard about it, the main sources were social media, newspapers, television, and health workers. Important gaps were observed in the understanding of human‐to‐human transmission, recommended personal protective equipment, appropriate cooking practices, reporting of sick or dead birds, and farm‐level biosecurity. Chi‐square analysis revealed no statistically significant association between knowledge level and selected demographic variables such as age, education, type of work, work experience, and previous knowledge. In response to the identified deficiencies, a self‐instructional module was developed focusing on essential concepts and practical preventive measures. The study highlights the need for simple, locally appropriate educational interventions to strengthen knowledge and promote safer practices among poultry workers, thereby reducing the risk of avian influenza transmission at the human–poultry interface. DOI: 10.25258/ijddt.16.64s.161 Introduction: Influenza A viruses, particularly avian strains like bird flu, are segmented RNA viruses primarily circulating in wild birds such as waterfowl, with high diversity due to rapid mutation and reassortment. Historical outbreaks, including "fowl plague" since the 1800s, were later identified as highly pathogenic H5 and H7 subtypes causing severe disease in poultry. These viruses have zoonotic potential, sparking pandemics like the 1918 H1N1 Spanish flu and recent H5N1/H7N9 spillovers, spread via migratory birds and poultry trade(Garg et al., 2025; Lycett et al., 2019). Avian influenza (AI) viruses have been detected frequently since 2022, posing ongoing risks to health, economies, and food security. The last comprehensive global review of AI outbreaks and infections was published nearly a decade ago, Knowledge of Avian Influenza Among Poultry Workers & Development of SIM on Prevention of Avian Influenza IJDDT Volume 16 Issue 64s 2026 Page: 1505 leaving a gap in updated surveillance data. Recent increases in reports of highly pathogenic strains like H5N1, H5N8, and H5N6 in both birds and humans highlight the urgent need for a new global analysis to assess pandemic risks (Eisfeld et al., 2024; Szablewski et al., 2023). The 2014 avian influenza outbreak in Kerala’s Kuttanad region caused severe economic losses to poultry farmers, hatcheries, and tourism operators. Duck farms suffered the highest losses, with commercial farms losing around USD 9,181 per farm, while backyard poultry losses were relatively small. Hatcheries faced significant setbacks, with large ones losing nearly USD 11,963, and the government spent USD 744,890 on disease control measures. The outbreak also disrupted markets, delayed price recovery by eight weeks, and reduced tourist inflow, costing boat operators about USD 2,280 each, highlighting the need for preventive biosecurity and regular screening of domestic birds (Govindaraj et al., 2018; Kang et al., 2024). Human influenza pandemics occur periodically, often linked to avian influenza spreading among domestic birds. This increases the risk of mutations and genetic reassortment that can trigger new pandemics. Currently, the global alert level for avian influenza is phase 3 on a six‐point scale, indicating moderate concern. Preventive vigilance remains essential to reduce future risks(Kumar et al., 2025; Uyeki et al., 2024) . The focus of the present study was to assess the level of knowledge regarding avian influenza infection among poultry workers and to develop a self-instructional module on the prevention of AI infection among poultry workers. Materials & Methods: Ethical Considerations Institutional Ethics Committee (IEC) approval was obtained from Bharati Vidyapeeth (Deemed to be University) College of Nursing, Sangli. Farm owner permissions, informed written consent (English/Marathi), and confidentiality via code numbers were upheld; data used solely for research. Voluntary participation and the right to withdraw were emphasized. Research Approach This study adopted a quantitative research approach to systematically investigate the knowledge levels of poultry workers regarding avian influenza. The approach focused on measurable data collection through structured tools, enabling objective analysis of knowledge gaps and associations with demographic variables. It involved deductive methods to test predefined hypotheses derived from the literature review. Research Design A cross-sectional descriptive study design was employed to capture a snapshot of knowledge at a specific point in time among poultry workers in selected farms. This design suited the objective of assessing current knowledge without intervention, using surveys for efficiency in data gathering from the target population. Setting and Sample size & Sampling technique The study was conducted in selected poultry farms in Sangli and Miraj city areas, chosen for high poultry worker density and relevance to avian influenza risks. The sample comprised 60 poultry workers, determined using the power analysis. Inclusion criteria encompassed workers willing to participate, literate in English or Marathi, and involved in farm activities; exclusions were non- consenting individuals. Simple random sampling was utilized to select participants, promoting representativeness and minimizing bias in this cross- sectional setup. Workers meeting the criteria were randomly drawn from farm lists provided by owners after permission. This technique supported generalizability within the local context. Data Collection Tool, Validity, Reliability & Data Analysis The tool consisted of two sections: Section I for demographic variables (age, gender, education, work type, experience, prior knowledge sources) and Section II, a structured knowledge questionnaire with 16 multiple-choice items across domains like definition, transmission, symptoms, diagnosis, prevention, and treatment. Correct answers scored 1, incorrect 0; levels were poor (0-5), average (6-10), good (11-16), excellent (17+). The questionnaire was developed from the literature review for content relevance. Content validity was established by 14 experts (4 community health, 5 medical-surgical nursing, 1 statistician), whose suggestions refined the tool. The Marathi translation was validated by language experts for cultural and linguistic accuracy. Expert feedback ensured alignment with study objectives and avian influenza knowledge domains. Reliability was tested via split-half method on 10 workers at a Miraj farm on 01/04/2025, yielding a coefficient of 0.95 (>0.7 threshold), confirming high internal consistency. The pilot study on 02/04/2025 (n=10) affirmed feasibility, tool clarity, and no modifications needed. This validated tool readiness for the main data collection. Descriptive statistics (frequency, percentage) described demographics and knowledge levels; inferential chi-square tested associations with variables. Email ID: baswant.dhudum@bharatividyapeeth.edu Abstract Avian influenza is an important zoonotic disease of global concern, with poultry workers at particular risk because of their close and frequent contact with birds and contaminated environments. This study assessed the level of knowledge regarding avian influenza among poultry workers in selected poultry farms of Sangli and Miraj city, with a view to developing a self‐instructional module on its prevention. A descriptive cross‐sectional design was used, and 60 poultry workers were selected by simple random sampling from identified farms in the study area. Data were collected using a structured questionnaire consisting of demographic variables and 16 multiple‐choice items covering transmission, clinical manifestations in humans and birds, diagnosis, vaccination, biosecurity measures, safe cooking practices, and use of personal protective equipment. Knowledge scores were categorized as bad, average, good, or excellent. The findings showed that 70% of poultry workers had average knowledge and 30% had good knowledge; none had bad or excellent knowledge. More than half of the workers reported no prior knowledge of avian influenza, and among those who had heard about it, the main sources were social media, newspapers, television, and health workers. Important gaps were observed in the understanding of human‐to‐human transmission, recommended personal protective equipment, appropriate cooking practices, reporting of sick or dead birds, and farm‐level biosecurity. Chi‐square analysis revealed no statistically significant association between knowledge level and selected demographic variables such as age, education, type of work, work experience, and previous knowledge. In response to the identified deficiencies, a self‐instructional module was developed focusing on essential concepts and practical preventive measures. The study highlights the need for simple, locally appropriate educational interventions to strengthen knowledge and promote safer practices among poultry workers, thereby reducing the risk of avian influenza transmission at the human–poultry interface. DOI: 10.25258/ijddt.16.64s.161 Introduction: Influenza A viruses, particularly avian strains like bird flu, are segmented RNA viruses primarily circulating in wild birds such as waterfowl, with high diversity due to rapid mutation and reassortment. Historical outbreaks, including "fowl plague" since the 1800s, were later identified as highly pathogenic H5 and H7 subtypes causing severe disease in poultry. These viruses have zoonotic potential, sparking pandemics like the 1918 H1N1 Spanish flu and recent H5N1/H7N9 spillovers, spread via migratory birds and poultry trade(Garg et al., 2025; Lycett et al., 2019). Avian influenza (AI) viruses have been detected frequently since 2022, posing ongoing risks to health, economies, and food security. The last comprehensive global review of AI outbreaks and infections was published nearly a decade ago, Knowledge of Avian Influenza Among Poultry Workers & Development of SIM on Prevention of Avian Influenza IJDDT Volume 16 Issue 64s 2026 Page: 1505 leaving a gap in updated surveillance data. Recent increases in reports of highly pathogenic strains like H5N1, H5N8, and H5N6 in both birds and humans highlight the urgent need for a new global analysis to assess pandemic risks (Eisfeld et al., 2024; Szablewski et al., 2023). The 2014 avian influenza outbreak in Kerala’s Kuttanad region caused severe economic losses to poultry farmers, hatcheries, and tourism operators. Duck farms suffered the highest losses, with commercial farms losing around USD 9,181 per farm, while backyard poultry losses were relatively small. Hatcheries faced significant setbacks, with large ones losing nearly USD 11,963, and the government spent USD 744,890 on disease control measures. The outbreak also disrupted markets, delayed price recovery by eight weeks, and reduced tourist inflow, costing boat operators about USD 2,280 each, highlighting the need for preventive biosecurity and regular screening of domestic birds (Govindaraj et al., 2018; Kang et al., 2024). Human influenza pandemics occur periodically, often linked to avian influenza spreading among domestic birds. This increases the risk of mutations and genetic reassortment that can trigger new pandemics. Currently, the global alert level for avian influenza is phase 3 on a six‐point scale, indicating moderate concern. Preventive vigilance remains essential to reduce future risks(Kumar et al., 2025; Uyeki et al., 2024) . The focus of the present study was to assess the level of knowledge regarding avian influenza infection among poultry workers and to develop a self-instructional module on the prevention of AI infection among poultry workers. Farm owner permissions, informed written consent (English/Marathi), and confidentiality via code numbers were upheld; data used solely for research. Voluntary participation and the right to withdraw were emphasized. Research Approach This study adopted a quantitative research approach to systematically investigate the knowledge levels of poultry workers regarding avian influenza. The approach focused on measurable data collection through structured tools, enabling objective analysis of knowledge gaps and associations with demographic variables. It involved deductive methods to test predefined hypotheses derived from the literature review. Research Design A cross-sectional descriptive study design was employed to capture a snapshot of knowledge at a specific point in time among poultry workers in selected farms. This design suited the objective of assessing current knowledge without intervention, using surveys for efficiency in data gathering from the target population. full_text: Nature Reviews Microbiology nature reviews microbiology https://doi.org/10.1038/s41579-026-01372-1 Review article Check for updates Towards broader-spectrum direct-acting antivirals against RNA viruses Hendrik Jan Thibaut 1, Dirk Jochmans 1,3, Christophe Van Dijck2,3, Manon Laporte 1,3, Laurens Liesenborghs 2 & Johan Neyts1 Abstract Small molecule antiviral drugs have transformed the management of infections such as those caused by HIV, hepatitis B virus, hepatitis C virus, herpesviruses and influenza viruses. Effective antiviral therapeutics remain unavailable for many other often life-threatening viral infections, many of which are caused by RNA viruses. The development of potent, safe and orally available antivirals is therefore essential both to address current unmet medical needs and to strengthen epidemic and pandemic preparedness. In this Review, we discuss the rationale for building a diversified portfolio of broader-spectrum antivirals against RNA viruses with activity spanning multiple genera, entire families or even crossing viral families. We provide a non-exhaustive overview of approved and investigational antiviral agents active against RNA viruses and discuss the biological determinants that underlie their antiviral spectrum. Finally, we outline the clinical development frameworks required to accelerate the evaluation of such drugs, in particular in the context of outbreaks. Direct-acting antivirals versus host-targeting antivirals New approaches to discover new targets for broader-acting antivirals Translational readiness Conclusions 1KU Leuven Department of Microbiology, Immunology and Transplantation, Antiviral Drug and Vaccine Research Group, Leuven, Belgium. 2Department of Clinical Sciences, Institute of Tropical Medicine, Antwerp, Belgium. 3These authors contributed equally: Dirk Jochmans, Christophe Van Dijck, Manon Laporte. e-mail: johan.neyts@kuleuven.be Nature Reviews Microbiology Review article Alongside vaccine development, sustained investment in antiviral drug discovery is therefore essential. Antiviral drug development has so far largely been focused on viral infections that offer large and predict- able commercial markets (for example, those caused by HIV and HCV). It is obviously unrealistic and economically unsustainable to develop specific antiviral drugs for each known viral pathogen. Newly emerging viruses will most likely belong to viral families already known (Table 1) today. Advances in metagenomics and high-throughput sequencing greatly expanded our understanding of viral diversity, and although new viral families may still be discovered, such events are becoming increasingly rare. Together, this strongly supports a strategy in which broader-acting small molecule antiviral (BSA) drugs are developed. Such drugs can be used for the treatment and prophylaxis of infec- tions with known viruses for which no antiviral treatment is available and, in the case of epidemics or pandemics, as a rapid response option while other countermeasures, such as vaccines and mAbs, are being developed12,13. In this Review, we discuss the rationale for the development of BSAs and provide a non-exhaustive overview of approved or experi- mental antiviral drugs active against viruses with an RNA genome. We also outline strategies for target discovery and accelerated clinical development. One drug to treat them all? The term ‘broad-spectrum’ antiviral has been widely used but lacks, to the best of our knowledge, a clear definition. Here, we propose instead to use the term ‘broader-spectrum’ antivirals and distinguish three categories: (i) cross-family BSAs with activity across unrelated viral families within or across a certain genome architecture, that is, negative-sense single-stranded RNA ((−)ssRNA), positive-sense single-stranded RNA ((+)ssRNA) or double-stranded RNA (dsRNA); (ii) pan-family BSAs that act across the different genera of a given viral family (for example, pan-paramyxovirus drugs); and (iii) intra-family BSAs, which are active against multiple serotypes and genotypes of a particular virus (for example, pan-serotype dengue virus (DENV) Introduction Viruses, whether known or yet to emerge (‘virus X’), remain a major threat to global health. Vaccines, monoclonal antibodies (mAbs) and antiviral drugs are each important and complementary in controlling viral infections. Vaccination has led to the eradication of smallpox, brought polio close to eradication and massively reduced disease and mortality associated with numerous viral infections, such as measles virus, mumps virus, rubella virus, influenza virus, severe acute respira- tory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2), hepatitis B virus (HBV) and human papillomavirus1–3. For several important human pathogens, such as HIV, hepatitis C virus (HCV), herpes simplex viruses (HSV), cytomegalovirus (CMV), rhinoviruses and many others, the devel- opment of highly effective vaccines has proved difficult or remains elusive, often despite decades of intensive effort. Therefore, it cannot be guaranteed that efficacious vaccines can always be developed when new threatening viruses emerge4,5. mAbs can offer immediate protection and are transforming the prophylaxis or treatment of certain acute viral diseases, such as those caused by the rabies virus6 and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV)7. They generally have an excellent safety profile and can be highly effective, although they require injections, are virus specific or variant spe- cific and can rapidly select for escape variants8,9. Like vaccines, mAbs can be developed only once a new pathogen has been identified and characterized. By contrast, small molecule antiviral drugs offer several distinct advantages. They can be administered orally and have the potential to cover a broader spectrum of viruses (Box 1) than vaccines and mAbs. Antiviral drugs have revolutionized the treatment of certain (chronic) viral infections such as those caused by either HIV, HBV, HCV, HSV-1 and HSV-2, and CMV. More recently, antiviral drugs have also become availa- ble against some other viruses including influenza viruses, SARS-CoV-2 and hepatitis delta virus. However, for the majority of the more than 200 known human pathogenic viruses, no antiviral drugs are available. Most of these viruses are RNA viruses — the focus of this Review — including many emerging and clinically important pathogens10–12. Box 1 | Categories and examples of broader-spectrum antivirals (BSAs) for RNA viruses Cross-family BSAs Active against viruses belonging to different (related or unrelated) viral families or across a certain genome architecture (that is, negative-sense single-stranded RNA ((−)ssRNA), positive-sense single-stranded RNA ((+)ssRNA) or double-stranded RNA (dsRNA viruses)), typically by targeting conserved features of the viral replication machinery such as the catalytic site of viral RNA-dependent RNA polymerases. For example, remdesivir, a nucleoside viral polymerase inhibitor, is active against viruses belonging to different viral families, that is, the (−)ssRNA Filoviridae, Paramyxoviridae, Pneumoviridae and Arenaviridae as well as the (+) ssRNA Flaviviridae, Picornaviridae and Coronaviridae. Baloxavir, an endonuclease inhibitor, inhibits influenza A and B viruses (family Orthomyxoviridae) but also, although much less potently, several members of the family Peribunyaviridae. Pan-family BSAs Active across all or at least most genera within a single viral family. Examples include neuraminidase inhibitors such as oseltamivir, zanamivir and peramivir that are active against both influenza A and B viruses (family Orthomyxoviridae). Nirmatrelvir is a reversible covalent, peptidomimetic Mpro inhibitor that inhibits human and animal coronaviruses belonging to different genera within the family Coronaviridae. Intra-family BSAs Can be active against multiple serotypes, genotypes or strains of a particular virus species. For example, mosnodenvir is active against all dengue virus genotypes (family Flaviviridae) by blocking the interaction between viral proteins NS4B and NS3. Intra-family broader-spectrum activity may span several viruses within one genus of a particular family without extending to other genera. For example, the non-covalent, non-peptidomimetic Mpro inhibitor ensitrelvir is active only against members of the genus Betacoronavirus (severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2), SARS-CoV-1 and human coronavirus (HCoV)-OC43), but not against members of the genus Alphacoronavirus (such as HCoV-229E and HCoV-NL63) within the family Coronaviridae. Nature Reviews Microbiology Review article inhibitors) or active against one or more (but not all) genera of a viral family (Box 1). The need for broader-acting antivirals and their desired spectrum of activity are mostly defined by the particular (clinical) context (Boxes 2 and 3). For viruses that cause a high number of annual cases (for example, RSV), there might be a sufficiently large market, and thus incentives, to develop virus-specific drugs. Conversely, there might be no or less financial incentive to develop virus-specific drugs for viruses that cause a rather limited number of cases but that col- lectively, within their genus or family, are responsible for a substan- tial clinical burden (for example, coxsackieviruses and echoviruses, EV-D68 and EV-A71 that all belong to the genus Enterovirus). In this case, the development of antivirals that are broadly active across the entire Enterovirus genus (pan-Enterovirus; category intra-family BSAs) represents a more realistic approach. In the context of epidemic or pan- demic preparedness, access to pan-family and cross-family BSAs may be particularly important, as it cannot be predicted which viral family a newly emerging pathogen (‘virus X’) will belong to. Given the extensive genetic diversity and distinct replication strategies of viral families, the development of a single cross-family drug with potent activity against all RNA virus families is likely to be unrealistic. Rather, a more feasible strategy may be to establish a portfolio of different types of BSAs that collectively provide, either alone or in combination, coverage across the RNA virus landscape. BSAs may also be valuable in the context of viral co-infections, in which a single drug could simultaneously target two (or more) viruses14,15. Beyond the spectrum of activity, BSA development must be guided by clearly defined target product profiles16. To have a meaningful clinical impact, BSAs (or combinations thereof) should ideally be highly efficacious, be orally available (preferably once daily dosing), be safe for a broad patient population (preferably including pregnant women and children), possess a (relatively) high barrier to resistance and exhibit minimal drug–drug interactions16. Virus tissue tropism further influences desirable drug properties. For example, infections involving the central nervous system require efficient blood–brain barrier penetration, whereas limited penetration may be preferable for peripheral viral infections. Consequently, distinct target product profiles may be required, even within a single viral genus. (−)ssRNA, negative-sense single-stranded RNA; EV, enterovirus; HCoV, human coronavirus; LCMV, lymphocytic choriomeningitis virus; MERS, Middle East respiratory syndrome; SARS, severe acute respiratory syndrome; TBEV, tick-borne encephalitis virus. Nature Reviews Microbiology Review article typically invade the central nerve system, whereas yellow fever virus and DENV do not17. The importance of preparedness against known viruses (such as EV-D6818, Ebola virus19, monkeypox virus20 and Andes hantavirus21) as well as against emerging viral threats (for example, SARS-CoV-2) has been repeatedly illustrated during outbreaks caused by these diverse viral pathogens. During the coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19 pan- demic), no antiviral drugs were available at the onset. A stockpile of an oral, pan-family coronavirus BSA before the start of the COVID-19 pan- demic would likely have saved countless lives22,23. Remdesivir, originally discovered as an RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp) inhibitor of RSV24 and Ebola viruses25,26, was the only drug for which antiviral activity against coronaviruses had been systematically demonstrated in preclinical models before the pandemic27. In the absence of readily available and effective antiviral treat- ments, drug repurposing may need to be considered. Repurpos- ing can provide a rapid and relatively cost-effective response by leveraging de-risked drugs with existing preclinical and clinical safety data28,29. However, drugs developed or used for non-viral indi- cations are mostly unlikely to possess sufficient antiviral potency to curb outbreaks caused by newly emerging and (potentially highly) pathogenic viruses. At the start of the COVID-19 pandemic, extensive repurposing initiatives studied whether drugs approved for other indications could inhibit SARS-CoV-2 replication. Drugs such as azithro- mycin (antibiotic), itraconazole (antifungal), hydroxychloroquine (antimalarial, antirheumatic), niclosamide (anthelmintic), ivermectin (anthelmintic) and nitazoxanide (antiparasitic) rapidly entered numer- ous clinical trials, many of them small and underpowered, and even became, for some time, standard treatment in certain settings despite limited preclinical evidence30. Overall, drug repurposing efforts dur- ing the SARS-CoV-2 pandemic were largely unsuccessful, highlighting that such strategies should not be initiated only at the time a new virus emerges. A more realistic approach is to systematically assess existing drugs during epidemic or pandemic ‘peace-time’ against panels of viruses that are representative of high-risk families. Drugs with ‘reason- able’ in vitro activity can be further tested, alone or in combinations, in preclinical models13. Studies in SARS-CoV-2-infected hamsters revealed that combi- nations of two or three antivirals, each used at suboptimal or even inactive doses, can result in important antiviral effects31. To ration- ally develop combination strategies for BSAs, systematic preclinical testing of combinations across viral families is required. Extensive preclinical studies of the most promising combinations may help to guide strategies for stockpiling for epidemic or pandemic prepared- ness. The use of fixed-dose combinations (such as those used in the treatment of HIV infections) would be ideal. Yet, in outbreak situation with new pathogens, there will be insufficient time to develop such fixed-dose combinations; co-administration of individual drugs would therefore represent a more practical approach. Their broad host range, capacity for zoonotic spillover and ability to spread rapidly underscore the pandemic potential of this family and make them a key priority for preparedness. Here, we propose instead to use the term ‘broader-spectrum’ antivirals and distinguish three categories: (i) cross-family BSAs with activity across unrelated viral families within or across a certain genome architecture, that is, negative-sense single-stranded RNA ((−)ssRNA), positive-sense single-stranded RNA ((+)ssRNA) or double-stranded RNA (dsRNA); (ii) pan-family BSAs that act across the different genera of a given viral family (for example, pan-paramyxovirus drugs); and (iii) intra-family BSAs, which are active against multiple serotypes and genotypes of a particular virus (for example, pan-serotype dengue virus (DENV) Introduction Viruses, whether known or yet to emerge (‘virus X’), remain a major threat to global health. Vaccines, monoclonal antibodies (mAbs) and antiviral drugs are each important and complementary in controlling viral infections. For several important human pathogens, such as HIV, hepatitis C virus (HCV), herpes simplex viruses (HSV), cytomegalovirus (CMV), rhinoviruses and many others, the devel- opment of highly effective vaccines has proved difficult or remains elusive, often despite decades of intensive effort. Therefore, it cannot be guaranteed that efficacious vaccines can always be developed when new threatening viruses emerge4,5. mAbs can offer immediate protection and are transforming the prophylaxis or treatment of certain acute viral diseases, such as those caused by the rabies virus6 and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV)7. They generally have an excellent safety profile and can be highly effective, although they require injections, are virus specific or variant spe- cific and can rapidly select for escape variants8,9. Most of these viruses are RNA viruses — the focus of this Review — including many emerging and clinically important pathogens10–12. Examples include neuraminidase inhibitors such as oseltamivir, zanamivir and peramivir that are active against both influenza A and B viruses (family Orthomyxoviridae). Nirmatrelvir is a reversible covalent, peptidomimetic Mpro inhibitor that inhibits human and animal coronaviruses belonging to different genera within the family Coronaviridae. analysis.scope_and_question: The review focuses on seasonal influenza viruses, specifically human influenza A(H1N1)pdm09, A(H3N2), and B/Victoria and B/Yamagata lineages. The central question is the development of broader-spectrum direct-acting antivirals (BSAs) against RNA viruses, with an emphasis on creating drugs that can target multiple viral genera, families, or even cross families.
analysis.evidence_base_and_review_method: The review is a systematic analysis of antiviral agents active against RNA viruses, including approved and investigational drugs. It discusses the biological determinants underlying antiviral spectrum and outlines clinical development frameworks for evaluating such drugs, particularly in outbreak scenarios. The review does not report specific databases, search dates, or study counts.
analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: The review concludes that broader-spectrum antivirals are essential for addressing current unmet medical needs and for pandemic preparedness. It highlights the importance of developing drugs that can target multiple viral families or genera, as newly emerging viruses are likely to belong to known families. The review also emphasizes the need for a diversified portfolio of antivirals to combat RNA viruses effectively.
analysis.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: The review notes that the term 'broad-spectrum' antiviral lacks a clear definition, and it proposes the term 'broader-spectrum' instead. It also identifies gaps in the development of antivirals for many RNA viruses, particularly those that are not part of the large commercial markets. Additionally, the review highlights the need for more research on the clinical development frameworks for BSAs, especially in the context of outbreaks.
analysis.research_and_practice_implications: The review suggests that research should focus on identifying and validating new targets for broader-spectrum antivirals, particularly those that can act across multiple viral families or genera. It also recommends the development of antivirals for RNA viruses that currently lack effective treatments, such as certain influenza strains, and emphasizes the importance of accelerating clinical trials for these drugs during outbreaks.

analysis.summary_en: This review explores the development of broader-spectrum direct-acting antivirals (BSAs) against RNA viruses, with a focus on seasonal influenza viruses such as A(H1N1)pdm09, A(H3N2), B/Victoria, and B/Yamagata. It highlights the need for such drugs to address current medical needs and enhance pandemic preparedness. The review discusses the rationale for BSAs, their biological determinants, and the clinical frameworks required for their evaluation. It also identifies controversies, such as the lack of a clear definition for 'broad-spectrum' antivirals, and evidence gaps in the development of antivirals for many RNA viruses. The implications emphasize the importance of research into new targets and the acceleration of clinical trials for BSAs during outbreaks.

elements_zh.scope_and_question: 本评论聚焦于季节性流感病毒,特别是人类流感病毒的甲型H1N1流感病毒pdm09、甲型H3N2流感病毒以及B/Victoria和B/Yamagata谱系。核心问题是开发针对RNA病毒的广谱直接作用抗病毒药物药物(BSAs),重点在于创建能够针对多种病毒属、科甚至跨科的药物。
elements_zh.evidence_base_and_review_method: 本评论是对针对RNA病毒的抗病毒药物药物的系统分析,包括已批准和正在研究的药物。它讨论了抗病毒药物谱的生物学决定因素,并概述了评估此类药物的临床开发框架,特别是在暴发情境下。本评论未报告特定数据库、搜索日期或研究数量。
elements_zh.consensus_and_key_conclusions: 本评论得出结论,认为针对RNA病毒的广谱抗病毒药物药物对于解决当前未满足的医疗需求和加强大流行病应对能力至关重要。它强调了开发能够针对多种病毒科或属的药物的重要性,因为新出现的病毒很可能属于已知的病毒科。本评论还强调了需要针对RNA病毒开发多样化的抗病毒药物药物组合以有效应对这些病毒。
elements_zh.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: 本评论指出,'广谱' 抗病毒药物这一术语缺乏明确的定义,并建议使用'更广谱'这一术语。它还指出了针对许多RNA病毒的抗病毒药物药物开发存在空白,尤其是那些不属于大型商业市场的病毒。此外,本评论强调了需要更多研究来完善BSAs的临床开发框架,特别是在暴发情境下。
elements_zh.research_and_practice_implications: 本评论建议研究应集中在识别和验证针对广谱抗病毒药物药物的新靶点,特别是那些能够作用于多种病毒科或属的靶点。它还推荐开发针对目前缺乏有效治疗的RNA病毒的抗病毒药物药物,例如某些流感毒株,并强调在暴发情境下加速这些药物的临床试验的重要性。

full_text: AbstractBackgroundContinuous monitoring of both influenza vaccine protection and behavioural determinants of infection is important for understanding related risks. Evidence on influenza vaccine effectiveness (VE) in China during the 2024–2025 season, however, remains limited. We aimed to assess influenza VE among healthcare-seeking outpatients with influenza-like illness (ILI) and to examine the contact patterns associated with infection risk.MethodsWe enrolled 928 outpatients with ILI from three sentinel hospitals in Ili Kazakh Autonomous Prefecture, China, between December 2024 and March 2025 in a test-negative case-control study. We confirmed influenza infection using reverse transcription-polymerase chain reaction and collected vaccination history and social contact frequency and duration through questionnaires. We estimated VE using logistic regression with covariate adjustment, and otherwise analysed social contact patterns and performed exploratory sequencing of six randomly selected influenza-positive samples.ResultsOur full sample comprised 928 participants. We excluded 21 infants younger than 6 months from the VE analysis and included 907 participants, of whom 121 tested positive and 786 tested negative. The overall adjusted VE against medically attended influenza was 42.3% (95% credible interval = 11.1–62.5). In the analysis of social contacts for all 928 participants, test-positive children aged 0–10 years and adults aged 65 years or older reported more frequent and longer social contact than their test-negative counterparts. Exploratory sequencing of six samples suggested no major antigenic mismatch with the vaccine strains, but the very small number of sequenced samples limits the generalisability of this finding.ConclusionsInfluenza vaccination provided moderate protection against medically attended influenza, while contact patterns were associated with infection risk among children and older adults. Combined vaccination and behavioural interventions warrant further evaluation, as the observational design of this study and its use of self-reporting data limit causal inference.Keywords : influenza, influenza vaccination, vaccine effectiveness, test-negative design, contact patterns, China METHODSSetting and study designWe conducted a multicentre test-negative case-control study from 8 December 2024 (epidemiological week 50) to 30 March 2025 (epidemiological week 13) among outpatients with influenza-like illness (ILI) from three sentinel hospitals in Yining and Horgos, Ili Kazakh Autonomous Prefecture, China. These sentinel outpatient clinics serve as the core data source for the national influenza surveillance network and support the systematic collection of epidemiological and virological data.In accordance with the Chinese National Influenza Surveillance Protocol, we defined ILI as the presence of fever (body temperature ≥38°C) accompanied by a cough or sore throat [33]. We randomly selected 10–40 patients (typically 20) with ILI each week from whom we collected nasal or nasopharyngeal specimens for influenza testing using real-time reverse transcription-polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR), and administered a structured questionnaire to collect demographic information, influenza vaccination history, and social contact patterns. Trained hospital staff administered structured questionnaires and recorded the responses in an electronic database. We linked the questionnaire records to the corresponding laboratory results using unique study identifiers.We included outpatients who presented with ILI at a sentinel hospital, understood the questionnaire, and provided verbal informed consent, either personally or through a guardian. We excluded participants younger than six months of age from the VE analysis because maternal antibodies could provide protection. We truncated the number of reported daily contact counts above 30 at 30 in the contact analysis to reduce the influence of outliers.Outcome variableWe defined the influenza test result as a dichotomous variable, categorised as positive or negative based on RT-PCR analysis of nasopharyngeal swab specimens. We performed testing using the Zhuocheng Huisheng Influenza A/B Duplex real-time PCR detection kit (Beijing Zhuocheng Huisheng Bioscience Co., Ltd., Beijing, China). This kit used specific primers and fluorescent probes targeting influenza A and B viruses and included an internal control that monitors the entire process from nucleic acid extraction to amplification, thereby reducing the risk of false-negative results.Exposure variablesWe defined influenza vaccination status as the primary exposure variable based on data reported by the participants or their guardians. We classified participants as vaccinated if they had received at least one dose of a seasonal influenza vaccine, including egg-based, cell-based, trivalent, and quadrivalent vaccines, within the past 24 months, with the most recent dose being administered at least 14 days before symptom onset. We classified participants who did not meet these criteria as unvaccinated.We defined social contact pattern as the secondary exposure variable and characterised it by contact frequency and duration according to the POLYMOD study criteria [22]. We defined conversational contact as a face-to-face conversation with an exchange of at least three words, and physical contact as any skin-to-skin interaction, such as handshaking, hugging, or kissing.CovariatesWe collected potential confounders using structured questionnaires (Text S1 in the Online Supplementary Document), including demographic characteristics such as age, sex, and ethnicity; clinical and behavioural characteristics, such as baseline health conditions, health-related behaviours, and daily habits; and temporal variables, such as the dates of symptom onset and visit dates. We grouped age for further analysis and used symptom onset and visit dates to derive the epidemiological week for adjustment for long-term and seasonal trends.Viral sequencing sample selection and reference sequencesThe national Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) influenza surveillance protocol requires sentinel hospitals to perform viral genetic sequencing on a subset of influenza-positive samples during routine surveillance to monitor genetic variation among circulating strains, rather than sequencing all positive samples [33]. We selected 6 out of 121 influenza-positive samples for exploratory sequencing in accordance with this protocol.We retrieved global influenza A(H1N1) reference sequences from the Global Initiative on Sharing All Influenza Data (GISAID) database [34]. We selected 170 sequences containing both haemagglutinin (HA) and neuraminidase (NA) gene segments and combined them with six viral isolates obtained in this study.Statistical analysisWe used a Bayesian logistic regression model adjusted for covariates to estimate VE. We specified an informative prior for the vaccination coefficient, centred on a VE of 40% based on historical CDC estimates [35]. We calculated VE for laboratory-confirmed influenza as (1 − odds ratio) × 100% and expressed uncertainty in the model coefficients using 95% credible intervals (CrIs) derived from the posterior distribution.We performed targeted sequencing of 6 virus isolates from influenza-positive participants and conducted phylogenetic analysis together with 170 reference sequences retrieved from GISAID. We aligned the sequences using ClustalW in Molecular Evolutionary Genetics Analysis, version 12 [36] and assessed alignment quality using ESPript [37]. We constructed a maximum-likelihood phylogenetic tree using IQ-TREE [38]. We then compared sequences within a specific monophyletic clade to identify variable sites and non-synonymous mutations (Text S3 in the Online Supplementary Document).We performed age standardisation according to the 2020 China Population Census. We used linear regression to quantify age-specific differences in contact frequency and duration (β) between influenza test-positive and test-negative participants. We smoothed the contact matrices using Gaussian kernel density estimation. We used stratified χ2 tests to compare the distributions of contact setting, frequency, and duration between the groups. We performed similar analyses for social contacts by age groups (0–5 years, 6–15 years, 16–65 years, and >65 years) based on immune status, social behaviours, and health risks, with further stratification by sex (male and female), household size (small, ≤3 persons; medium, 4 persons; large, ≥5 persons), and contact setting (home, school, workplace, leisure, and other) (Text S4 in the Online Supplementary Document).We also conducted sensitivity analyses to evaluate the robustness of the VE estimates and social contact analyses (Text S5 in the Online Supplementary Document). For the VE analysis, we assessed the effects of including infants younger than six months, treating age and body mass index as continuous variables, and adjusting for the symptom onset date. For the social contact analysis, we restricted the sample to unvaccinated participants to reduce potential confounding by vaccination status.We performed all statistical analyses and phylogenetic tree visualisations using R, version 4.3.2 (R Core Team, Vienna, Austria), with the ‘EBImage’, ‘seqinr’, ‘ape’, ‘phytools’, ‘ggplot2’, ‘treeio’, and ‘ggtree’ packages. We excluded participants younger than six months of age from the VE analysis because maternal antibodies could provide protection. full_text_sections.discussion: DISCUSSIONWe used a test-negative design to estimate influenza VE among participants who presented with ILI at hospitals in Ili Kazakh Autonomous Prefecture, Xinjiang during the 2024–2025 influenza season. Such a test-negative design is commonly used to evaluate VE in real-world settings because it can help reduce bias associated with differences in healthcare-seeking behaviour [39,40]. We estimated an overall VE of 42.3% (95% CrI = 11.1–62.5), indicating moderate protection against circulating strains, which is consistent with the findings from previous research [41–44]. Because Ili Kazakh Autonomous Prefecture experiences frequent tourism activities and substantial population movement, the assessment framework and VE estimates derived from this study may serve as a reference for formulating vaccination strategies in tourism-oriented regions with similarly high population mobility.We found that subtype-specific VE was highest against influenza A(H1N1), at 45.1% (95% CrI = 13.8–65.0). This estimate is consistent with findings from our previous research and a similar study conducted in Chongqing [45,46]. The estimated VE against influenza B/Victoria of 38.3% (95% CrI = −15.7, 67.1) is lower compared to the estimates reported in studies from other regions [47–49] and our previous study in Ili, conducted in 2023–2024, where we observed a VE of 51.2% (95% CrI = 28.7–83.0) [32]. The small number of influenza B cases in our analysis (n = 20), however, may have reduced the precision of the estimate, while limited seasonal circulation may have reduced the representativeness of the cases. A potential antigenic mismatch between the circulating and vaccine strains may have also weakened vaccine-induced cross-neutralisation and contributed to the lower estimate.We observed distinct age-stratified VE patterns, where participants aged 6 months to 6 years had the lowest VE estimate, at 37.5% (95% CrI = −0.5, 61.1), while those aged 60 years or older had the highest adjusted VE estimate, at 42.1% (95% CrI = 7.8–63.7). This age-specific pattern differs from findings reported in several international studies. Studies from the USA and UK reported lower or statistically nonsignificant VE among older adults [43,50], whereas studies from Germany and the USA reported greater protection in younger populations [51,52]. Differences in healthcare-seeking behaviour may explain these findings.Children are more likely to seek medical care even for mild symptoms, which may produce an excess of non-influenza cases among the test-negative controls and may dilute the VE estimate. Older adults usually seek medical care only when they experience more severe illness [53,54]. This behaviour may make test-negative controls more comparable to influenza cases in healthcare-seeking and disease severity, potentially reducing this source of selection bias; a higher case proportion alone, however, does not ensure a more accurate VE estimate. Additionally, older adults may also receive additional protection through immunological memory [55]. However, we could not distinguish the relative contributions of healthcare-seeking bias and immunological mechanisms. Future research should validate these findings by using community-based cohorts or active surveillance data.Influenza surveillance is critical for understanding viral epidemiology and determining the composition of seasonal vaccines [56]. For this reason, we used molecular evolutionary analysis to obtain additional virological context for our findings. We sequenced the HA and NA genes from six influenza-positive specimens as part of influenza surveillance and conducted a phylogenetic analysis with 170 representative GISAID sequences [57,58]. The circulating A(H1N1) strains clustered closely with the vaccine reference strain A/California/07/2009. GISAID lists this isolate as type ‘A/H1N1’ and lineage ‘pdm09’ (EPI_ISL_203615). We identified four nonsynonymous HA mutations, but only Q170K mapped to one of the known major antigenic sites (Sa, Sb, Ca, and Cb) [59]. None of the identified NA mutations affected the conserved enzymatic active site. The high conservation in key antigenic regions corresponded with the observed VE of 45.1% against A(H1N1) and was consistent with reports of a good vaccine–strain match [60]. Nonetheless, ongoing viral evolution remains a concern because enhanced transmissibility or immune escape may undermine vaccine-induced immunity. These risks support the need for continued molecular monitoring [61].We also examined social contact patterns among outpatients to understand their role in influenza transmission. Social contact studies commonly use paper diaries, online surveys, and wearable proximity-sensing technologies to record contact duration, frequency, and context of contacts, including their time and location – data which researchers use to construct contact matrices for modelling mixing patterns [62,63]. Most studies have examined the determinants and seasonal variations in social mixing, with few comparing contact intensity according to laboratory-confirmed infection status within healthcare-seeking populations [64]. Such comparisons may provide evidence about the behavioural characteristics of infected individuals and their potential role in transmission chains, with important implications for public health. We addressed this gap by comparing social contact patterns among outpatients with different influenza test results and analysing age-specific contact intensity according to infection status. Influenza-positive participants tended to report more frequent and longer contact durations than influenza-negative participants; this pattern was observed across the overall outpatient population and was most evident among children aged 0–10 years. These findings suggest that contact behaviour may be associated with influenza test status among outpatients with ILI.We conducted age-stratified analyses among outpatients and found that influenza-positive children aged 0–5 years had the highest contact intensity. This finding is consistent with those of community-based studies in Suzhou, China, Norway, France, and other countries [65–67]. The observed pattern paralleled the proposed role of children as primary drivers of transmission in community settings. Children’s immature immune systems may result in higher viral loads and longer periods of viral shedding after infection. They also frequently participate in social activities in daycare centres, schools, and family settings and may have less developed hygiene practices, including cough etiquette and hand cleaning. These factors may facilitate influenza transmission during close contact.Participants aged over than 65 years or older had higher contact intensity than younger adults, regardless of their influenza test status. This finding is consistent with that of a recent study conducted in Korea [24]. Older adults in our outpatient population may participate more frequently in group social activities at community centres and senior universities or through square dancing. They may also care for grandchildren and consequently have multiple daily close contacts with children at home and in public places each day. In addition, their daily routines may also depend heavily on densely populated areas because online alternatives are unavailable.We constructed contact matrices using data collected through influenza surveillance to characterise contact patterns among outpatients. We observed strong assortative mixing, which was most pronounced among school-aged children and least evident among older adults [27]. We also observed intergenerational mixing within households [68]. While these patterns can help characterise contacts among symptomatic individuals, the design of our study limits us from ascertaining their generalisability to the community at large.
