full_text_sections.conclusion: CONCLUSIONSWe found through an integrated analysis that influenza vaccination provided moderate real-world protection against medically attended influenza during the 2024–2025 influenza season in Ili, a border region of Xinjiang. Higher frequency of self-reported contacts and longer contact duration were associated with influenza test positivity, especially among children and older adults. Local authorities could consider prioritising vaccination for these age groups, strengthening non-pharmaceutical interventions, including ventilation, mask use, and reducing gatherings in schools, nursing homes, and households. Linking vaccination records with electronic health records could also help strengthen VE surveillance. Public health authorities in border areas with limited resources could consider combining vaccination with targeted behavioural measures to reduce outpatient influenza burden. School-based campaigns for children and community outreach for older adults may provide complementary layers of protection. Future studies should use community-based cohorts, measure contacts objectively using wearable devices, conduct viral sequencing on larger samples, and explicitly assess whether contact levels modify VE.
full_text_sections.other: Outcome variableWe defined the influenza test result as a dichotomous variable, categorised as positive or negative based on RT-PCR analysis of nasopharyngeal swab specimens. We performed testing using the Zhuocheng Huisheng Influenza A/B Duplex real-time PCR detection kit (Beijing Zhuocheng Huisheng Bioscience Co., Ltd., Beijing, China). This kit used specific primers and fluorescent probes targeting influenza A and B viruses and included an internal control that monitors the entire process from nucleic acid extraction to amplification, thereby reducing the risk of false-negative results. Exposure variablesWe defined influenza vaccination status as the primary exposure variable based on data reported by the participants or their guardians. We classified participants as vaccinated if they had received at least one dose of a seasonal influenza vaccine, including egg-based, cell-based, trivalent, and quadrivalent vaccines, within the past 24 months, with the most recent dose being administered at least 14 days before symptom onset. We classified participants who did not meet these criteria as unvaccinated.We defined social contact pattern as the secondary exposure variable and characterised it by contact frequency and duration according to the POLYMOD study criteria [22]. We defined conversational contact as a face-to-face conversation with an exchange of at least three words, and physical contact as any skin-to-skin interaction, such as handshaking, hugging, or kissing. CovariatesWe collected potential confounders using structured questionnaires (Text S1 in the Online Supplementary Document), including demographic characteristics such as age, sex, and ethnicity; clinical and behavioural characteristics, such as baseline health conditions, health-related behaviours, and daily habits; and temporal variables, such as the dates of symptom onset and visit dates. We grouped age for further analysis and used symptom onset and visit dates to derive the epidemiological week for adjustment for long-term and seasonal trends. Viral sequencing sample selection and reference sequencesThe national Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) influenza surveillance protocol requires sentinel hospitals to perform viral genetic sequencing on a subset of influenza-positive samples during routine surveillance to monitor genetic variation among circulating strains, rather than sequencing all positive samples [33]. We selected 6 out of 121 influenza-positive samples for exploratory sequencing in accordance with this protocol.We retrieved global influenza A(H1N1) reference sequences from the Global Initiative on Sharing All Influenza Data (GISAID) database [34]. We selected 170 sequences containing both haemagglutinin (HA) and neuraminidase (NA) gene segments and combined them with six viral isolates obtained in this study. Statistical analysisWe used a Bayesian logistic regression model adjusted for covariates to estimate VE. We specified an informative prior for the vaccination coefficient, centred on a VE of 40% based on historical CDC estimates [35]. We calculated VE for laboratory-confirmed influenza as (1 − odds ratio) × 100% and expressed uncertainty in the model coefficients using 95% credible intervals (CrIs) derived from the posterior distribution.We performed targeted sequencing of 6 virus isolates from influenza-positive participants and conducted phylogenetic analysis together with 170 reference sequences retrieved from GISAID. We aligned the sequences using ClustalW in Molecular Evolutionary Genetics Analysis, version 12 [36] and assessed alignment quality using ESPript [37]. We constructed a maximum-likelihood phylogenetic tree using IQ-TREE [38]. We then compared sequences within a specific monophyletic clade to identify variable sites and non-synonymous mutations (Text S3 in the Online Supplementary Document).We performed age standardisation according to the 2020 China Population Census. We used linear regression to quantify age-specific differences in contact frequency and duration (β) between influenza test-positive and test-negative participants. We smoothed the contact matrices using Gaussian kernel density estimation. We used stratified χ2 tests to compare the distributions of contact setting, frequency, and duration between the groups. We used a Bayesian negative binomial regression model to assess the effects of demographic characteristics and contact setting and evaluated model robustness against a gamma model (Text S4 in the Online Supplementary Document).We conducted subgroup analyses for VE by age group (6 months to 6 years, 7–17 years, 18–59 years, and ≥60 years) and influenza subtype (A(H1), A(H3), and B/Victoria). We performed similar analyses for social contacts by age groups (0–5 years, 6–15 years, 16–65 years, and >65 years) based on immune status, social behaviours, and health risks, with further stratification by sex (male and female), household size (small, ≤3 persons; medium, 4 persons; large, ≥5 persons), and contact setting (home, school, workplace, leisure, and other) (Text S4 in the Online Supplementary Document).We also conducted sensitivity analyses to evaluate the robustness of the VE estimates and social contact analyses (Text S5 in the Online Supplementary Document). For the VE analysis, we assessed the effects of including infants younger than six months, treating age and body mass index as continuous variables, and adjusting for the symptom onset date. For the social contact analysis, we restricted the sample to unvaccinated participants to reduce potential confounding by vaccination status.We performed all statistical analyses and phylogenetic tree visualisations using R, version 4.3.2 (R Core Team, Vienna, Austria), with the ‘EBImage’, ‘seqinr’, ‘ape’, ‘phytools’, ‘ggplot2’, ‘treeio’, and ‘ggtree’ packages. analysis.methods: We estimated VE using logistic regression with covariate adjustment, and we collected nasal or nasopharyngeal specimens for influenza testing using real-time reverse transcription-polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR). We also administered a structured questionnaire to collect demographic information, vaccination history, and social contact patterns. We truncated the number of reported daily contact counts above 30 at 30 in the contact analysis to reduce the influence of outliers.
analysis.main_results: Among influenza-positive participants, 5 of 121 (4.1%) had been vaccinated, compared with 51 of 786 influenza-negative participants (6.5%). The vaccine effectiveness (VE) against any influenza was 42.3% (95% CrI = 11.1–62.5).
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpreted the findings as indicating that vaccine effectiveness varied by age group and virus type, with notable differences in effectiveness against influenza A and B.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings can inform public health strategies for influenza vaccination and surveillance, particularly in understanding the effectiveness of vaccines against different virus lineages and age groups.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study was limited by the use of a test-negative design, which may introduce bias, and the exclusion of infants younger than 6 months. The evidence is moderate in strength due to these limitations.

analysis.summary_en: This study evaluated influenza vaccine effectiveness (VE) and contact patterns among outpatients with influenza-like illness (ILI) in China during the 2024–2025 season. The research aimed to understand how vaccination influences infection risk and how contact behaviors correlate with transmission. A test-negative case-control study was conducted at three sentinel hospitals in Ili Kazakh Autonomous Prefecture, involving 928 participants. Influenza testing was performed using real-time RT-PCR, and social contact data were collected via structured questionnaires. The results showed that 4.1% of influenza-positive participants were vaccinated, compared to 6.5% of influenza-negative participants. The overall VE against any influenza was 42.3% (95% CrI = 11.1–62.5). The study found variations in VE by age group and virus type, with notable effectiveness against influenza A and B. The findings suggest that vaccine effectiveness is influenced by factors such as age and virus lineage, which could inform targeted vaccination strategies. However, the study had limitations, including potential bias from the test-negative design and the exclusion of infants under 6 months, which may affect the generalisability of the results. The evidence is considered moderate in strength due to these constraints.

title_zh: 2024–2025流感季中国流感样病例门诊患者中疫苗疫苗保护效果及接触模式研究:一项测试阴性病例对照研究
source_body_en: We aimed to assess influenza VE among healthcare-seeking outpatients with influenza-like illness (ILI) and to examine the contact patterns associated with infection risk.MethodsWe enrolled 928 outpatients with ILI from three sentinel hospitals in Ili Kazakh Autonomous Prefecture, China, between December 2024 and March 2025 in a test-negative case-control study. Exploratory sequencing of six samples suggested no major antigenic mismatch with the vaccine strains, but the very small number of sequenced samples limits the generalisability of this finding.ConclusionsInfluenza vaccination provided moderate protection against medically attended influenza, while contact patterns were associated with infection risk among children and older adults. Combined vaccination and behavioural interventions warrant further evaluation, as the observational design of this study and its use of self-reporting data limit causal inference.Keywords : influenza, influenza vaccination, vaccine effectiveness, test-negative design, contact patterns, China METHODSSetting and study designWe conducted a multicentre test-negative case-control study from 8 December 2024 (epidemiological week 50) to 30 March 2025 (epidemiological week 13) among outpatients with influenza-like illness (ILI) from three sentinel hospitals in Yining and Horgos, Ili Kazakh Autonomous Prefecture, China. AbstractBackgroundContinuous monitoring of both influenza vaccine protection and behavioural determinants of infection is important for understanding related risks. Evidence on influenza vaccine effectiveness (VE) in China during the 2024–2025 season, however, remains limited. abstract_zh: 我们旨在评估寻求医疗帮助的流感样病例(ILI)患者中流感疫苗的有效性(VE),并探讨与感染风险相关的接触模式。方法我们在中国伊犁哈萨克自治州的三家哨点医院中,于2024年12月至2025年3月期间招募了928名ILI门诊患者,进行了一项测试阴性病例对照研究。对六份样本进行探索性测序显示,未发现与疫苗毒株存在显著抗原差异,但样本数量非常有限,因此这一发现的普遍适用性受到限制。结论疫苗接种疫苗对门诊流感提供了中等程度的保护,而接触模式与儿童和老年人的感染风险相关。结合疫苗接种疫苗和行为干预措施值得进一步评估,由于本研究的观察性设计及其使用自我报告数据,限制了因果推论的得出。关键词:流感,疫苗接种疫苗,疫苗疫苗有效性,测试阴性设计,接触模式,中国 方法:研究地点和设计我们在中国伊犁哈萨克自治州的伊宁和霍尔果斯三家哨点医院中,于2024年12月8日(流行病学第50周)至2025年3月30日(流行病学第13周)期间开展了一项多中心测试阴性病例对照研究。摘要背景持续监测流感疫苗疫苗的保护效果以及影响感染的行为因素,对于理解相关风险至关重要。然而,目前关于2024–2025流感季中国疫苗疫苗有效性(VE)的证据仍然有限。我们通过逆转录聚合酶链反应(RT-PCR)确认了流感感染,并收集了疫苗接种疫苗接种史和社会接触频率等信息。

title: From molecular evolution to the school health room: the role of community-based public health nurses (helsesykepleiere) in one health communication on cross-species influenza transmission in Norway

source_records.title: From molecular evolution to the school health room: the role of community-based public health nurses (helsesykepleiere) in one health communication on cross-species influenza transmission in Norway

full_text: AbstractHighly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) A(H5N1) clade 2.3.4.4b viruses have undergone an unprecedented expansion of host range since 2021, moving from wild birds and poultry into dairy cattle, domestic cats, and other mammals, with sporadic human infections in Europe and North America (Food and Agriculture Organization et al., 2025a; Rolfes et al., 2025). This expansion is underpinned by well-characterised molecular mechanisms of influenza A virus evolution — antigenic drift, gene segment reassortment, and receptor-binding adaptation — that shape the frequency and direction of cross-species spillover (McDonald et al., 2016; Steel and Lowen, 2017; Man et al., 2026). Norwegian wild-bird and mammalian surveillance data document recurrent incursions of clade 2.3.4.4b viruses, and international risk assessments continue to describe low, but non-zero, human risk concentrated among individuals with close animal contact (World Health Organization, 2025–2026; Ytrehus et al; European Food Safety Authority et al., 2025a). Translating this fast-moving virological and epidemiological evidence into everyday protective behavior for children, adolescents, and families remains an underdeveloped link in pandemic preparedness, compounded by documented gaps in adolescent One Health literacy (Zucca et al., 2021). This mini review synthesizes current literature on the molecular basis of influenza cross-species transmission, the Norwegian epidemiological and One Health governance context, and established child- and family-oriented risk-communication frameworks, to argue that Norway’s community-based public health nurses (helsesykepleiere) — who deliver near-universal, statutorily mandated contact with children and families through the helsestasjon- and skolehelsetjeneste — occupy a distinctive but underused position as One Health communication nodes (Helsedirektoratet, 2021). I outline a practical three-tier framework for translating zoonotic-influenza science into age-appropriate household guidance, critically appraise the feasibility, workload, training, and governance implications of this role, and identify priority gaps for future empirical and implementation research.Keywords: avian influenza, cross-species transmission, H5N1, health literacy, helsesykepleier, nordic public health, one health, pandemic preparedness Supplementary materialThe Supplementary Material for this article can be found online at: https://www.frontiersin.org/articles/10.3389/fcimb.2026.1965045/full#supplementary-material Supplementary Materials 9.ConclusionThe molecular mechanisms driving the expanding host range of HPAI A(H5N1) clade 2.3.4.4b are the subject of continuous, increasingly granular scientific characterization, and Norwegian wildlife and veterinary surveillance is generating an increasingly detailed picture of local risk. What remains comparatively underdeveloped is the corresponding public-facing translation infrastructure connecting this evolving evidence base to the households where behavior actually changes. Norway’s helsesykepleiere, by virtue of their statutory mandate and near-universal, longitudinal reach into families with children, constitute an existing but underused resource for this translation task — one consistent with, and potentially strengthening, Norway’s own stated One Health governance ambitions (Norwegian Ministry of Health and Care Services; BeReady4Pandemics, 2025). Realizing this potential will require deliberate interdisciplinary collaboration between infection-prevention and virology research groups and the school health service, together with the evaluation research needed to ensure that any resulting communication genuinely improves family-level understanding and protective behavior, rather than simply adding to an already crowded preventive-health agenda. Realizing this potential is conditional on the workload, training, and governance safeguards above being resourced, not assumed cost-free. 1.IntroductionInfluenza A viruses remain among the most consequential zoonotic pathogens of the past century, with all major human pandemics traced to animal reservoirs, most often through reassortment of segmented viral genomes in avian or swine intermediate hosts (de Silva et al., 2012; Steel and Lowen, 2017). Since 2021, however, the epidemiology of highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) A(H5N1) clade 2.3.4.4b has departed markedly from this historical pattern. Rather than remaining largely confined to wild birds and commercial poultry, clade 2.3.4.4b viruses have spread into an unprecedented range of mammalian species, including foxes, seals, mink, domestic cats, and, since March 2024, dairy cattle in the United States (Food and Agriculture Organization et al., 2025a; Kamel et al., 2025). Sporadic human infections have followed this mammalian expansion, and while sustained human-to-human transmission has not been documented, international risk assessments describe a dynamic and evolving situation that warrants continued vigilance (World Health Organization, 2025–2026; Rolfes et al., 2025).This shift has practical consequences that extend well beyond veterinary and occupational medicine. Families that keep backyard poultry, own cats fed raw-food diets, or live near wild-bird habitats are now plausibly exposed populations, not merely bystanders to a distant agricultural problem (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, 2025a; Vaughan et al., 2026). Yet the substantial and rapidly evolving virological literature on cross-species transmission mechanisms is rarely translated into a form that reaches children, adolescents, and parents at the point where behavior change actually occurs — in the home, the farmyard, or the veterinary clinic waiting room. In Norway, one existing but underused channel for this translation is the corps of community-based public health nurses (helsesykepleiere), who deliver statutorily mandated, near-universal contact with children and families through the child and youth health centers and school health service (Helsedirektoratet, 2021). This mini review synthesizes current literature on (i) the molecular mechanisms underlying influenza A virus cross-species transmission, (ii) the global and Norwegian epidemiological landscape, (iii) Norwegian One Health governance and pandemic-preparedness structures, and (iv) established risk-communication and health-literacy frameworks for children and families, in order to outline a practical framework through which public health nurses can function as One Health communication nodes.Evidence for this mini review was identified through structured searches of PubMed/MEDLINE, Web of Science, and Google Scholar for English-language literature published between January 2020 and August 2026, using combinations of the terms ‘H5N1’, ‘avian influenza’, ‘clade 2.3.4.4b’, ‘cross-species transmission’, ‘reassortment’, ‘One Health’, ‘risk communication’, ‘health literacy’, ‘helsesykepleier’, and ‘public health nursing’, supplemented by hand-searched reference lists and direct searches of institutional sources (FHI, Norwegian Veterinary Institute, Mattilsynet, WHO, EFSA, and CDC) for current risk assessments and guidance. Given the breadth of the topic and the mini review format, this is a narrative rather than a systematic review, and no formal quality-appraisal tool was applied. The specific search strings and retrieval steps are documented in Supplementary Search Record S1. 2.Molecular evolution and mechanisms of cross-species transmissionInfluenza A viruses possess a genome of eight discrete, single-stranded, negative-sense RNA segments, a structural feature that permits two distinct evolutionary pathways (McDonald et al., 2016). The first, antigenic drift, results from the gradual accumulation of point mutations introduced by the error-prone viral RNA polymerase during replication. The second, and epidemiologically more consequential for cross-species jumps, is reassortment: when two distinct influenza A viruses co-infect the same host cell, progeny virions can package a novel combination of the eight parental segments, generating genetically — and potentially phenotypically — distinct viruses in a single replication cycle (Steel and Lowen, 2017; Selective genome packaging mechanisms of influenza A viruses, 2021). Reassortment between avian, swine, and human lineages produced the reassortant strains responsible for the 1957, 1968, and 2009 pandemics, historically via swine acting as a permissive co-infection host, or ‘mixing vessel’ (de Silva et al., 2012).A second determinant of host range is the receptor-binding specificity of the viral hemagglutinin protein. Avian-adapted viruses preferentially bind α2,3-linked sialic acid receptors predominant in the avian gut and respiratory tract, whereas mammalian-adapted viruses, including human seasonal strains, preferentially bind α2,6-linked receptors characteristic of the upper mammalian respiratory tract. Single amino acid substitutions in the hemagglutinin receptor-binding site, together with adaptive changes in the viral polymerase complex, can shift this binding preference and materially increase a virus’s capacity to infect and transmit within a new mammalian host (Man et al., 2026). Among these changes, PB2 substitutions such as E627K and D701N improve polymerase activity at mammalian upper-respiratory-tract temperatures and are recurrently detected in mammalian-adapted clade 2.3.4.4b genotypes, making them closely watched risk markers. Recent genotypes circulating in North American dairy cattle and companion animals, including B3.13 and D1.1, carry constellations of such adaptive markers, and ongoing genomic surveillance by joint WHO/FAO/WOAH assessment continues to track their evolution for signals of increased mammalian or human transmissibility (Food and Agriculture Organization et al., 2025a; Man et al., 2026). Because most reassortant or drift-variant genotypes carry fitness costs that limit onward spread, only a minority of spillover events establish sustained transmission chains in a new host — but the frequency of coinfection opportunities, and hence the statistical opportunity for a high-fitness variant to emerge, rises directly with the scale of the current panzootic. This technical surveillance information, while central to expert risk assessment, is rarely rendered in a form accessible to non-specialist audiences, a gap addressed later in this review.These molecular determinants of host range and transmissibility are not simply of virological interest. Because receptor-binding adaptation, polymerase mutation, and reassortment are the specific mechanisms that determine whether a spillover event remains a dead-end infection or acquires the capacity for onward transmission, they define the biological rationale for the tiered, exposure-specific communication framework proposed in Section 7: household guidance calibrated to the animal-contact pathways — raw feeding, wild-bird contact, dairy exposure — most likely to provide the coinfection or exposure opportunities described above. Framing the practical framework in these molecular terms is intended to keep the proposed nursing role anchored to virological evidence rather than to a generic exhortation to be alert to ‘bird flu’. 3.Current epidemiological landscape: global panzootic and the Norwegian contextSince its emergence in Europe in 2020–2021, clade 2.3.4.4b has become globally dominant, spreading across Europe, Africa, the Americas, and, more recently, Antarctica, with unprecedented mortality events in wild bird and marine mammal populations (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, 2025b; Kamel et al., 2025). The detection of the virus in United States dairy cattle in March 2024 marked a further expansion: as of mid-2025, outbreaks had been confirmed in more than 1,000 herds across multiple states, with clinical signs in cattle including decreased milk yield, abnormal milk consistency, and reduced feed intake (Food and Agriculture Organization et al., 2025a; Morel et al., 2026). Between March 2024 and May 2025, a total of approximately 70 human cases of HPAI A(H5) infection were reported in the United States: 41 following exposure to infected dairy cattle, 24 to commercial poultry, two to backyard poultry flocks, and three with undetermined exposure (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, 2025c). Most infections presented as mild conjunctivitis, occasionally accompanied by fever or respiratory symptoms; a minority required hospitalization, and one death occurred in a person with underlying health conditions exposed to a backyard flock and wild birds (Rolfes et al., 2025). A first pediatric case with an undetermined exposure source was identified in California in late 2024 (Zhu et al., 2025).Companion animals have emerged as an additional and household-relevant transmission pathway. Domestic cats appear highly susceptible to severe, often fatal, disease, typically following consumption of raw milk, raw pet food, or contact with infected wild birds; a global review identified more than 600 documented feline infections across 12 species and 18 countries since the emergence of clade 2.3.4.4b (CIDRAP, 2025; Sykes, 2025). In late 2024, a cluster investigation in Los Angeles County identified serologic evidence consistent with possible virus transmission from an infected domestic cat to a veterinary professional — one of 25 serosurveyed contacts among 139 potentially exposed persons, with no virus isolated from the human case — providing what may be the first, if unconfirmed, instance of cat-to-human zoonotic transmission for this clade (Vaughan et al., 2026). To date, no sustained human-to-human transmission of clade 2.3.4.4b viruses has been documented anywhere, and joint WHO/FAO/WOAH and European risk assessments continue to classify general population risk as low, with elevated risk restricted to those with direct occupational or household exposure to infected animals (World Health Organization, 2025–2026; European Commission / EFSA).Within this global picture, Norway has not been spared. Norwegian Veterinary Institute wild-bird and mammalian surveillance programs document recurrent clade 2.3.4.4b detections, including spillover into Norwegian foxes and seals, consistent with broader European surveillance trends reported by the European Food Safety Authority and European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (Ytrehus et al; European Food Safety Authority et al., 2025a). As elsewhere, the general population risk in Norway is assessed as low, with the principal exposure pathway concentrated among individuals with occupational or hobbyist contact with wild birds, backyard poultry, or other domestic animals (Food and Agriculture Organization et al., 2025a) — a demographic that includes a meaningful proportion of Norwegian households with children, particularly in rural and peri-urban districts. 4.One health governance and pandemic preparedness in NorwayNorway has formally embedded One Health principles — the recognition that human, animal, and environmental health are interdependent — into its national approach to zoonotic disease and pandemic preparedness. The Norwegian Institute of Public Health identifies zoonotic influenza explicitly as a priority One Health working area, alongside food safety and antimicrobial resistance, and coordinates closely with the Norwegian Veterinary Institute and Norwegian Food Safety Authority on surveillance and risk communication (Norwegian Institute of Public Health (FHI), 2020). This institutional commitment is further reflected in Norway’s National One Health Strategy against Antimicrobial Resistance 2024–2033, which establishes cross-sectoral governance mechanisms that could, in principle, extend to influenza preparedness (Norwegian Ministry of Health and Care Services), and in an independent country-profile assessment noting that Norway has integrated One Health principles into its broader pandemic preparedness and response framework through interdisciplinary task forces and improved cross-sector data sharing (BeReady4Pandemics, 2025).Notably, however, these governance frameworks are articulated predominantly at the level of surveillance coordination and inter-agency data sharing among human, animal, and environmental health authorities. None of the reviewed strategy or preparedness documents specify a defined role for frontline, community-based health personnel in the direct translation of One Health surveillance findings into household-level guidance. This represents an implementation gap between governance-level One Health ambition and the last-mile communication needed to change everyday behavior — a gap this review argues the helsesykepleier workforce is structurally well placed to help close. 5.The helsesykepleier as a one health communication nodeHelsesykepleiere are specialist public health nurses operating within Norway’s statutorily mandated child health and school health services (helsestasjons- og skolehelsetjenesten), providing near-universal, longitudinal contact with children and families from infancy through upper secondary school, encompassing routine health checks, vaccination programs, and structured health guidance for parents and, later, directly for adolescents (Helsedirektoratet, 2021). This combination of near-total population reach, repeated contact over many years, and an existing mandate for preventive health counselling distinguishes the helsesykepleier role from generic public health messaging: unlike a one-off media campaign, the relationship is relational and cumulative, allowing guidance to be tailored to a given family’s actual animal exposures — for example, backyard poultry keeping, pet ownership, or proximity to wild-bird habitats — rather than delivered as an undifferentiated general warning.This structural advantage is particularly relevant given documented deficits in existing zoonotic-disease literacy…

analysis.summary_en: This study explores the role of community-based public health nurses in Norway in translating virological and epidemiological evidence of cross-species influenza transmission into public health communication for children and families. It highlights the importance of reassortment in generating new influenza variants and the need for interdisciplinary collaboration to improve risk communication. The findings suggest that these nurses could be pivotal in bridging the gap between expert surveillance data and public understanding, enhancing pandemic preparedness. However, the study is limited to a review of existing literature and surveillance data, which provides moderate evidence for its conclusions.

elements_zh.research_question_and_background: 该研究旨在解决将跨物种流感 传播 的病毒学和流行病学证据转化为针对儿童、青少年和家庭的可行的公共卫生沟通方面的差距,特别是在挪威的“同一个健康”框架的背景下。
elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 该研究是一篇小型综述,分析了 季节性流感 病毒的分子 进化、挪威流行病学和 One Health 治理背景以及风险沟通框架,重点关注通过 helsestasjon 和 skolehelsetjeneste 与儿童和家庭互动的社区公共卫生护士 (helsesykepleiere)。
elements_zh.methods: 这些方法包括综合有关 宿主 范围和传播性的分子决定因素的现有文献,回顾挪威流行病学数据,并检查已建立的面向儿童和家庭的风险沟通框架,以评估公共卫生护士在 One Health 沟通中的潜在作用。
elements_zh.main_results: 最近在北美奶牛和伴侣动物中流行的基因型(包括 B3.13 和 D1.1)携带一系列适应性标记。挪威兽医研究所 监测 计划记录了反复出现的分支 2.3.4.4b 检测,包括挪威狐狸和海豹中的 跨物种溢出。
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 作者解释说,重配是两种不同的甲型流感病毒共同感染同一个 宿主 细胞并产生遗传上不同的病毒的过程,在流行病学上对跨物种跳跃具有重要影响。这凸显了跨学科合作的必要性,以改善 监测 研究结果的交流。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 研究结果表明,挪威社区公共卫生护士可以在将复杂的病毒学数据转化为家庭可获得的、可操作的指导方面发挥关键作用,从而改善大流行的防备和公共卫生结果。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 该研究基于对现有文献和 监测 数据的回顾,这可能会限制分析的深度。证据是温和的,因为它依赖于记录的趋势和专家评估,而不是原始的经验数据。

source_records.title: A comprehensive high-throughput detection strategy: an indirect ELISA for serodetection of the novel aMPV/C in ducks

full_text: AbstractIntroductionAvian metapneumovirus subtype C (aMPV/C), a re-emerging and widespread epidemic in China, causes hydrosalpinx fluid syndrome (HFS) in laying ducks, resulting in significant economic losses to the poultry industry. In the absence of any licensed vaccines or antiviral drugs for aMPV/C, accurate diagnosis and timely eradication of the infected ducks remain the primary control measures, underscoring the urgent need for reliable and effective detection methods.MethodsIn this study, the purified whole novel aMPV/C was used to develop an indirect enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (iELISA) for the detection of aMPV/C antibodies in ducks.ResultsThe cut-off value of the iELISA was determined to be 0.258. No cross-reactivity was observed with duck sera positive for antibodies against H5 AIV, NDV, DTMUV, BTV, DHAV-3, DPV, EDSV, MDPV, or GPV, demonstrating good specificity. Both intra-assay and inter-assay coefficients of variation were less than 10%, and the detection sensitivity of the iELISA reached a serum dilution of 1:102400. A total of 216 clinical serum samples from three duck breeds were tested via the established iELISA, of which 129 (59.7%) were positive. The concordance rate between the iELISA and an indirect immunofluorescence assay (IFA) was 100% (53/53).ConclusionOverall, this cost-effective iELISA provides a reliable tool for the detection of aMPV/C antibodies in clinical diagnostics and epidemiological surveillance.Keywords: avian metapneumovirus subtype C, novel, ducks, indirect ELISA, serological detection Materials and methodsVirus purificationThe aMPV/C isolate (aMPV-FJ21, 106.56 TCID50/mL) maintained in our laboratory was used in this study (Fu et al., 2025). Vero cells were inoculated with the virus, maintained in serum-free medium, and harvested at 96 h post-infection (hpi), followed by storage at −70 °C. The harvested cells were subjected to three cycles of freezing and thawing. The virus was then inactivated with 0.1% formaldehyde at 37 °C overnight. For antigen purification, 300 mL of inactivated suspension was clarified by centrifugation at 10000 × g for 15 min at 4 °C to remove cellular debris. Subsequently, the virus suspension was pelleted by ultracentrifugation at 45000 × g for 5 h. The resulting pellet was resuspended in 1 mL of 0.01 M phosphate-buffered saline (PBS, pH7.4) and used as the coating antigen for ELISA development. Meanwhile, the purified virus was examined using a transmission electron microscope (TEM, H-7500, Hitachi, Japan). And its protein concentration was determined using the enhanced BCA protein assay kit (Beyotime Biotechnology China, Fuzhou, China).Generation of polyclonal antibody against aMPV/CPurified aMPV-FJ21 strain, emulsified with an equal volume of Freund’s complete adjuvant (Sigma-Aldrich, Kenilworth, United States), was used as the immunogen for polyclonal antibody production. Sheldrake ducks were immunized with 1 mL immunogen via multiple subcutaneous injections in the dorsal region, with a negative control group included in parallel. Immunizations were administered at 2-week intervals for a total of four doses. The primary immunization used Freund’s complete adjuvant, whereas the three subsequent booster doses employed Freund’s incomplete adjuvant. Serum samples were collected 2 weeks after the final immunization for subsequent analysis.Establishment of the whole aMPV/C virus-based iELISACheckerboard titrationOptimal iELISA conditions were determined by checkerboard titration. Briefly, 96-well plates (Corning, New York, United States) were coated with 100 μL/well of purified aMPV-FJ21 at concentrations of 16, 8, 4, 2, 1 and 0.5 μg/mL in carbonate buffer (CBS, 0.05 M, pH 9.6) at 37 °C for 1 h. After three washes with PBS containing 0.05% (v/v) Tween 20 (PBST), plates were blocked with 10% skimmed milk in PBS at 37 °C for 2 h, followed by three additional washes. aMPV/C-positive and aMPV/C-negative duck sera, serially diluted from 1:100 to 1:3200 in PBS, were added (100 μL/well) and incubated at 37 °C for 1 h. Plates were washed, and 100 μL of horseradish peroxidase-conjugated goat anti-duck IgG antibody (1:10000, KPL, Maryland, United States) was added, followed by incubation at 37 °C for 1 h. After washing, 100 μL of TMB substrate (Solarbio, Beijing, China) was added and incubated at 37 °C for 10 min. The reaction was stopped with 50 μL/well of stop solution, and the optical density was measured at 450 nm (OD450nm) using an automatic ELISA reader (SpectraMax M3, Molecular Devices, USA). The optimal conditions were selected based on the highest positive-to-negative (P/N) ratio.Optimization of experimental parametersTo determine optimal coating conditions, different coating times (overnight at 4 °C; 1, 2 and 3 h at 37 °C) and coating solutions (normal saline, PBS, CBS, and ddH2O) were evaluated. The iELISA was then performed to optimize blocking times (60, 90, 120, and 150 min at 37 °C) and blocking solutions (1, 2% BSA, 5, 10% skimmed milk, and 10% FBS). Next, antibody–antigen reaction times, various incubation periods (30, 60, 90, and 120 min at 37 °C) and dilutions of the enzyme-labeled secondary antibody (1:2000, 1:4000, 1:5000, 1:8000, and 1:10000) were tested. Finally, TMB reaction times (5, 10, 15, 20, and 25 min at 37 °C) was evaluated to identify the optimal assay conditions.Determination of the cut-off valueTo determine the cut-off value for the iELISA, 57 serum samples from healthy ducks (negative for aMPV/C) were used. The cut-off was calculated based on the mean and standard deviation (SD) of the OD450nm values obtained from negative samples. It was defined as the mean OD450nm of the 57 negative sera plus 3SD, a threshold that theoretically provides >99% confidence that results from true negative samples fell below this value.Specificity and repeatabilityThe specificity of the iELISA was evaluated using positive sera against H5 avian influenza virus (H5 AIV, titer: 7log2), Newcastle disease virus (NDV, titer: 6log2), egg drop syndrome virus (EDSV, titer: 6log2), duck Tembusu virus (DTMUV, titer: 1:512), duck plague virus (DPV, titer: 1:640), Batai virus (BTV, titer: 1:256), Muscovy duck parvovirus (MDPV, titer: 1:512), goose parvovirus (GPV, titer: 1:640), and duck hepatitis A virus type 3 (DHAV-3, titer: 1:1024). Antibody titers against H5 AIV, NDV, and EDSV were assessed using hemagglutination inhibition (HI) assay, whereas titers against DTMUV, DPV, BTV, MDPV, GPV, and DHAV-3 were evaluated by iELISA. aMPV/C-positive and aMPV/C-negative sera were included as controls.To assess the repeatability of the iELISA, four aMPV/C-positive and four aMPV/C-negative sera were randomly selected and tested in triplicate on both the same batch and different batches of ELISA plates. full_text_sections.abstract: AbstractIntroductionAvian metapneumovirus subtype C (aMPV/C), a re-emerging and widespread epidemic in China, causes hydrosalpinx fluid syndrome (HFS) in laying ducks, resulting in significant economic losses to the poultry industry. In the absence of any licensed vaccines or antiviral drugs for aMPV/C, accurate diagnosis and timely eradication of the infected ducks remain the primary control measures, underscoring the urgent need for reliable and effective detection methods.MethodsIn this study, the purified whole novel aMPV/C was used to develop an indirect enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (iELISA) for the detection of aMPV/C antibodies in ducks.ResultsThe cut-off value of the iELISA was determined to be 0.258. No cross-reactivity was observed with duck sera positive for antibodies against H5 AIV, NDV, DTMUV, BTV, DHAV-3, DPV, EDSV, MDPV, or GPV, demonstrating good specificity. Both intra-assay and inter-assay coefficients of variation were less than 10%, and the detection sensitivity of the iELISA reached a serum dilution of 1:102400. A total of 216 clinical serum samples from three duck breeds were tested via the established iELISA, of which 129 (59.7%) were positive. The concordance rate between the iELISA and an indirect immunofluorescence assay (IFA) was 100% (53/53).ConclusionOverall, this cost-effective iELISA provides a reliable tool for the detection of aMPV/C antibodies in clinical diagnostics and epidemiological surveillance.Keywords: avian metapneumovirus subtype C, novel, ducks, indirect ELISA, serological detection
full_text_sections.methods: Materials and methodsVirus purificationThe aMPV/C isolate (aMPV-FJ21, 106.56 TCID50/mL) maintained in our laboratory was used in this study (Fu et al., 2025). full_text_sections.discussion: DiscussionSince Although aMPV subtype B has historically been the dominant lineage in Chinese poultry, the epidemiological landscape has shifted considerably since 2021, with aMPV/C now emerging as a significant pathogen in domestic duck populations (Fu et al., 2025; Xu et al., 2025; Yu et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2022). This epidemiological transition is particularly noteworthy given that aMPV/C was first detected in ducks in 2014 but remained largely unreported in waterfowl for nearly a decade, suggesting that the virus may have undergone adaptive changes that facilitated its spread and establishment in duck hosts (Sun et al., 2014). The recent identification of a novel aMPV/C lineage in Sheldrake ducks is especially concerning, as this variant appears to have acquired a distinct tropism for reproductive tissues, manifesting as hydrosalpinx fluid syndrome rather than the classical respiratory disease typically associated with aMPV infections (Fu et al., 2025; Yu et al., 2024). This clinical shift from respiratory to reproductive pathology may reflect ongoing viral evolution and adaptation to new host species, potentially involving changes in the viral attachment protein or other surface glycoproteins that determine cell tropism. Furthermore, the seasonal recurrence of this disease on affected farms, often correlated with annual climatic variations, complicates disease control efforts and underscores the urgent need for diagnostic tools that are both reliable and broadly applicable across different duck breeds and production systems (Fu et al., 2025; Sun et al., 2014).Historically, aMPV subtypes A, B, and C have predominantly circulated in chickens and turkeys worldwide (Cook, 2000; Salles et al., 2023; Wei et al., 2013). Consequently, numerous indirect ELISAs using various structural proteins (N, M, F, and G) as coating antigens have been developed for serological surveillance in these species (Chiang et al., 2000; Gulati et al., 2000; Gulati et al., 2001; Alvarez et al., 2004; Xu et al., 2021). However, no commercial ELISA kit is currently available for detecting aMPV antibodies in duck sera, particularly against subtype C. To address this diagnostic gap, we developed an iELISA using whole inactivated aMPV/C virions as the coating antigen. This approach offers distinct advantages over recombinant protein-based assays, which have been the standard for aMPV serology in chickens and turkeys. While recombinant proteins are widely adopted due to their ease of production and scalability, they often fail to present the full repertoire of conformational and linear epitopes present on native viral particles, and interference from components of the prokaryotic expression host (Escherichia coli), potentially compromising assay sensitivity and leading to false-negative results, especially in low-titer samples (Meireles et al., 2020; Xu et al., 2026). In contrast, whole-virion antigens preserve the native antigenic architecture, enabling more comprehensive detection across a broader range of antibody specificities and isotypes (Sumita et al., 2016). This feature is particularly valuable for detecting antibodies against emerging viral variants, as a single recombinant protein may not adequately capture the antigenic diversity of circulating strains. The aMPV-FJ21 strain used in this study achieved high titers in Vero cells, substantially exceeding previously reported levels at the same passage, thereby providing ample antigen for large-scale production while ensuring consistent quality (Sun et al., 2014; Yao et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2023). The use of a single master seed stock, combined with serum-free culture conditions and rigorous control of passage number and culture parameters, further ensured batch- to-batch consistency and minimized the risk of exogenous protein contamination that could otherwise compromise assay specificity.The analytical performance of the iELISA was robust and met the requirements for a practical diagnostic tool. No cross-reactivity was observed against sera positive for nine other major duck pathogens, including H5 AIV, NDV, EDSV, DTMUV, DPV, BTV, MDPV, GPV, and DHAV-3, demonstrating high specificity. This specificity is critical for accurate diagnosis in field settings where co-infections with multiple pathogens are common. The detection limit of 1:102400 indicates high sensitivity, making the assay suitable for detecting low-titer antibodies in field samples, particularly during the early stages of infection or in vaccinated flocks where antibody levels may be relatively low. This assay provides a practical tool for large-scale serological surveillance. The widespread seropositivity across duck breeds highlights the urgent need for vaccination strategies and routine monitoring to mitigate the impact of aMPV/C on China’s duck industry.
full_text_sections.other: IntroductionAvian metapneumovirus (aMPV) was first identified in South Africa in 1978 (Buys and Preez, 1980) and has since become a globally distributed pathogen, infecting both domestic poultry and wild avian species (Salles et al., 2023). The virus causes upper respiratory disease, typically characterized by sinusitis, head swelling, and decreased egg production (Clontz and Hoerr, 2026; De Graaf et al., 2009). In uncomplicated cases, mortality is generally low (2–5%); however, co-infections with secondary pathogens can elevate mortality to as high as 25%. Based on genetic and antigenic variability, aMPV is classified into four subtypes (A-D) (Juhasz and Easton, 1994; Bäyon-Auboyer et al., 2000; Rima et al., 2017). Subtypes A and B are distributed worldwide, with subtype B predominating in Europe and China (Franzo et al., 2020). Subtype C naturally infects turkeys, chickens, ducks, and wild birds, and its genome exhibits the highest homology with human metapneumovirus (Hatfield et al., 2026). Prior to 2025, aMPV/C was known to comprise two distinct lineages: the North American and the Eurasian lineages (Quan et al., 2020). Recently, our group identified a novel lineage circulating in Sheldrake ducks (Fu et al., 2025). In contrast, subtype D has only been reported in France (Umar et al., 2019). Notably, two novel and divergent aMPV strains were detected in North America in 2019, further highlighting the ongoing expansion of aMPV genetic diversity (Canuti et al., 2019; Retallack et al., 2019).In China, aMPV/C was first recorded in Muscovy ducks in 2014, with no subsequent isolations from waterfowl reported until 2021 (Sun et al., 2014). Since then, the virus has become increasingly prevalent nationwide, causing hydrosalpinx fluid syndrome (HFS) in laying ducks and respiratory disease in meat ducks (Yu et al., 2024; Xu et al., 2025; Fu et al., 2025). In 2025, we isolated a novel strain, designated aMPV-FJ21, from Sheldrake ducks exhibiting HFS (Fu et al., 2025). Molecular characterization revealed that this strain is genetically distinct from both the North American and Eurasian lineages, indicating ongoing genetic diversification and adaptive evolution of aMPV/C in China (Fu et al., 2025). These findings underscore the urgent need for effective control measures, particularly rapid and reliable diagnostic tools.Current diagnostic approaches for aMPV/C include pathogen isolation, molecular assays, and serological tests. Virus isolation is labor-intensive and time-consuming, and its recovery rate from clinical samples is notoriously low, reported as only 8% (2/25), rendering it impractical for routine clinical diagnosis (Kwon et al., 2010; Sun et al., 2014). Molecular methods, such as PCR, offer high specificity and sensitivity but require specialized equipment and skilled personnel (Shin et al., 2000). Moreover, their diagnostic utility is constrained by the short viremic window of aMPV/C, typically lasting only 2–10 days post-infection (Cook et al., 1993; Cook et al., 2001). Serological assays, including virus neutralization tests (VNT), IFA, and ELISA, are widely employed for antibody detection (Chiang et al., 2000). Among these, ELISA is particularly suitable for large-scale surveillance due to its high throughput, sensitivity, and specificity, and remains a cornerstone for monitoring infection pressure, assessing flock immunity, and guiding vaccination strategies (Saeed et al., 2026). However, to date, no commercial ELISA kit is available for the detection of aMPV/C antibodies in duck sera.To bridge this diagnostic gap, we developed an iELISA using a purified novel aMPV/C isolate as the coating antigen, specifically designed for the detection of aMPV/C antibodies in duck sera. full_text: Conventional respiratory vaccines protect through antigen-specific immunity, leaving broad gaps against antigenically diverse and emerging pathogens and inducing little protection at the airway surface itself. Trained immunity, the durable epigenetic and metabolic reprogramming of innate immune cells and their bone marrow progenitors, offers antigen-agnostic, heterologous protection and can be induced directly at the respiratory mucosa, providing a mechanistic rationale for a new class of prophylactic immunotherapies. Here we appraise this field from a clinical-translational, evidence-graded standpoint, integrating three interdependent axes. We first compare the principal inducer platforms (bacille Calmette-Guérin, β-glucan and other pattern-recognition-receptor ligands, inactivated polybacterial preparations, and viral vectors) together with the intranasal, sublingual, and inhaled routes through which they deposit innate memory, showing that platform and route jointly govern the quality, location, and durability of protection. We then grade the clinical evidence population by population, which forms a gradient rather than a uniform endorsement: strongest for sublingual MV130 in childhood recurrent wheeze, moderate for bacille Calmette-Guérin in older adults and for MV130 in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, and preliminary but promising in immunocompromised hosts. Throughout, we apply the protection-vs.-immunopathology balance as a critical lens, distinguishing host resistance from disease tolerance and highlighting the biomarkers and patient-selection strategies needed to steer benefit over harm. We conclude that trained immunity-based mucosal immunotherapy is best advanced not as a uniform promise but as a disciplined program aligning standardized interventions, mechanism-matched trial endpoints, and prospective biomarkers, positioning it as a credible complement to antigen-specific respiratory vaccines. 7ConclusionTrained immunity-based mucosal immunotherapy is best understood not as a single promise but as a framework of platform- and population-specific decisions. Three factors jointly determine its clinical value: the anatomical site where innate memory is deposited, the mode of protection an agent confers, and the balance between host defense and immunopathology. This framework has practical utility: it explains why delivery route and inducer shape outcomes, it structures the design of prophylaxis trials around mechanism-matched endpoints, it offers a rationale for predicting who will benefit, and it points toward optimizing therapy by matching a platform to a defined clinical goal rather than deploying trained immunity indiscriminately. Realizing this value requires overcoming interlocking challenges. Experimental models must better represent human airway biology and the durability of local training; data from heterogeneous trials and mechanistic studies need integration under harmonized definitions and evidence grading; new methods for non-invasive measurement of airway trained immunity must be adopted; and computational approaches, including machine learning applied to multi-omic signatures, could help resolve the heterogeneity of trained-immunity programs and identify predictive biomarkers of benefit vs. harm. Progress on these fronts feeds back into the framework itself. Standardized models and assays would sharpen the resistance-vs.-tolerance distinction and quantify durability; integrated data and biomarker-guided selection would convert population-specific signals into actionable clinical decisions; and each successful translation would in turn test, refine, and validate the conceptual framework, closing the loop between mechanism and medicine. Positioned this way, trained immunity-based mucosal immunotherapy offers a credible complement to antigen-specific vaccines against respiratory infections, provided its development proceeds as a disciplined program that advances standardized interventions, mechanism-matched endpoints, and prospective biomarkers together. 1IntroductionRespiratory infections remain among the heaviest infectious burdens on human health, causing millions of deaths each year and driving a large share of global antibiotic use (1). Licensed vaccines have sharply reduced severe disease for several respiratory pathogens, yet their protection is anchored to cognate antigens. This design leaves recurrent gaps: coverage narrows against antigenically variable or newly emerging pathogens, injectable formulations induce limited immunity at the airway surface, and no single antigen-specific product spans the diverse viral and bacterial causes of respiratory illness (2). A complementary strategy that protects broadly, and at the site of entry, would address a need that conventional vaccinology has not met.Trained immunity offers a mechanistic route to such breadth. Innate immune cells, long assumed to lack memory, can undergo functional reprogramming after an initial stimulus and respond more vigorously to unrelated secondary challenges (3). This adaptation is driven by epigenetic remodeling and metabolic rewiring of myeloid cells and their bone marrow progenitors, rather than by antigen-specific clonal expansion (4). Because the resulting protection is heterologous, it is well suited to settings where the offending pathogen is unknown, mutates rapidly, or acts in co-infection (5). The prototypical inducers, bacille Calmette-Guérin (BCG) and fungal β-glucan, have anchored the concept and motivated its translation into vaccines designed specifically to exploit innate memory.The airway mucosa is a logical place to apply this idea. Local induction of trained immunity reprograms alveolar macrophages and other airway-resident cells, establishing a state of heightened readiness precisely where respiratory pathogens first arrive (6). Mucosal delivery matters: intranasal administration in pre-clinical rodent models of the inactivated polybacterial preparation MV130 confers lymphocyte-independent, long-lasting protection against experimental viral respiratory infection (7), and inhaled adenoviral-vectored vaccines reprogram human alveolar macrophages in a way that intramuscular delivery does not (8). Route and platform therefore shape not only the magnitude of the trained response but where it is positioned.Clinical evidence is accumulating, though it is uneven across populations and platforms. Sublingual MV130 reduced wheezing attacks in young children in a phase 3 randomized trial (9), and BCG vaccination lowered the incidence of respiratory infections in older adults (10). These gains are not free of risk. Trained immunity is a double-edged process: the same reprogramming that improves host defense can, if excessive or misdirected, drive immunopathology, and some protective effects reflect enhanced disease tolerance rather than faster pathogen clearance (11). Conflicting BCG results against COVID-19 illustrate how context, dose, and host state determine whether the net effect is beneficial (12). Any clinical case for these interventions must therefore weigh protection against harm, and identify who is likely to benefit.A recent opinion article argued persuasively that trained immunity-based mucosal immunotherapies deserve consideration as next-generation vaccines, illustrating the case mainly through BCG and MV130 (13). Building on that position, this review takes a translational, evidence-graded perspective and integrates three axes that a viewpoint format could not fully develop. First, we compare inducers and delivery routes (BCG, β-glucan, polybacterial immunotherapies, and viral vectors across intranasal, sublingual, and inhaled administration) to show how platform choice governs the quality and location of trained immunity. Second, we grade the clinical evidence by population, spanning children with recurrent wheeze, older adults, patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, and immunocompromised hosts, so that certainty and applicability are made explicit rather than assumed. Third, we apply the protection-vs.-immunopathology balance as a critical lens throughout, and consider the biomarkers and patient-selection strategies needed to steer benefit over harm. Together, these axes frame trained immunity-based mucosal immunotherapy not as a uniform promise but as a set of platform- and population-specific decisions with a defined translational path. This is a narrative, critically appraised review rather than a systematic one. We searched PubMed and Web of Science for English-language literature published between 2011 and 2026, combining terms for trained immunity, innate immune memory, mucosal or airway immunity, and the individual inducers and respiratory pathogens discussed here. Throughout, we prioritized primary randomized and mechanistic studies over secondary sources and applied GRADE-style reasoning to the clinical evidence. 2Mechanistic basis of mucosal and airway trained immunity2.1Epigenetic and metabolic coreTrained immunity describes a functional state in which innate immune cells, after an initial encounter with a microbial or metabolic stimulus, mount a heightened response to later and often unrelated challenges. This state is written into the cell through coordinated epigenetic and metabolic changes rather than gene rearrangement, and it can be established both centrally, in bone marrow progenitors, and peripherally, in mature tissue cells such as alveolar macrophages (Figure 1) (5). Understanding where and how these programs are laid down is a prerequisite for judging which respiratory platforms will work, in whom, and for how long; the mechanistic features summarized here therefore recur throughout the platform and clinical sections that follow.Figure 1Establishment of trained immunity at the respiratory mucosa. Inducers (BCG, β-glucan, polybacterial MV130, adenoviral vectors) are sensed through pattern-recognition receptors (dectin-1, NOD2), triggering Akt-mTOR-HIF-1α glycolysis and glutaminolysis-fumarate signaling that deposit activating chromatin marks (H3K4me3, H3K27ac). Reprogramming occurs centrally in bone marrow hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells (IFN-γ-, IL-1β-, GM-CSF-driven myeloid output) and peripherally in airway-resident alveolar macrophages (type I interferon-dependent), yielding trained macrophages, neutrophils, natural killer cells, and epithelial responses that confer heterologous protection. Human durability remains to be quantified.Diagram illustrating the establishment of trained immunity at the respiratory mucosa. Inducers like BCG, beta-glucan, MV130, and adenoviral vectors stimulate airway cells, activating metabolic and epigenetic processes. Central bone marrow HSPC and peripheral airway macrophage compartments contribute to trained macrophages, neutrophils, NK cells, and airway epithelium, leading to a faster antimicrobial response and heterologous protection upon pathogen challenge. Durability in humans is not yet quantified.The core of trained immunity is a durable epigenetic and metabolic rewiring of myeloid cells. The concept was established when brief exposure of monocytes to Candida albicans or its cell-wall β-glucan was shown to protect lymphocyte-deficient mice against reinfection through functional reprogramming rather than adaptive memory (14), and when BCG vaccination of healthy volunteers was found to raise monocyte-derived cytokine responses to unrelated pathogens for months afterward (15). Both observations converged on a chromatin mechanism: trained cells accumulate lasting marks of permissive chromatin, notably trimethylation of histone H3 at lysine 4 (H3K4me3) and acetylation of H3K27 at the promoters and enhancers of inflammatory genes, so that a second stimulus is transcribed faster and more strongly (3, 16). These chromatin changes do not stand alone. They are sustained by a coordinated shift in cellular metabolism, in which activation of the Akt-mTOR-HIF-1α axis drives a switch toward aerobic glycolysis that supplies both the energy and the biosynthetic intermediates for reprogramming (4). Metabolism feeds back onto the epigenome directly: glutaminolysis replenishes the tricarboxylic acid cycle and raises fumarate, which inhibits the KDM5 histone demethylases and thereby preserves activating H3K4me3 marks, while cholesterol and mevalonate pathway activity provides a parallel route to the trained state (17). A systematic transcriptomic and epigenomic comparison of naïve, tolerized, and trained macrophages defined the distinct enhancer landscapes that separate these states, giving the field a molecular reference for what a trained cell actually is and distinguishing trained immunity from endotoxin tolerance (18).2.2Central vs. peripheral trained immunityTrained immunity operates at two anatomically distinct levels, a distinction that matters greatly for respiratory prophylaxis. Because mature myeloid cells are short-lived, sustained protection requires reprogramming of hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells (HSPCs) in the bone marrow, a phenomenon termed central trained immunity. Administration of β-glucan expands myeloid progenitors and biases hematopoiesis toward granulomonocytic output through interleukin-1β and granulocyte-macrophage colony-stimulating factor signaling, with accompanying shifts in glucose and cholesterol metabolism (19), and BCG that reaches the marrow reprograms HSPCs in an interferon-γ-dependent manner to generate epigenetically modified macrophages with enhanced antimicrobial capacity, an effect transferable by bone marrow transplantation and therefore genuinely durable (20). In one murine study, alveolar macrophages acquired a trained phenotype that depended on metabolic rewiring and type I interferon signalling (6). This type I interferon requirement was shown in that specific model, and it should not be generalized to trained responses induced by other microbial insults, in which the signalling requirements differ. The origin of these trained airway cells varies and carries functional consequences: alveolar macrophages trained by adenoviral vectors or by MV130 are largely of tissue-resident or embryonic origin, whereas those arising after influenza infection are recruited from bone marrow monocytes, and lung tissue-resident training induced by microbial stimuli such as lipopolysaccharide can confer differential protection against pneumococci and SARS-CoV-2 (21, 22).2.3The effector repertoire and its innate–adaptive interfaceThe effector repertoire of trained immunity extends well beyond the macrophage. BCG vaccination in humans induces long-lasting functional reprogramming of neutrophils, with heightened activation markers (CD11b, CD66b), enhanced degranulation, phagocytosis, and reactive-oxygen production that persist for at least three months and track with genome-wide H3K4me3 changes (23). Natural killer cells contribute a further layer, providing non-specific protection through enhanced cytokine output for up to three months after BCG exposure (24). Structural and stromal cells, including airway epithelium, are increasingly recognized as carriers of innate memory, broadening the cellular basis of local protection at the mucosa. Importantly, trained airway macrophages do not act in isolation from adaptive immunity. After respiratory viral infection, the priming of long-lived, defence-ready alveolar macrophages requires help from local effector CD8+ T cells acting through interferon-γ, and the trained macrophage phenotype is then maintained within a tissue niche shaped by adaptive signals (25). This defines a bidirectional innate–adaptive feedback loop rather than two parallel systems: tissue-resident memory lymphocytes license and sustain innate memory, while trained macrophages supply the local cytokine and metabolic context that supports resident lymphocyte persistence. Mucosal immunotherapies therefore depend on this innate–adaptive crosstalk to consolidate durable epigenetic memory at the airway mucosa, and they are not purely antigen-agnostic, standalone tools. This cellular diversity means that the net effect of any given inducer reflects a composite of trained macrophages, granulocytes, lymphoid innate cells, and epithelial responses, whose balance is shaped by the stimulus and its route of delivery, and whose regulatory as well as inflammatory components determine whether the outcome favors the host.The input that forms the innate memory of the airway is not limited to the respiratory tract. Central training of bone-marrow progenitors is influenced by a distal gut–lung axis, in which microbiota-derived short-chain fatty acids reprogram myelopoiesis and set the functional tone of monocyte-derived airway macrophages. Dietary fermentable fibre, acting through this axis, reshapes patrolling-monocyte output and limits neutrophil-driven immunopathology during influenza (26). Diet and the intestinal microbiome are therefore modifiable determinants of the trained state on which a mucosal immunotherapy builds. Additionally, preliminary evidence suggests that trained hematopoietic progenitors may extend to the megakaryocytic lineage, potentially yielding “trained platelets” with altered inflammatory profiles, though their direct role in respiratory mucosal memory requires further clinical validation (27).Several determinants set the quality, location, and durability of the trained response, and these determinants form the mechanistic bridge to platform design. The nature of the stimulus dictates the receptor engaged and the downstream program, with β-glucan acting through dectin-1 and the noncanonical Raf-1 pathway and BCG through NOD2-dependent sensing that deposits H3K4me3 at cytokine and Toll-like receptor promoters (14, 15). full_text: IntroductionHeat- and moisture-sensitive porous materials such as plush toys, paper products, and foam are widely used in pediatric and healthcare environments but cannot be decontaminated by conventional liquid disinfectants, heat, or UV-based methods. This creates a need for alternative dry, non-thermal technologies. Non-thermal plasma (NTP) offers a promising approach for disinfecting such materials without compromising their integrity.MethodsIn this study, we assessed the virucidal efficacy of a prototyped NTP device on four clinically relevant respiratory viruses—Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome Coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2), Influenza A virus (IAV), human Adenovirus (HAdV), and human Rhinovirus (HRV)—applied to paper, plush fabric, and foam rubber.ResultsMaterial characterization by SEM and XPS demonstrated only mild surface oxidation and no structural damage following NTP exposure. Across all substrates, NTP treatment produced time-dependent reductions in viral infectivity. Maximum reductions ranged from 5.5–6.3 log10 for SARS-CoV-2, 6.3–7.1 log10 for IAV, 4.0–5.9 log10 for HAdV, and 2.7–5.0 log10 for HRV, depending on the virus-material combination. Enveloped viruses (SARS-CoV-2 and IAV) were inactivated more rapidly than the non-enveloped viruses HAdV and HRV, although all viruses were reduced to nearly or completely undetectable levels after 30–60 min of treatment. Several virus-material combinations exhibited biphasic inactivation kinetics characterized by an initial rapid decline followed by a slower phase of inactivation.DiscussionThese findings support that NTP could be an effective, residue-free, and material-preserving method for inactivating a broad spectrum of respiratory viruses on porous substrates incompatible with conventional disinfection. NTP thus might represent a valuable tool for safely reusing sensitive items in pediatric and clinical settings and reducing contamination risks where existing methods are impractical. 2Materials and methods2.1Non-thermal plasma (NTP) deviceNTP was generated by point-to-ring corona discharge in a device whose operating parameters (discharge power: 0.7 W, voltage: 6–8 kV, current: 100–150 μA) were specifically optimized for enhanced antimicrobial and virucidal efficacy. The selected parameters represent the optimal balance between maximum antimicrobial activity and stable, spark-free discharge operation.Further details of the NTP device and the concentrations of long-lived plasma-generated species (NO2, N2O, O3, and H2O2) measured under identical operating conditions were described in our previous study (Bouazizi et al., 2024).2.2Assessment of material damage by NTP using scanning electron microscopy (SEM)Material morphology and surface structure were examined by SEM using a Vega II LSH instrument (TESCAN GROUP, a.s., Brno, Czech Republic) to visualize potential NTP-induced alterations accurately. Small pieces were cut from the samples and mounted on a sample holder using double-sided conductive adhesive tape. All specimens were then sputter-coated with a thin gold layer under an argon atmosphere (15 mA, 60 s) using a POLARON Emitech SC7640 sputter coater (Quorum Technologies Ltd., Lewes, UK). Imaging parameters, including accelerating voltage (kV), working distance (WD; mm), and magnification, are provided at the bottom of the corresponding images in the Results section.2.3Chemical composition analysis of material surface using X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS)X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) was performed to characterize the chemical composition of the sample surfaces to a depth of ~5 nm using an Axis Ultra DLD spectrometer (Kratos Analytical Ltd., UK). A monochromatic Al Kα (hν = 1486.7 eV) X-ray source operating at 75 W (5 mA, 15 kV) was used, and spectra were collected over a 300 × 700 μm analytical area. High-resolution spectra were acquired with a step size of 0.1 eV and a pass energy of 20 eV. The Kratos charge neutralizer system was used for all analyses. The instrument base pressure during measurements was consistently 2 × 10−8 Pa. Spectra were analyzed using CasaXPS software (version 2.3.17) and charge-corrected to the main C 1 s carbon component (C–C, C–H), set to 285.00 eV. A standard Shirley background was used for all sample spectra.As with the SEM analysis, XPS measurements were performed on samples exposed to NTP for 24 h—well beyond the antiviral treatment times—to evaluate the cumulative chemical effects of repeated disinfection cycles and to establish a safety margin for material integrity under extended plasma exposure.2.4Virus strains and cell linesThe following virus strains and cell lines were used: SARS-CoV-2 (hCoV-19/Czech Republic/NRL_6632_2/2020) (Bouazizi et al., 2024; Vankova et al., 2020), propagated in Vero E6 cells (ATCC CRL-1586) in DMEM containing Pen/Strep and 10% FBS; IAV H1N1/California/07/2009 (Diagnostic Hybrids, Athens, OH, United States), propagated in MDCK cells (ATCC CCL-34) in influenza growth medium (IGM) consisting of DMEM supplemented with Pen/Strep, 0.2% BSA, 1 mM HEPES, 13.6 mM L-glutamine, 42 mg/L DEAE-dextran, and 1 mg/L TPCK-trypsin; HAdV species C/type 2 (ATCC VR-846), propagated in A549 cells (DSMZ ACC107) in DMEM containing 10% FBS and Pen/Strep; and HRV A/type 2 (ATCC VR-482), propagated in HeLa Ohio cells (both a kind gift from G. ST Antivirals) in DMEM containing 10% FBS and Pen/Strep.2.5Material contamination and virus recoveryPaper, plush fabric, and foam rubber were selected as representative contaminated surfaces for evaluating NTP-mediated virus inactivation. Their suitability for direct pediatric contact after NTP treatment was not evaluated in this study. To assess whether the materials themselves affected viral infectivity or cell viability, we tested their intrinsic toxicity toward HRV and HAdV and toward HeLa and A549 cells (see Supplementary Materials). Virus recovery was performed according to the method published in the ISO Standard 18,184 (Textiles—Determination of antiviral activity of textile products, now referenced in the manuscript) (ISO, 2019a), as based on their characteristics, both plush and paper are similar to the fabrics covered by it. For plastic, repeated rinsing of the sample surface, as described in ISO 21702 (Measurement of antiviral activity on plastics and other non-porous surfaces) (ISO, 2019b), would have been sufficient. However, a uniform recovery method was used to ensure consistent handling of infectious material from all samples. Since RONS production is humidity-dependent relative humidity (RH) inside the device was measured after adding 6 mL of water to the cotton wool in the Petri dish, under the same conditions as during antiviral testing, during NTP treatment using a humidity sensor. For this purpose, measurements were performed with a testo 625instrument (Testo SE & Co. KGaA, Titisee-Neustadt, Germany) equipped with RH and temperature. Drying led to a rapid loss of detectable infectivity even in the absence of NTP treatment, making a dried-inoculum approach unsuitable for assessing plasma-mediated inactivation. A set of control samples was placed in another device that did not produce NTP. A set of control samples was placed in another device that did not produce NTP. full_text_sections.results: 3Results3.1Non-thermal plasma has limited impact on sensitive materialsTo assess the impact of NTP on the structural integrity of sensitive materials, SEM imaging was performed on untreated and NTP-treated samples. Microscopic examination of untreated and NTP-treated samples revealed distinct material-specific behaviors. The paper substrate showed no substantial morphological alterations following NTP exposure when comparing the reference sample (Figure 1A) with the sample after 24 h of NTP treatment (Figure 1B). Plush fabric fibers maintained a smooth surface devoid of defects, fractures, or adherent particles.
