full_text_sections.discussion: 4DiscussionThis study supports that NTP is an efficient and material-compatible method for inactivating a broad spectrum of human respiratory viruses on porous, heat- and moisture-sensitive substrates. By evaluating four epidemiologically relevant viruses—SARS-CoV-2, IAV, HAdV and HRV—across three commonly used materials in pediatric and healthcare settings (paper, plush fabric, foam rubber), we showed that NTP consistently was able to reduce viral infectivity to at least nearly undetectable levels of infectivity after 30 to 60 min, depending on virus–material combinations. These findings expand on our previous work demonstrating the virucidal effects of NTP on surface contaminants, including SARS-CoV-2 and IAV on mask filters and other materials (Obrova et al., 2022; Bouazizi et al., 2024).Material characterization provided essential insight into why all three substrates tolerated NTP exposure without major structural or chemical compromise. SEM analysis confirmed no change in structural attributes at all for paper, only minor changes for plush and foam rubber maintained its structure after treatment. XPS revealed mainly superficial oxidation—manifested as increased oxygen-containing functional groups—consistent with the mild oxidative surface modification described in prior NTP–material interaction studies (Obrova et al., 2022; Scholtz et al., 2023). Crucially, these observations were made after 24 h of continuous NTP exposure, substantially exceeding the antiviral treatment times (5–60 min), thereby providing a conservative assessment of plasma-induced surface alterations under prolonged exposure. Importantly, no detrimental alterations in material morphology were observed, supporting the suitability of NTP for items that cannot undergo heat-, moisture-, or solvent-based decontamination (Rutala et al., 2023). However, the present assessment was limited to surface morphology (SEM) and surface chemistry (XPS) and therefore could not provide a comprehensive evaluation of the mechanical performance or long-term durability of the tested materials. Regarding the durability of NTP-treated materials under realistic conditions, mechanical properties of paper exposed to NTP under comparable discharge parameters were previously evaluated and shown to remain unchanged even after 120 min of treatment (Scholtz et al., 2023). For plush fabric and foam rubber, our SEM and XPS analyses suggested that plasma treatment induces predominantly superficial surface modifications, which are unlikely to result in substantial changes in mechanical integrity. A comprehensive assessment of multi-cycle durability and mechanical properties across all tested materials is currently in progress and will be the subject of a future study.The differences in susceptibility observed among the four viruses can by some extent be explained by their structural organization and the primary molecular targets of plasma-generated RONS (Mumtaz and Rana, 2026; Ahmed et al., 2025). The more pronounced initial reductions observed for SARS-CoV-2 and IAV are consistent with the high susceptibility of enveloped viruses to oxidative damage. Lipid peroxidation and modification of envelope glycoproteins can rapidly abolish infectivity even before substantial genome degradation occurs, leading to steep early declines in viable virus counts (Obrova et al., 2022; Mumtaz and Rana, 2026; Lan et al., 2024; Huang et al., 2025). SARS-CoV-2 was the most susceptible virus, which is consistent with its fragile lipid envelope and the critical role of the spike glycoprotein in host-cell attachment. Oxidative damage to membrane lipids and envelope proteins can rapidly abolish infectivity even before extensive genome degradation occurs. IAV, although also enveloped, exhibited slightly greater persistence under some conditions. This may reflect differences in envelope composition, virion morphology, and the organization of its surface glycoproteins, which can influence susceptibility to oxidative modification (Obrova et al., 2022; Mumtaz and Rana, 2026; Lan et al., 2024; Huang et al., 2025). In contrast, non-enveloped viruses generally depend on the accumulation of damage to capsid proteins and nucleic acids before infectivity is lost, which may result in a more gradual reduction profile (Lion, 2019; Lan et al., 2024; Huang et al., 2025; Birmpa et al., 2016). HAdV possesses a highly stable icosahedral protein capsid composed of tightly packed structural proteins that protect the viral genome from environmental stress. Effective inactivation therefore requires the accumulation of damage to capsid proteins and/or nucleic acids, resulting in slower loss of infectivity (Lion, 2019). HRV is likewise non-enveloped and contains a compact protein capsid that contributes to its well-established environmental stability (Wang et al., 2017; Reagan et al., 1981). However, its smaller particle size and less complex capsid architecture compared with adenovirus may facilitate access of reactive species to critical viral structures, potentially explaining why HRV appeared more susceptible than HAdV despite also being non-enveloped (Huang et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2017; Reagan et al., 1981). Collectively, the observed susceptibility ranking is consistent with a hierarchy in which viruses protected only by a lipid envelope are most readily inactivated, whereas viruses relying on highly stable protein capsids require more extensive molecular damage before infectivity is lost. Recent plasma-biological interface studies further indicate that plasma-generated RONS and charged particles can act synergistically on biomolecular targets by oxidizing lipids, proteins, and nucleic acids, while also inducing downstream biological responses such as oxidative stress and immune modulation, with the relative contribution of each pathway depending on virion structure (Mumtaz and Rana, 2026; Ahmed et al., 2025; Lan et al., 2024).However, the dependence of inactivation kinetics seems to rely on both the material properties and virus type. Beyond the overall reduction in infectivity, the shape of the inactivation curves may provide additional insight into the underlying mechanisms of NTP-mediated viral inactivation. Several virus-material combinations exhibited biphasic kinetics characterized by a rapid initial decrease in infectious titer followed by a slower phase of inactivation. Such tailing behavior has frequently been reported during plasma-based microbial decontamination and is generally attributed to population heterogeneity and limitations in agent accessibility rather than changes in plasma activity itself (Mošovská et al., 2023; Zhang and Wang, 2025). RONS are expected to rapidly inactivate virions that are directly exposed at the material surface, resulting in an initial steep decline. The remaining infectious fraction may consist of particles embedded within surface irregularities, retained in pores or fiber networks, or protected by aggregation and local microenvironmental effects, thereby requiring longer exposure times to achieve non-detectable levels of infectivity (Bouazizi et al., 2024; Mumtaz and Rana, 2026; Huang et al., 2025; Birmpa et al., 2016; Mošovská et al., 2023; Zhang and Wang, 2025). Material-dependent differences further support the importance of physical accessibility during treatment. Because virus application and drying conditions had to be adapted to the absorbency and drying tolerance of each substrate, cross-substrate comparisons should be interpreted cautiously and mainly as indicators of material-dependent viral accessibility. The delayed inactivation of HAdV on plush fabric compared with paper and foam rubber suggests that the dense fibrous structure may partially shield virions from direct exposure to reactive species. Porous and textured materials can create protected microenvironments where local RONS concentrations are lower and diffusion is restricted, producing extended tailing phases despite continued plas…
full_text_sections.other: 1IntroductionRespiratory viruses are major global pathogens because of their high transmissibility, ability to persist on surfaces, and potential to cause epidemics. Although airborne spread is the principal route of transmission, contaminated surfaces and shared objects represent important secondary reservoirs, particularly in communal and healthcare settings (Haas et al., 2023). This risk is especially pronounced in hospitals, daycare centers, and pediatric wards, where high-touch items are frequently reused without adequate decontamination between uses. To address this challenge, the present study examines the virucidal efficacy of non-thermal plasma (NTP), a dry, low-temperature disinfection technology, against four clinically relevant respiratory viruses with distinct biological properties: severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2), influenza A virus (IAV), human rhinovirus (HRV), and human adenovirus (HAdV).SARS-CoV-2, an enveloped RNA virus, demonstrated remarkable epidemic potential during the recent pandemic (Fathizadeh et al., 2020). Although enveloped viruses are generally more susceptible to disinfectants, the prolonged stability of SARS-CoV-2 on surfaces and in aerosols underscores the need for reliable decontamination strategies (van Doremalen et al., 2020). Moreover, repeated outbreaks caused by related coronaviruses, including SARS-CoV and MERS-CoV, indicate that members of the Coronaviridae family are likely to remain relevant targets for future infection-control efforts (Civljak et al., 2020). IAV, another enveloped RNA virus, is a frequent cause of seasonal and localized epidemic outbreaks (Moa et al., 2001). Its persistence in aerosols, low infectious dose, and rapid antigenic evolution make it a continuing public health challenge and a priority target for improved disinfection approaches (Tellier, 2009; Wu et al., 2020).Non-enveloped viruses such as HRV and HAdV present additional challenges because of their marked environmental stability. HRV, a ubiquitous cause of respiratory tract infections, can remain infectious on surfaces and is difficult to eliminate from porous substrates because of its small particle size and structural resilience. HAdV is among the most resistant human viruses; its robust non-enveloped capsid and stable DNA genome make it particularly difficult to inactivate and therefore a useful indicator organism for evaluating disinfection technologies (Lion, 2014; Lion, 2019). Although adenovirus infections are often self-limiting in immunocompetent individuals, they can cause severe outbreaks in crowded settings and life-threatening disease in immunocompromised patients (Hiwarkar et al., 2018; Sammons et al., 2019).Standard decontamination approaches, including ultraviolet (UV) irradiation, gamma irradiation, and chemical disinfectants, are often poorly suited to sensitive materials. UV light has limited penetration, and its efficacy is substantially reduced by surface irregularities and shadowing (Deng et al., 2020; Derraik et al., 2020; Kayani et al., 2021; Mills et al., 2018). Gamma irradiation requires specialized infrastructure and may compromise material integrity (Derraik et al., 2020; Rutala et al., 2023). Conventional liquid disinfectants are incompatible with many moisture- or heat-sensitive items and may leave residues that are undesirable in pediatric or clinical environments (Rutala et al., 2023; Obrova et al., 2022).These limitations are particularly relevant for porous, soft, and absorbent materials such as plush toys, foam rubber, paper, and cardboard. Plush toys, often composed of polyester or cotton fibers with sponge-like inner structures, can trap microbes deep within multiple layers. Foam rubber, including polyurethane-based materials used in cushions, child seating, and packaging, readily absorbs fluids and resists complete drying. Paper and cardboard, which are common in books, educational toys, and packaging, may deform or degrade when exposed to heat or moisture (Rutala et al., 2023; Scholtz et al., 2023).Such materials are ubiquitous in pediatric environments, where tactile play, frequent handling, and hand-to-mouth behavior increase the risk of contamination and transmission. Children are also more susceptible to infection because their immune systems are still developing, and viral shedding may be greater and more prolonged than in adults (Costa et al., 2012; Prendergast et al., 2012). Consistent with this vulnerability, contaminated toys and shared supplies in hospitals and daycare centers have repeatedly been implicated in outbreaks of influenza and adenovirus infections among children (Bearden and Casanova, 2016).Against this background, NTP has emerged as a promising alternative disinfection technology. NTP is a partially ionized gas generated at room temperature and atmospheric pressure that contains reactive oxygen and nitrogen species (RONS), UV photons, ions, and electrons (Scholtz et al., 2023; Graves, 2012). In contrast to conventional methods, NTP provides dry, non-thermal, and non-wetting disinfection, making it particularly suitable for soft and porous materials that would otherwise need to be discarded after contamination (Obrova et al., 2022; Scholtz et al., 2023). Previous studies have shown that NTP can inactivate SARS-CoV-2, IAV, HRV, and HAdV on parafilm, P3 R filter material, foam, and other filter-based substrates, with dose-dependent reductions in viral titers (Obrova et al., 2022; Bouazizi et al., 2024).A further advance has been the development of portable, affordable, 3D-printed plasma devices optimized for microbiocidal performance and improved surface coverage of irregular materials such as plush toys and layered foams. By promoting deeper penetration and more uniform exposure, these devices may enable the safe reuse of items in pediatric care while reducing waste, lowering transmission risk, and extending the availability of essential resources during periods of shortage, including pandemics (Obrova et al., 2022; Scholtz et al., 2023; Bouazizi et al., 2024; Klenivskyi et al., 2024). 2.1Non-thermal plasma (NTP) deviceNTP was generated by point-to-ring corona discharge in a device whose operating parameters (discharge power: 0.7 W, voltage: 6–8 kV, current: 100–150 μA) were specifically optimized for enhanced antimicrobial and virucidal efficacy. The optimization process is described in detail in our previous works (Bouazizi et al., 2024; Klenivskyi et al., 2024), which involved systematic variation of the interelectrode distance (0–8 mm) and discharge current (50–500 μA) and assessment of the bactericidal effect on Escherichia coli. The selected parameters represent the optimal balance between maximum antimicrobial activity and stable, spark-free discharge operation.Further details of the NTP device and the concentrations of long-lived plasma-generated species (NO2, N2O, O3, and H2O2) measured under identical operating conditions were described in our previous study (Bouazizi et al., 2024). 2.4Virus strains and cell linesThe following virus strains and cell lines were used: SARS-CoV-2 (hCoV-19/Czech Republic/NRL_6632_2/2020) (Bouazizi et al., 2024; Vankova et al., 2020), propagated in Vero E6 cells (ATCC CRL-1586) in DMEM containing Pen/Strep and 10% FBS; IAV H1N1/California/07/2009 (Diagnostic Hybrids, Athens, OH, United States), propagated in MDCK cells (ATCC CCL-34) in influenza growth medium (IGM) consisting of DMEM supplemented with Pen/Strep, 0.2% BSA, 1 mM HEPES, 13.6 mM L-glutamine, 42 mg/L DEAE-dextran, and 1 mg/L TPCK-trypsin; HAdV species C/type 2 (ATCC VR-846), propagated in A549 cells (DSMZ ACC107) in DMEM containing 10% FBS and Pen/Strep; and HRV A/type 2 (ATCC VR-482), propagated in HeLa Ohio cells (both a kind gift from G. title_original: Non-thermal plasma efficiently decontaminates sensitive materials from respiratory viruses

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to evaluate the effectiveness of non-thermal plasma (NTP) in decontaminating sensitive materials from respiratory viruses without compromising their structural integrity.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study assessed the virucidal efficacy of a prototyped NTP device on four clinically relevant respiratory viruses—SARS-CoV-2, Influenza A virus (IAV), human Adenovirus (HAdV), and human Rhinovirus (HRV)—applied to paper, plush fabric, and foam rubber. The experiment was conducted under controlled conditions to evaluate the cumulative chemical effects of repeated disinfection cycles.
analysis.methods: The virucidal efficacy of NTP was assessed using plaque assays and TCID50 assays for viral titration. Material characterization was performed using scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) to evaluate surface oxidation and structural damage. The study also included intrinsic toxicity testing of materials toward HRV and HAdV and toward HeLa and A549 cells.
analysis.main_results: Material characterization by SEM and XPS demonstrated only mild surface oxidation and no structural damage following NTP exposure. Results with p-values < 0.05 were considered significant, and the log10 reduction was reported as the primary effect size.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The findings suggest that NTP treatment effectively inactivates respiratory viruses while preserving material integrity, offering a promising alternative for disinfection of sensitive surfaces.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The results provide evidence for the potential use of NTP in decontaminating materials contaminated with respiratory viruses, which could inform the development of safer and more effective disinfection protocols in healthcare and public settings.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study did not perform a prospective power analysis, and the additional power calculations are retrospective planning aids. The evidence is moderate, as the results are based on a limited set of materials and viruses, and the interpretation is grounded in the observed outcomes.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigated the effectiveness of non-thermal plasma (NTP) in decontaminating sensitive materials from respiratory viruses such as SARS-CoV-2, Influenza A virus (IAV), human Adenovirus (HAdV), and human Rhinovirus (HRV). The research aimed to determine if NTP could inactivate these viruses without damaging the materials. Using plaque assays, TCID50 assays, scanning electron microscopy (SEM), and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS), the study found that NTP treatment led to significant virucidal effects while causing only mild surface oxidation and no structural damage. The results suggest that NTP could be a viable method for disinfecting surfaces in healthcare and public environments. However, the study lacked a prospective power analysis, and the evidence is considered moderate due to the limited scope of materials and viruses tested.

elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 本研究未进行前瞻性功效分析,附加的功效计算是回顾性计划辅助工具。证据强度中等,因为结果基于有限的材料和病毒种类,且解释基于观察到的结果。

analysis_en.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to evaluate the effectiveness of non-thermal plasma (NTP) in decontaminating sensitive materials from respiratory viruses without compromising their structural integrity.
analysis_en.study_design_and_population: The study assessed the virucidal efficacy of a prototyped NTP device on four clinically relevant respiratory viruses—SARS-CoV-2, Influenza A virus (IAV), human Adenovirus (HAdV), and human Rhinovirus (HRV)—applied to paper, plush fabric, and foam rubber. The experiment was conducted under controlled conditions to evaluate the cumulative chemical effects of repeated disinfection cycles.
analysis_en.methods: The virucidal efficacy of NTP was assessed using plaque assays and TCID50 assays for viral titration. Material characterization was performed using scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) to evaluate surface oxidation and structural damage. The study also included intrinsic toxicity testing of materials toward HRV and HAdV and toward HeLa and A549 cells.
analysis_en.main_results: Material characterization by SEM and XPS demonstrated only mild surface oxidation and no structural damage following NTP exposure. Results with p-values < 0.05 were considered significant, and the log10 reduction was reported as the primary effect size.
analysis_en.interpretation_and_novelty: The findings suggest that NTP treatment effectively inactivates respiratory viruses while preserving material integrity, offering a promising alternative for disinfection of sensitive surfaces.
analysis_en.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The results provide evidence for the potential use of NTP in decontaminating materials contaminated with respiratory viruses, which could inform the development of safer and more effective disinfection protocols in healthcare and public settings.
analysis_en.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study did not perform a prospective power analysis, and the additional power calculations are retrospective planning aids. The evidence is moderate, as the results are based on a limited set of materials and viruses, and the interpretation is grounded in the observed outcomes.

title_zh: 非热等离子体高效去除呼吸道病毒对敏感材料的污染
source_body_en: IntroductionHeat- and moisture-sensitive porous materials such as plush toys, paper products, and foam are widely used in pediatric and healthcare environments but cannot be decontaminated by conventional liquid disinfectants, heat, or UV-based methods. Non-thermal plasma (NTP) offers a promising approach for disinfecting such materials without compromising their integrity.MethodsIn this study, we assessed the virucidal efficacy of a prototyped NTP device on four clinically relevant respiratory viruses—Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome Coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2), Influenza A virus (IAV), human Adenovirus (HAdV), and human Rhinovirus (HRV)—applied to paper, plush fabric, and foam rubber.ResultsMaterial characterization by SEM and XPS demonstrated only mild surface oxidation and no structural damage following NTP exposure. Several virus-material combinations exhibited biphasic inactivation kinetics characterized by an initial rapid decline followed by a slower phase of inactivation.DiscussionThese findings support that NTP could be an effective, residue-free, and material-preserving method for inactivating a broad spectrum of respiratory viruses on porous substrates incompatible with conventional disinfection. This creates a need for alternative dry, non-thermal technologies. Across all substrates, NTP treatment produced time-dependent reductions in viral infectivity. Maximum reductions ranged from 5.5–6.3 log10 for SARS-CoV-2, 6.3–7.1 log10 for IAV, 4.0–5.9 log10 for HAdV, and 2.7–5.0 log10 for HRV, depending on the virus-material combination. Enveloped viruses (SARS-CoV-2 and IAV) were inactivated more rapidly than the non-enveloped viruses HAdV and HRV, although all viruses were reduced to nearly or completely undetectable levels after 30–60 min of treatment. analysis_zh.research_question_and_background: 本研究旨在评估非热等离子体(NTP)在不损害其结构完整性的情况下,对呼吸道病毒污染的敏感材料进行消毒的有效性。
analysis_zh.study_design_and_population: 本研究评估了原型NTP设备对四种临床相关的呼吸道病毒——SARS-CoV-2、流感A病毒(IAV)、人类腺病毒(HAdV)和人类鼻病毒(HRV)——在纸张、 plush织物和泡沫橡胶上的灭活效果。实验在受控条件下进行,以评估重复消毒周期的累积化学效应。
analysis_zh.methods: NTP的灭活效果通过斑块形成试验和TCID50试验进行评估,用于病毒滴度测定。材料表征使用扫描电子显微镜(SEM)和X射线光电子能谱(XPS)进行,以评估表面氧化和结构损伤。研究还包括对材料对HRV和HAdV以及对HeLa和A549细胞的内在毒性测试。
analysis_zh.main_results: 通过扫描电子显微镜(SEM)和X射线光电子能谱(XPS)对材料进行表征,结果显示NTP暴露后仅出现轻微的表面氧化,且无结构损伤。p值<0.05的结果被视为显著,且log10减少量被报告为主要效应量。
analysis_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 这些发现表明,NTP 治疗能够有效灭活呼吸道病毒,同时保持材料的完整性,为敏感表面的消毒提供了一种有前景的替代方法。
analysis_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 这些结果为NTP在去除呼吸道病毒污染材料中的潜在应用提供了证据,可能有助于在医疗和公共环境中开发更安全、更有效的消毒协议。
analysis_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 本研究未进行前瞻性功效分析,附加的功效计算是回顾性计划辅助工具。证据强度中等,因为结果基于有限的材料和病毒种类,且解释基于观察到的结果。

full_text: Viral-bacterial co-infections represent a major contributor to global morbidity and mortality. In influenza virus infections, secondary bacterial pneumonia occurs in approximately 20–30% of cases and is associated with an increased risk of shock, mechanical ventilation, and even mortality. Bacterial superinfections are frequent causes of mortality in influenza severe infections and have been a major cause of morbidity and mortality also in COVID-19 patients. Staphylococcus aureus has been identified as one of the most prevalent bacterial pathogens among hospitalized and non-hospitalized patients who have tested positive for SARS-CoV-2 or influenza virus infections. Generally, antibiotic therapy is administered to at-risk patients to preclude bacterial over-infections by eliminating susceptible pathogens, increasing selective pressure favoring antibiotic-resistant bacteria. Due to the recognized public health problem of antibiotic resistance, the exploration of alternative therapies to counteract or prevent the development of serious virus/bacteria co-infections has become a critical research priority. The present study aimed to investigate the interactions between coronavirus or influenza A virus, and S. aureus in a co-infection model and to investigate the ability of a known antiviral/antibacterial compound, the bithiazole derivative MR335, to counteract the interaction between the two pathogens. The co-infection models were established using the pulmonary cell line A549 and the bronchial cell line BEAS-2B. The synergistic interaction between virus and bacteria were assessed through standard viral titration assays and bacterial adhesion and invasion assays. The bithiazole compound, MR335, showed both antiviral and antibacterial activity at distinct concentrations. In particular, it effectively counteracted the synergistic interactions between respiratory viruses and S. aureus at concentration that retained antiviral but not antibacterial activity. Notably, eradication of viruses impaired bacterial invasion, suggesting their synergistic cooperation and opening the way to alternative therapies that prevent bacterial superinfection without resorting to conventional antibiotics. Materials and methodsCell culture and viruses’ productionHuman lung adenocarcinoma cells (A549 cell line) were grown in DMEM medium supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS), 0.3mg/ml glutamine, 100 U/ml penicillin, and 100 μg/ml streptomycin. Influenza virus A/Puerto Rico/8/34H1N1 (PR8/H1N1), influenza virus A/California/7/2009/H1N1 (pH1N1), influenza A/parrot/Ulster/73 (H7N1) or parainfluenza virus Sendai type 1 (SeV) were grown in allantoic cavities of 11-day-old embryonated chicken eggs. Viral suspension was inoculated in the allantoic cavity and incubated for 48 h at 37 °C, then infected eggs were maintained overnight at 4 °C. The allantoic fluid was collected and clarified by centrifugation (2500xg for 30 min). The recovered virus was used for the infection of A549 cells. Allantoic fluid from uninfected eggs was used as reference for mock infection.Confluent monolayers of BEAS-2B were challenged with the Human Coronavirus (HCoV-229E) seasonal strain. After the viral adsorption, the cells were washed with phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) and then incubated with the medium supplemented with 2% FBS for 24 h. Virus production was determined in the supernatants of the infected cells by TCID50 (tissue culture infectious dose 50%) assay. Briefly, MRC-5 (Medical Research Council cell strain 5) cells were seeded in 96-well plates at a density of 2×104 cells/well for 24 hours at 37 °C in an atmosphere of 5% CO2. Subsequently, cell monolayers were infected for 1 hour at 37 °C, using 10-fold dilutions of the samples, previously collected upon infection. After viral adsorption, cells were washed with PBS and 100 μL of fresh medium supplemented with 2% FBS will be added to each well for 24 hours at 37 °C. The number of wells showing positive CPE was then scored. TCID50/mL will be evaluated by means of the Reed and Muench method.Bacterial strainsA collection strain of Staphylococcus aureus ATCC 6538 was used in the study. The strain was stored at -80 °C in glycerol stocks. For experimental procedures, S. aureus was cultured directly from glycerol stock on Triptone Soy Agar plates (TSA, Oxoid, Basingstoke, UK) and incubated aerobically overnight at 37°C. A colony grown on TSA plate was inoculated in Brain Heart Infusion Broth (BHI, Oxoid, Basingstoke, UK) and incubated overnight at 37 °C with agitation (180 rpm). The concentration of the overnight bacterial suspension was then measured spectrophotometrically (BioPhotometer, Eppendorf, Hamburg, Germany).CompoundsThe compound used was supplied in powder form, resuspended in 100% dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO) (Sigma-Aldrich, St. Louis, MO, USA). Chemical structure, published data and reference to its synthesis are reported in Table 1.Table 1Chemical structure of MR335.CompoundReference paper to synthesis, characterization and biological evaluation Chemical structure diagram of MR335, displaying an arrangement of rings, nitrogen, sulfur, trifluoromethyl, and carboxylic acid groups, with lines indicating bonds between atoms in the molecular structure. Martina, M. G.; Sannio, F.; Crespan, E.; Pavone, M.; Simoncini, A.; Barbieri, F.; Perini, C.; Pesce, E.; Maga, G.; Pedemonte, N.; Docquier, J-D.; Radi, M.ChemMedChem 2022, 17, e202200277.(compound 8b)IC50 (PI4KB) = 7.1 ± 0.65 μMCytotoxicity assayThe cytotoxicity of MR335 compound was assessed by using MTT (3-(4,5- dimethylthiazol-2-yl)-2,5-diphenyl tetrazolium bromide) reagent (Sigma-Aldrich, St. Louis, MO, USA) assay on A549 cell line. In a 96-well plate, 200 μl of cell suspension (104 cells/well) were added to each well and the plates were incubated at 37 °C, 5% CO2. After 24 h, the culture medium was replaced with 200 μl of medium supplemented with MR335 compound at different concentrations (500, 400, 300, 200, 150, 100, 80, 60, 40, 20 μM). Untreated cells were used as control. After 24 h of contact, the culture medium was replaced with 200 μl of fresh medium added with 3-(4, 5-dimethylthiazol-2-yl)-2, 5-diphenyltetrazolium bromide (MTT) (5 mg/ml) (SERVA Electrophoresis GmbH, Heidelberg, Germany), then the plates were incubated for 4h at 37 °C, in a 5% CO2 atmosphere. Next, the culture medium with MTT was removed and 200 μl of dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO) (Sigma-Aldrich, St. Louis, MO, USA) were added to each well to dissolve the formazan crystals formed in the live cells. After 15 minutes of incubation, absorbance was measured at 570 nm, with the reference set at 620 nm, using the automatic microplate reader, Tecan Sunrise (Kumar et al., 2018). For solvent control, the cell viability was compared with the DMSO-treated cells, at the same volumes used for MR335 dilutions.Co-infection modelsCo-infection models between respiratory viruses and S. aureus were settled, referring to previous studies with some modifications (Oliva and Terrier, 2021; Sura et al., 2022; Goncheva and Heinrichs, 2023). In particular, co-infection models of S. aureus and PR8/H1N1 strain on A549 alveolar cell line and of S. aureus and HCoV-229E strain on BEAS-2B bronchial cell line were set up.For this purpose, A549 or BEAS-2B cells were seeded in 24-well culture plates at a concentration of 1,5×105 cells/mL, resuspended in complete DMEM medium and incubated at 37°C, 5% CO2. After 24 h of incubation, the cells were infected with PR8/H1N1 or HCoV-229E virus at MOI 0,1, in DMEM at 2% FBS, without antibiotics. After 22 h of viral infection, the cell monolayers were infected with S. aureus at a multiplicity of infection of 1 for A549 and 10 for BEAS cell line. The MOI was independently optimized for each cell line based on preliminary experiments aimed at identifying conditions yielding reproducible and quantifiable adhesion and invasion.The cells were then incubated for 2 h at 37 °C, 5% CO2. At the end of the 2 h of infection, supernatants were collected for viral titration assays. In addition, bacterial adhesion and invasion were evaluated. Cells were infected with S. aureus alone or virus alone in order to compare the results with those of the co-infection models. In parallel, the same experimental conditions were used to evaluate the efficacy of MR335 compound in interfering with virus-bacteria synergistic interactions. To this aim, the compound was added after viral adsorption and maintained for the following 24 h post-infection.Antiviral activity of bithiazole compoundConfluent monolayers of A549 or BEAS-2B cells were challenged with influenza virus A/Puerto Rico/8/34 H1N1 (PR8) or HCoV-229E, respectively, for 1 h at 37 °C. Then, cells were washed with PBS and incubated or not with MR335 compound diluted in medium supplemented with 2% of FBS for 24 h post-infection. Mock infection was performed with the same dilution of allantoic fluid. Viral titration was performed by TCID50 or Hemagglutination assay (HAU) method.In-cell western assayA549 cells were grown in 96-well plates (2 × 104 cells/well) and incubated with the supernatants of infected and treated cells for 1 h at 37 °C. After 24 h of infection, cells were fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde (Santa Cruz Dallas, TX, USA), permeabilized with 0.1% Triton X-100, and incubated with Odyssey Blocking buffer (LI-COR Biosciences, Lincoln, NE, USA) for 1 h. Anti-Hemagglutinin (HA) or anti-influenza (Flu) antibodies (Santa Cruz Biotechnology, Santa Cruz, CA, USA) diluted in Odyssey Blocking Buffer were used to stain the cell monolayer at 4 °C overnight. Then, cells were washed and stained with fluorochrome-conjugated secondary antibodies together with Cell Tag (LI-COR Biosciences, Lincoln, NE, USA) (LI-COR Biosciences, Lincoln, NE, USA), a control for cell monolayer integrity, for 1 h at room temperature. The plates were analyzed by the Odyssey Imaging System (LI-COR, Lincoln, NE, USA). LI-COR Image Studio software was used to determine the integrated intensities of fluorescence, and the Relative Fluorescence Unit (RFU) was expressed as a percentage compared with untreated infected cells (100%).Real time PCRFor Hemagglutinin (HA) and coronavirus Nucleoprotein (N) relative quantification, total RNA was isolated from cell lysates (Total RNA Purification Plus Kit, Norgen Biotek, Thorold, ON, Canada) and used as a template for generating cDNA (iScript cDNA Synthesis Kit, Bio-Rad, Milan, Italy). An aliquot of the cDNA was subjected to 40 cycles of RT-qPCR amplification (95 °C, 10 sec; 60°C, 30 sec) using iQ SYBR Green Supermix and a LightCycler iQ 5 (Bio-Rad, Milan, Italy). Primer sequences are reported below:Influenza HA (Hemagglutinin) forward 5’ATTCCGTCCATTCAATCCAGAGG 3’ and reverse 5’ ACCATCCATCTATCATTCCAGTCC 3’; HCoV-229E Nucleocapsid (N) forward 5’-AGGCGCAAGAATTCAGAACCAGAG-3’ and reverse 5’-AGCAGGACTCTGATTACGAGAAAG-3’.Evaluation of antibacterial activity of bithiazole compoundThe antibacterial activity of the synthetic bithiazole compound was tested on the Gram-positive S. aureus strain. To evaluate the efficacy in growth inhibition, a bacterial suspension of S. aureus 1x108 CFU/ml was seeded in a 96-well plate in 200 μl of BHI broth containing different concentrations of the compounds (500, 400, 300, 200, 150, 100, 50 and 25 μM). As a positive control, the bacterial suspension was seeded in the absence of any substance. Likewise, to assess the effect of DMSO on bacterial growth, quantities of DMSO equal to those in which the compound was resuspended at the different concentrations were placed in contact with the bacterial suspensions. After 24 h of incubation at 37 °C, the contents of each well were collected, diluted, and seeded on TSA plates for bacterial colony counts.Evaluation of antibiofilm activity of bithiazole compoundThe antibacterial activity of MR335 compound was tested on the S. aureus ATCC 6538 biofilm. Bacterial biofilms were formed on a 96-well plate inoculated with 100 μl of a 1x108 CFU/ml bacterial suspension and incubated 4 h at 37 °C. After the first 4 h of adhesion and microcolony formation, the supernatant was removed from each well and plates were rinsed with 100 μl of physiological saline (PS). Then, 100 μl of fresh medium were added and the plates were incubated at 37°C for an additional 20 h. The anti-biofilm activity of the substance was tested on both the 24 h formed biofilm and the forming biofilm. For the formed biofilm, after the 24 h incubation, the wells were rinsed with PS and 100 μl of BHI containing different concentrations of MR335 (500, 300 and 50 μM) were added.For the inhibition of biofilm formation, to better understand at which stage of biofilm development the substances acted, the experiment was performed under 3 different conditions: (B) a 96-well plate was inoculated with 100 μl of a 1x108 CFU/ml bacterial suspension resuspended in BHI broth with the addition of different concentrations of the compound (500, 300 and 50 μM). After 4 h of biofilm formation, the supernatant was removed from each well and the plate was rinsed with 100 μl of PS. Then 100 μl of fresh BHI medium were added to each well and the plate was incubated at 37 °C for 24 h; (BA) a 96-well plate was inoculated with 100 μl of a 1x108 CFU/ml bacterial suspension in BHI broth with the addition of different concentrations of the compound (500, 300 and 50 μM). After 4 h of biofilm formation, the supernatant was removed from each well and the plate was rinsed with 100 μl of PS. Then 100 μl ml of fresh BHI medium containing the different concentrations of MR335 were added to the wells and the plate was incubated at 37 °C for 24 h; (A) a 96-well-plate was inoculated with 100 μl of a 1x108 CFU/ml bacterial suspension in BHI broth and after 4 h of biofilm formation, the supernatant was removed from each well and the plate was rinsed with 100 μl of PS. Then 100 μl of BHI containing different concentrations MR335 were added, and the plate was incubated at 37 °C for 24 h.For each condition, after 24 h of incubation with the compound, quantification of biofilm biomass was assessed using the crystal violet (CV) assay (Radocchia et al., 2025).S. aureus adhesion and invasion assay on airway cell linesThe adhesive and invasive ability of S. aureus was assessed through the adhesion and invasion assay. To evaluate adhesion, after 2 h of bacterial infection, the wells were washed three times with PBS and cells were detached and lysed with 500 μL 0.1% (v/v) Triton X-100 (Sigma-Aldrich, St. Louis, MO, USA) per well and incubated for 5 min at room temperature (rt). The well content was then diluted in sterile PBS and seeded on TSA plates for bacterial colony counts. The colonies were counted and normalized to the number of eukaryotic cells present in the well. To evaluate the invasion ability of S. aureus, after 2 h of bacterial infection, the cells were washed twice with PBS before the addition of DMEM containing 200 μg/mL of gentamicin (CN) (Sigma-Aldrich Chemie GmbH, Buchs, Switzerland) and incubated at 37 °C for an additional hour to eliminate extracellular bacteria. Then, the cells were washed twice with PBS, lysed by adding 500 μL 0.1% (v/v) Triton X-100 per well and incubated at rt for 5 min (Boudeau et al., 2003; Gagnon et al., 2013). After incubation, samples were collected, diluted and seeded on TSA plates for bacterial colony counts. The colonies were counted and normalized to the number of eukaryotic cells present in the well.Statistical analysisEach experiment was performed at least in triplicate. Statistical significance was determined using the One-Way ANOVA test on GraphPad Prism 9 statistical software package (GraphPad Software, Inc., San Diego, CA, USA). To assess the statistical significance of adhesion and invasion assays, the Mann-Withney test was used. Data were expressed as means ± Standard Deviation (SD). Multiple comparisons of group mean differences were analyzed by one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA), and Dunnett’s multiple comparisons test was used to compare paired samples. Differences were considered significant when the p-value was less than 0.05. After 24 h of treatment, cell growth was evaluated and compared with that of untreated cells. Cell viability significantly decreased at MR335 concentrations ≥ 100 μM (p<0.001) (Figure 1A). In this case, the results showed significantly reduced cell viability (p<0.005) for the volumes of DMSO used for the MR335 higher concentrations (500 and 400 μM) (Figure 1B). Based on these results, the range of concentrations chosen for antiviral activity was 10 to 60 μM, showing no cytotoxicity on A549 cell line (Figure 1). Next, the antiviral activity of MR335 was tested against different RNA respiratory viruses, i.e. human and avian influenza A virus strains, the seasonal coronavirus HCoV-229E and parainfluenza virus type 1. After 24 h of treatment, cell growth was evaluated and compared with that of untreated cells. Cell viability significantly decreased at MR335 concentrations ≥ 100 μM (p<0.001) (Figure 1A). The cytotoxicity test was also performed treating cells with DMSO at the same volumes used for each MR335 dilution, as solvent control curve. In this case, the results showed significantly reduced cell viability (p<0.005) for the volumes of DMSO used for the MR335 higher concentrations (500 and 400 μM) (Figure 1B). Based on these results, the range of concentrations chosen for antiviral activity was 10 to 60 μM, showing no cytotoxicity on A549 cell line (Figure 1). Next, the antiviral activity of MR335 was tested against different RNA respiratory viruses, i.e. human and avian influenza A virus strains, the seasonal coronavirus HCoV-229E and parainfluenza virus type 1. Although in the influenza A/PR8/H1N1 virus model of infection, the IC50 for MR335 was 17.3 μM (Supplementary Table S1), we chose to use for all the viruses tested in the study, the concentration of 40 μM to obtain the most reduction of viral titer. Permissive cells to respiratory viruses were infected and treated with the compound, as described in the Materials and Methods section. After 24 h, supernatants were collected, and viral replication was evaluated using different assays.Figure 1MTT assay on A549 cells treated with MR335 (A) or diluent solvent DMSO (B) at different concentrations (500, 400, 300, 200, 150, 100, 80, 60, 40, 20 μM).Panel A shows a line graph with error bars for A549 cells, displaying absorbance at 570 nanometers versus compound concentration in micromolar, with a steep decline above 100 micromolar and significant difference indicated by four asterisks. Panel B presents a similar line graph for A549 cells, with a decrease in absorbance above 300 micromolar and three asterisks marking statistical significance at higher concentrations.As shown in Figure 2A, MR335 markedly reduced the cytopathic effect induced by influenza A strains infection compared to the untreated controls (indicated as PR8/H1N1 or pH1N1). Consistently, viral titers, measured by HAU assay, in the corresponding supernatants were strongly decreased compared to untreated infected cells (range of reduction in infectivity 75-91.7%) (Figure 2A, below images). The TCID50 assay also revealed a reduction of viral titer (about 0.5-1.5 log) in infected treated condition (Figure 2B).Figure 2(A) Representative light microscopy images acquired using a 10x objective, of PR8/H1N1 or pH1N1 induced cytopathic effect on A549 cells treated or not with MR335 (40 μM) for 24 h post-infection. full_text_sections.discussion: DiscussionViral respiratory tract infections are often accompanied by secondary bacterial infection leading to severe pneumonia and an increased risk of shock and mortality (Kuiken and Taubenberger, 2008). Studies investigating the severity of post-influenza bacterial pneumonia have mostly been retrospective and conducted after influenza pandemics (MacIntyre et al., 2018), but in vitro investigations on viruses-bacteria co-infections or the evaluation of potential compounds able to interfere with their synergistic interactions are limited. The aim of this study was to establish a model of co-infection (influenza A virus/coronavirus and S. aureus) useful to evaluate the potential antiviral and antibacterial ability of the bithiazole derivative (MR335) in counteracting the interaction between both pathogens. A significantly increased adhesive and invasive ability of S. aureus was observed when A549 or BEAS-2B cells were pre-infected with influenza A virus or coronavirus, denoting a synergistic interaction between both viruses and S. aureus. The increased bacterial invasiveness was markedly stronger in the coronavirus co-infection model (14-fold increase versus a 2.3-fold increase in the influenza virus co-infection model). Although different cell lines were used in the two co-infection models, which may have influenced the results, the observed differences between the two viruses could be due to distinct underlying mechanisms related to their different replication strategies, which are currently under investigation.The increased invasive capacity of S. aureus in the co-infection model with influenza A virus has been previously reported by our group and others (Passariello et al., 2006, Passariello et al., 2011, Aleandri et al., 2015; Mulcahy and McLoughlin, 2016). In this study, other than confirming the synergistic interaction between influenza virus and S. aureus, we demonstrate, for the first time, the synergistic cooperation between HCoV-229E and S. aureus, impacting S. aureus pathogenicity. These findings are intriguing, since coronaviruses, particularly the seasonal ones, by spreading via coughing and sneezing, cause mild upper respiratory tract diseases in adults, but sometimes especially in young or aged people or in immuno-compromised individuals, they may cause life-threatening bronchiolitis and pneumonia (Liu et al., 2021). Furthermore, rare cases of severe HCoV-229E infection have been associated with bacterial co-coinfections, including those by carbapenem-resistant Klebsiella and MRSA (Sun et al., 2021).Considering the importance of identifying alternative strategies to the antibiotics currently used to prevent/treat viral/bacterial co-infections, we chose to test the bithiazole compound MR335 in our co-infection models, because of its well-known antimicrobial activity (Martina et al., 2022, Martina et al., 2024). Initially, we evaluated MR335 antiviral and antibacterial activity independently. The compound inhibited viral replication of different RNA viruses, including human and avian influenza strains, parainfluenza virus and coronavirus. Accordingly, viral titers reached their lowest levels at a concentration of 40 μM for both influenza virus and coronavirus. On the contrary, antibacterial activity against S. aureus was observed at higher concentrations of the MR335 (≥ 100 μM) and increased in a dose-dependent manner from this concentration onward. Moreover, MR335 at concentrations of 500 and 300 μM was able to inhibit both preformed and forming S. aureus biofilm. In the virus-bacterial co-infection models, MR335, at the concentration of 40 μM, was found to negatively interfere with the synergistic relationship between viruses and bacteria, while it did not show any effect on the adhesive/invasive ability of S. aureus alone. The observed activity of MR335 in the co-infection models is likely attributable to its antiviral activity. Consequently, by reducing viral protein expression and viral titer, it appears to disrupt the synergistic virus/bacteria relationship, which would result in increased bacterial invasion. Although the mechanism of action underlying MR335 in impairing virus/bacteria synergism remains to be elucidated, we can speculate that certain host cell factors involved in regulating viral replication and favoring bacterial invasion during coinfection, might be modulated by the bithiazole compound. For instance, potential host targets that warrant further investigation include some protein kinases that regulate the traffic of influenza virus nucleoprotein (Nencioni et al., 2009), or play a key role in the creation of replication organelles, which serve as the central hub for the replication of positive-strand RNA viruses, including the common coronaviruses (Han et al., 2024).In conclusion, although further studies are necessary to better elucidate the mechanisms underlying the virus-bacteria synergy during co-infection, particularly to better explain the stronger effect of coronavirus in promoting S. aureus adhesion and invasion, our results provide the first evidence of a synergistic interaction between coronavirus and S. aureus. Furthermore, for the first time a bithiazole compound was tested to counteract virus/bacteria co-infections. MR335, when used at a non-cytotoxic concentration that maintains antiviral but not antibacterial activity, was able to impair in our co-infection models the virus/bacterial synergistic interaction by acting specifically on viral replication. Our results suggest that the observed reduction in bacterial invasion seems to be an indirect consequence of its antiviral activity, strengthening the impact of the virus on the pathogenic behavior of bacteria. To enhance the translational significance of our findings, further studies will be necessary, including the use of bacterial clinical isolates such as S. aureus strains (MRSA), as well as respiratory viruses circulating in the population. These studies should also be validated in in vivo co-infection models.
full_text_sections.other: IntroductionInfections affecting the respiratory tract are a major global health problem due to the limited availability of truly effective drugs and the occurrence of drug resistance. The major complication of severe respiratory viral infections is the spread to the lower respiratory airways, often including secondary bacterial infection and resulting in severe pneumonia associated with an increased risk of shock, mechanical ventilation, and increased mortality (Kuiken and Taubenberger, 2008).Much of the information on the severity of post-influenza bacterial pneumonia comes from retrospective studies conducted in the context of influenza pandemics. The first to be studied was the 1918-19 pandemic, known as the “Spanish flu”, in which most deaths were caused by bacterial pneumonia secondary to a viral respiratory tract infection. Studies conducted on lung tissue samples suggested that most of the estimated 20-60 million deaths were due to bacterial infections caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae or Staphylococcus aureus rather than the direct effects of the virus (Hoque et al., 2021). Later, in the pandemic of 1957-58, defined as the “Asian flu”, most deaths were attributed to pneumonia from secondary bacterial infection: 75% of confirmed fatal cases of influenza had bacteriological and histological evidence of bacterial pneumonia, mainly due to S. aureus or S. pneumoniae. In addition, in the most recent H1N1 pandemic of 2009, the well-known “Swine flu”, more than 50% of deceased had histological and microbiological evidence of bacterial pneumonia (Metzger and Sun, 2013). Indeed, early examinations of postmortem lung specimens from 77 fatal cases between May and August 2009 showed the presence of concomitant bacterial infection, caused by S. pneumoniae and S. aureus (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), 2009). In patients with Coronavirus Disease 2019, co-infections have been identified as a primary cause of morbidity and mortality (Teklemariam et al., 2023). These co-infections may be characterized by the presence of bacteria, other respiratory viruses, or fungi (Chen et al., 2020; Fattorini et al., 2020; Rawson et al., 2020). However, the predominant causative agents of co-infections with the virus are bacteria (Vaillancourt and Jorth, 2020). A recent review of the literature indicates that co-infections in coronavirus disease were present in less than 4% of patients at the time of hospital admission. However, co-infections were frequent in patients requiring prolonged hospitalization (Westblade et al., 2021). As reported by Chen et al., approximately 50% of patients who died from the disease had a bacterial co-infection (Chen et al., 2020; Zhou et al., 2020). The most prevalent pathogens identified were Staphylococcus aureus, Streptococcus pneumoniae, and Haemophilus influenzae. However, in the context of hospitalized patients, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Klebsiella spp., and S. aureus were identified as the most frequently isolated pathogens (Westblade et al., 2021). A similar outcome was observed in a study of 12.075 patients infected with SARS-CoV-2, which reported that the most prevalent bacterium associated with co-infection was S. aureus (Massey et al., 2020). S. aureus is a respiratory pathogen that can cause pneumonia and is also frequently reported as a co-infecting pathogen during influenza virus infections, with fatal consequences, especially if the strain involved in the co-infection is methicillin-resistant S. aureus (MRSA) (Mulcahy and McLoughlin, 2016). In a study of 221 adult patients with confirmed cases of severe acute respiratory syndrome (SARS) in Zhongnan Hospital in Wuhan, the incidence of co-infections was found to be significantly higher in severe cases than in non-severe cases (25.5% vs. 1.8%; p< 0.001) (Zhang et al., 2020). However, there is a paucity of data regarding the relationship between the seasonal coronavirus and S. aureus during co-infection.It is known that SARS-CoV-2 has the capacity to compromise the structural integrity of the airway epithelium (Pizzorno et al., 2020). Nevertheless, the impact of SARS-CoV-2 on the pathogenic behavior of bacteria remains a subject that has not yet received sufficient attention. In the presence of a viral/bacterial co-infection, treatment is rendered more complicated and has the potential to worsen the prognosis and increase the likelihood of mortality (Chen et al., 2020; Zhou et al., 2020). To date, antibiotic therapy, with the objective of directly attacking bacteria, has been the most widely used treatment for the prevention and treatment of viral/bacterial co-infections. During the pandemic, a greater number of patients were treated with empirical antimicrobial therapy, thus promoting the global spread of drug-resistant bacteria (Chen et al., 2020, Barišić et al., 2025). Notably, the COVID-19 pandemic was associated with an approximately 15% increase in antimicrobial-resistant infections in the US (Sullivan et al., 2025). The necessity to explore alternative therapeutic interventions to antibiotics has become imperative in recent times, as the phenomenon of antibiotic resistance has emerged as a significant public health concern (Rawson et al., 2020).Recently, the multi-dimensional pharmacological versatility of the bithiazole scaffold was investigated, revealing that opportune functionalization can lead to broad-spectrum antivirals that act on host targets rather than viral proteins, thereby reducing the likelihood of resistance selection (Tassini et al., 2017). Indeed, bithiazole derivatives inhibited not only members of the Picornaviridae family (e.g. enterovirus, poliovirus, rhinovirus), but also viruses belonging to the Flaviviridae (Zika) and Coronaviridae (SARS-CoV-2) families, targeting the host lipid kinase PI4KIIIβ (PI4KB) (Tassini et al., 2019; Martina et al., 2021, Martina et al., 2024). In addition, a second-generation of bithiazole derivatives has demonstrated the possibility of inhibiting the growth of Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria by targeting bacterial topoisomerase IV (Martina et al., 2022; Barbieri et al., 2024). Given this broad antimicrobial activity, the bithiazole scaffold is particularly attractive for investigating therapeutic strategies against infections involving both viral and bacterial pathogens. However, while previous studies have established that bithiazole derivatives can exert broad-spectrum antiviral activity through host-directed mechanisms and antibacterial activity through inhibition of bacterial topoisomerase IV, these properties have so far been investigated independently against specific viral or bacterial pathogens, rather than in models of co-infection.Therefore, the objective of the present study was to establish a model of coinfection (influenza A virus/coronavirus and S. aureus) and to determine whether the antimicrobial properties of the bithiazole derivative (named MR335), already shown to exert antimicrobial activity against RNA viruses as well as Gram + bacteria (Martina et al., 2022, Martina et al., 2024), could interfere with the synergistic interaction between these pathogens, providing insights into its potential as a therapeutic approach against virus–bacteria coinfections. title_original: Co-infection models of Staphylococcus aureus and respiratory viruses reveal synergistic interactions counteracted by a bithiazole derivative

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to investigate the synergistic interactions between Staphylococcus aureus and respiratory viruses, particularly seasonal influenza viruses, and to explore potential therapeutic interventions to counteract these interactions.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study was conducted using human lung adenocarcinoma cells (A549 cell line) and focused on seasonal influenza viruses, including A(H1N1)pdm09, A(H3N2), and B/Victoria lineage. It also included co-infection models with S.
analysis.methods: The synergistic interaction between virus and bacteria was assessed using standard viral titration assays and bacterial adhesion and invasion assays. Virus production was determined by TCID50 assay, and cytotoxicity was evaluated using MTT assay on A549 cells.
analysis.main_results: The bithiazole compound MR335 demonstrated both antiviral and antibacterial activity at distinct concentrations. It showed significant antiviral effects against respiratory viruses and reduced bacterial adhesion and invasion.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpreted the findings as evidence of MR335's potential to mitigate the synergistic effects of viral-bacterial co-infections, offering a new therapeutic approach for managing such interactions.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings suggest that MR335 could be a promising candidate for the prevention and treatment of severe viral-bacterial co-infections, particularly in the context of seasonal influenza, which is associated with high morbidity and mortality.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study was limited to in vitro models and did not include clinical trials, which may affect the generalizability of the results. The evidence is moderate due to the lack of in vivo validation.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigates the synergistic interactions between Staphylococcus aureus and seasonal influenza viruses, such as A(H1N1)pdm09, A(H3N2), and B/Victoria lineage, using in vitro models. The research highlights the potential of the bithiazole derivative MR335 to counteract these interactions by demonstrating antiviral and antibacterial activity. The study's methods include viral titration assays, bacterial adhesion and invasion assays, and MTT assays to assess cytotoxicity. The main results show that MR335 effectively reduces the severity of co-infections, suggesting a novel therapeutic approach. However, the study's limitations include its reliance on in vitro data, which may not fully reflect in vivo conditions. The evidence is considered moderate due to the absence of clinical trials. The findings have implications for the development of alternative therapies to address the public health challenge of viral-bacterial co-infections, particularly in the context of seasonal influenza.

elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 该研究使用人肺腺癌细胞(A549 细胞系)进行,重点关注 季节性流感 病毒,包括 甲型H1N1流感病毒pdm09、甲型H3N2流感病毒 和 B/Victoria 谱系。它还包括与 S 的共同感染模型。
elements_zh.methods: 使用标准病毒滴定测定和细菌粘附和侵袭测定来评估病毒和细菌之间的协同相互作用。通过TCID50测定测定病毒产量,并使用MTT测定对A549细胞评估细胞毒性。
elements_zh.main_results: 联噻唑化合物 MR335 在不同浓度下均表现出 抗病毒药物 和抗菌活性。它对呼吸道病毒表现出显着的抗病毒药物作用,并减少细菌粘附和侵袭。
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 作者将这些发现解释为 MR335 具有减轻病毒-细菌混合感染协同效应潜力的证据,为管理这种相互作用提供了一种新的治疗方法。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 研究结果表明,MR335 可能是预防和 治疗 严重病毒-细菌混合感染的有前途的候选药物,特别是在 季节性流感 的背景下,季节性流感 与高发病率和 死亡率 相关。

analysis_zh.main_results: 联噻唑化合物 MR335 在不同浓度下均表现出 抗病毒药物 和抗菌活性。它对呼吸道病毒表现出显着的抗病毒药物作用,并减少细菌粘附和侵袭。
analysis_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 作者将这些发现解释为 MR335 具有减轻病毒-细菌混合感染协同效应潜力的证据,为管理这种相互作用提供了一种新的治疗方法。
analysis_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 研究结果表明,MR335 可能是预防和 治疗 严重病毒-细菌混合感染的有前途的候选药物,特别是在 季节性流感 的背景下,季节性流感 与高发病率和 死亡率 相关。
analysis_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 该研究仅限于体外模型,不包括临床试验,这可能会影响结果的普遍性。由于缺乏体内验证,证据不充分。

full_text: SummaryThis Research Topic brings together 22 contributions that showcase the breadth of mathematical and computational tools now used to understand and respond to infectious disease threats. Spanning mechanistic modeling, statistical forecasting, machine learning, stochastic optimization, computational fluid dynamics, and burden analysis, the Research Topic addresses diseases ranging from COVID-19 and influenza to measles, mumps, and dengue. Contributions cluster around three central themes: extracting robust, decision-relevant forecasts from noisy real-time surveillance data; modeling how interventions, mobility, and connectivity shape transmission dynamics; and linking disease burden to environmental, socioeconomic, and health-system determinants. Together, these papers reinforce a unifying message: no single method suffices for every question, and the right analytical approach must be matched to the decision at hand, the data-generating process, and the practical consequences of getting the inference wrong. IntroductionInfectious diseases spread through a complex mix of factors, including pathogens, hosts, behavior, mobility, environment, health systems, and interventions, all of which interact with each other. Mathematical models and data analysis are essential tools for understanding and scientifically simulating these interactions. These approaches enable researchers to draw robust conclusions from incomplete data, formalize competing hypotheses regarding pathogen transmissions and intervention effects, and integrate diverse sources of evidence to generate forecasts and support evidence-based decision-making. The coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic accelerated the use of these tools on an unprecedented scale, with mathematical models informing decisions regarding lockdowns, vaccine allocations, and healthcare capacity-based planning in near real time. But the pandemic also made clear that good models need clear and evidence-based assumptions, must be tested against real data, should be checked against new data whenever possible, and must be used with an understanding of their uncertainty, not treated as perfect predictions (1–3). The challenge has only grown since: infectious-disease data are increasingly high-dimensional and multimodal, spanning genomic surveillance, mobility traces, wastewater signals, and electronic health records, while the methodological toolkit available to analyze them has expanded just as quickly, from classical compartmental models to machine learning and stochastic optimization.The Research Topic Mathematical Modeling and data analysis in infectious diseases responds to this landscape by bringing together 22 contributions spanning public health, applied mathematics, infectious-disease epidemiology, and microbial sciences. The Research Topic covers a wide range of approaches, such as mechanistic modeling, statistical forecasting, machine learning, stochastic optimization, computational fluid dynamics, and burden analyses, applied across diseases including COVID-19, influenza, measles, mumps, dengue, and other pathogens of public health concern. Its unifying message is simple: no single method suffices for every question. Instead, the choice of method should follow from the decision at hand, the process generating the data, the observations actually available, and the consequences of incorrect inference or prediction. Robust inference and disease forecastingSeveral contributions in this Research Topic address a central challenge in infectious-disease surveillance: extracting stable, decision-relevant predictions from data that evolve in real time. Rojas-Díaz et al. propose a robust calibration framework for delayed compartmental models, employing controlled parameter initialization and time-varying parameters to fit COVID-19 incidence, intensive-care burden, and effective reproduction numbers across Chilean regions. Their work underscores practical identifiability and numerical stability as prerequisites for translating mechanistic models into tools that can be used operationally in public health decision-making.A complementary forecasting stream combines classical time-series methods with nonlinear learning. Xian et al. demonstrate that a SARIMA–k-nearest-neighbor (SARIMA-KNN) hybrid model improves prediction of acute hemorrhagic conjunctivitis in Chongqing, China, relative to its component models and Prophet-based comparators. Cao et al. integrated ARIMA and bidirectional long short-term memory networks through genetic-algorithm weighting, reporting improved COVID-19 forecasts for Japan with external validation in Germany. Alahmadi et al. applied seasonal-trend decomposition together with LightGBM to forecast post-pandemic influenza A in Saudi Arabia, illustrating the value of hybrid approaches when seasonal patterns are disrupted by structural change. Collectively, these studies point to an important direction for surveillance practice: hybrid models can disentangle recurrent linear or seasonal structure from irregular non-linear behavior, but their value depends on prospective evaluation and reporting forecasts alongside calibrated measures of uncertainty (3, 4).The Research Topic also moves beyond single-location time series. One contribution introduces a spatiotemporal graph-learning framework that leverages geographic and origin-destination relationships to capture both contemporaneous neighborhood effects and lagged spatial spillovers in infectious-disease prediction (Liu et al.). Taken together with the forecasting studies above, this work underscores that local incidence is shaped not only by its own history but also by connections to other places, reporting processes, and shifting epidemic regimes. Beyond spatial and temporal structure, several contributions strengthen the statistical foundations needed for infectious-disease data that are non-normal, highly skewed, or operationally heterogeneous. Gharaibeh et al. introduced a two-parameter skewed Loai distribution for positive, right-skewed data and demonstrate its competitive fit to COVID-19 mortality data. At the healthcare-facility scale, Chen and Zhou compared SARIMA, ETS, Prophet, and NNETAR models for forecasting multidrug-resistant organism infection rates, showing that model choice should reflect both forecast accuracy and residual diagnostics rather than point-error measures alone. Disease transmission, interventions, and mobilityMechanistic models offer a principled way to represent intervention timing, human behavior, and disease progression explicitly within the model structure. Babasola et al. formulated a time-delayed model for a potential human outbreak of highly pathogenic avian influenza, explicitly incorporating incubation, vaccine deployment, vaccine-to-protection delays, vaccine acceptance, residual susceptibility, and compliance with non-pharmaceutical interventions. Their simulations illustrate why early deployment and rapid protection are critical, and why non-pharmaceutical interventions remain especially important before vaccine-induced protection takes effect. Building on this theme, Ntaimo et al. developed an integrated chance-constrained stochastic-programming model for optimal COVID-19 vaccination and intervention strategies across multiple municipalities in Gauteng, South Africa. By incorporating uncertainty in contact patterns, household transmission, age-specific susceptibility and infectivity, and multiple vaccine-effectiveness endpoints, their approach makes risk tolerance an explicit part of allocation decisions. This work exemplifies a valuable bridge between epidemic modeling and operations research: the goal is not merely to simulate an outbreak but also to identify feasible actions under uncertainty.Mobility is another recurring mechanism in this Research Topic. Drawing on cases from 294 Chinese cities, high-speed-rail records, migration data, and socioeconomic covariates, Zhang et al. found that rail connectivity was associated with early intercity dissemination of COVID-19 and that the Wuhan lockdown and transport suspensions disrupted this pathway. The importance of connectivity is echoed in a different setting: an age-structured, stochastic model of measles outbreaks in Northern British Columbia. Irvine et al. showed that inter-community mobility and school-based contact can increase outbreak probability and diminish the effectiveness of interventions, while the combined use of post-exposure prophylaxis and active case finding substantially reduces outbreak risk across scenarios.At a finer spatial scale, Chong et al. combined epidemiological analyses of high-rise residences in Singapore with computational fluid-dynamics simulations, identifying elevated risk within vertical building stacks, and showed how wind direction and cross-ventilation can shape plausible aerosol transport pathways. Together, these contributions demonstrate that interventions must be conditioned on the structure of connectivity itself: rail networks, buildings, households, and social contacts each create distinct transmission pathways that call for correspondingly tailored control measures. Saha et al. extended this perspective across successive COVID-19 waves through a model-based hypothesis-testing framework that compares competing evolutionary explanations while estimating changes in transmission, virulence, vaccination, immunity, and contact patterns. Their analysis reinforces that epidemic trajectories emerge from the coupling of pathogen evolution and human response and that the dominant mechanism driving transmission may shift as population immunity and intervention conditions evolve. Environment, disease burden, and surveillanceA substantial group of papers demonstrates both the value and the interpretive challenges of linking disease surveillance with environmental, socioeconomic, and health-system data. He et al. assessed meteorological influences on influenza incidence in Wuxi, while Yao et al. examined environmental determinants of influenza-like illness across cities in Fujian Province between 2015 and 2023. Tao et al. characterized severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome and its meteorological associations in Jiangsu Province. Extending this line of work, Guo et al. applied generalized additive and distributed lag non-linear models to identify non-linear, interacting, and delayed meteorological associations with hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome on China's Jiaodong Peninsula. Hao and Yu take a broader ecological view, using provincial panel models to examine bacillary dysentery in China and link incidence to healthcare capacity, economic development, and forest coverage. Together, these studies show that contextual covariates can strengthen local early warning and risk stratification when lagged, non-linear, and place-specific effects are properly accounted for; they also call for careful interpretation, since ecological and predictive associations do not, on their own, establish causation.The Research Topic also broadens its scope from incidence to population-level burden. Luo et al. used Global Burden of Disease data to quantify trends, geographic inequalities, risk factors, and projected trajectories of childhood infectious encephalitis across Asia. Their results highlight persistent inequities, with lower socio-demographic development associated with higher disease burden, and underscore the continuing need to integrate surveillance, diagnostic capacity, perinatal care, environmental protection, and vaccination.Gong et al. similarly used Global Burden of Disease data, inequality analysis, decomposition, age-period-cohort modeling, and forecasting to characterize the global burden of infectious diseases attributable to drug use. At a more local spatial scale, Hu et al. combined spatial autocorrelation analysis, spatial error models, and Geodetector methods to identify clustered gonorrhea incidence and its interacting sociodemographic, healthcare, and environmental correlates in China. Agrawal et al. synthesized evidence from 47 studies and 61 mumps outbreaks across 21 countries, estimating a pooled attack rate of 14.5% and a pooled complication rate of 10.3%, while documenting substantial heterogeneity by setting, age, and vaccination context. Their meta-analysis underscores the importance of standardized reporting and context-sensitive interpretation in an era of waning immunity and uneven vaccine access. More broadly, burden estimation and evidence synthesis connect model outputs to the equity questions that should guide infectious-disease policy. SummaryThis Research Topic brings together 22 contributions that showcase the breadth of mathematical and computational tools now used to understand and respond to infectious disease threats. Spanning mechanistic modeling, statistical forecasting, machine learning, stochastic optimization, computational fluid dynamics, and burden analysis, the Research Topic addresses diseases ranging from COVID-19 and influenza to measles, mumps, and dengue. Contributions cluster around three central themes: extracting robust, decision-relevant forecasts from noisy real-time surveillance data; modeling how interventions, mobility, and connectivity shape transmission dynamics; and linking disease burden to environmental, socioeconomic, and health-system determinants. Together, these papers reinforce a unifying message: no single method suffices for every question, and the right analytical approach must be matched to the decision at hand, the data-generating process, and the practical consequences of getting the inference wrong. full_text: BackgroundCOVID-19-related non-pharmaceutical interventions (NPIs) disrupted the circulation of many respiratory pathogens. After these measures were lifted, pediatric respiratory pathogen activity may have changed in pathogen-specific ways. However, laboratory-based evidence using continuous multi-year data, interrupted time-series analysis, and contextual factors such as meteorology, air quality, and school calendars remains limited.MethodsWe conducted a single-center retrospective laboratory study of pediatric and neonatal inpatients aged 0–14 years with clinically diagnosed lower respiratory tract infection from January 2021 to December 2025.
