During 7-day deduplication, only the first testing record from the same child within a 7-day window was retained. NPI, non-pharmaceutical intervention.Flowchart of study record selection and analysis. A total of 21,132 pediatric 13-pathogen respiratory nucleic acid testing records were screened; 836 records were excluded during data cleaning, leaving 20,296 preliminary records. After excluding 46 non-first repeat tests within 7 days, 20,250 records remained. These were classified into the NPI period (January 2021-December 2022; n = 6,490) and post-NPI period (January 2023–December 2025; n = 13,760), followed by risk-ratio, interrupted time-series, multivariable, age-stratified, co-detection, and sensitivity analyses.Children were categorized into four age groups: <1, 1–<3, 3–<6, and 6–14 years. This age stratification was selected according to commonly used pediatric respiratory infection epidemiology and the social contact patterns of children in China, broadly corresponding to infancy, early childhood mainly under home care, kindergarten age, and school age.2.3Respiratory pathogen testing and pathogen definitionsRespiratory pathogen nucleic acid testing was performed using a multiplex detection kit for 13 respiratory pathogens based on fluorescence PCR followed by capillary electrophoresis (PN: 1060071; Health GeneTech Co., Ltd., Ningbo, China). Nucleic acid extraction was performed using a TANBead SLA-32 automated nucleic acid extraction system. PCR amplification was performed using a SLAN-96P real-time PCR system. Amplification products were detected using an Applied Biosystems 3500 Dx Genetic Analyzer for capillary electrophoresis-based detection and fragment analysis. Sample processing, nucleic acid extraction, PCR amplification, capillary electrophoresis, quality control, and result interpretation were performed according to the manufacturer's instructions and local standard operating procedures.The main analysis included 13 respiratory pathogen categories: influenza A virus not further classified by this panel (InfA-NFC), influenza A H1N1 (2009) virus, seasonal influenza A (H3N2) virus, influenza B virus, human respiratory syncytial virus, human parainfluenza virus, human metapneumovirus, human rhinovirus, human adenovirus, seasonal human coronaviruses, human bocavirus, Mycoplasma pneumoniae, and Chlamydia spp. In this study, InfA-NFC referred to records positive for the manufacturer-reported generic influenza A target, listed as InfA in the manufacturer's instructions, but not classified as influenza A H1N1 (2009) virus or seasonal influenza A (H3N2) virus. The seasonal human coronaviruses category did not include SARS-CoV-2. Throughout the study period, SARS-CoV-2 testing, when clinically indicated, was performed through a separate dedicated nucleic acid testing pathway and was therefore not included in the fixed 13-target respiratory pathogen panel analyzed in this study. The Chlamydia category was not further differentiated into C. trachomatis or C. pneumoniae. Pathogen abbreviations, full pathogen names, manufacturer-reported detection targets, and limits of detection are provided in Supplementary Table S1.A composite influenza A variable was defined as positivity for any influenza A-related analytic category, including InfA-NFC, influenza A H1N1 (2009) virus, or seasonal influenza A(H3N2) virus. This composite variable was used only for descriptive summaries and was not included as an additional category in the main risk ratio, multiple-comparison, interrupted time-series, or multivariable regression analyses to avoid double counting. Overall positivity was defined as positivity for at least one of the 13 main respiratory pathogen categories. Co-detection was defined as positivity for two or more of the 13 main pathogen categories in the same testing record. Positivity and co-detection rates were calculated using the corresponding number of testing records as the denominator. A 13-target-negative record was defined as a testing record in which none of the 13 main respiratory pathogen categories was detected. Overall positivity and 13-target-negative proportions describe laboratory detection among tested pediatric and neonatal inpatients and were not intended as estimates of community incidence or prevalence.2.4Study periods, seasons, and school-term statusThe study period was divided according to the timing of COVID-19 policy adjustment in China and the monthly structure of the dataset. January 2021 to December 2022 was defined as the NPI period, and January 2023 to December 2025 was defined as the post-NPI period. In interrupted time-series analyses, January 2023 was treated as the first post-intervention month. Seasons were defined by calendar month: spring, March to May; summer, June to August; autumn, September to November; and winter, December to February. School-term status was defined at the calendar-day level according to the official local school calendar rather than by calendar month alone and assigned to each testing record based on the application date. Each testing record was classified as occurring during an in-school term or a vacation period. This variable was used as a population-level contextual indicator of periods with increased or decreased community contact networks related to kindergarten and school attendance.2.5Meteorological and air-quality dataDaily meteorological observations for Nanchong, Sichuan Province, China were obtained from RP5 (Reliable Prognosis), a publicly available weather data platform providing observational data from ground weather stations. Before monthly aggregation, extracted AQI records were checked for completeness, date consistency, plausible value ranges, and temporal continuity. Daily temperature, relative humidity, and AQI records were aggregated into monthly means for each calendar month and linked to individual testing records by year-month. Temperature was modeled per 1 °C increase, relative humidity per 10% increase, and AQI per 10-unit increase. Categorical variables were summarized as counts and percentages. Continuous variables were summarized as medians with interquartile ranges or means with standard deviations, as appropriate. All tests were two-sided, and P < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. For multiple comparisons across the 13 main pathogen categories, the Benjamini–Hochberg method was used to control the false discovery rate (FDR). Categorical variables were compared using the χ2 test or Fisher's exact test, as appropriate. Continuous variables were compared using the Mann–Whitney U test or t test, depending on distributional characteristics. Continuous age is presented as median (interquartile range) and was compared between the NPI and post-NPI periods using the Mann–Whitney U test.2.6.2Risk ratio analysisDetection risks for the 13 main respiratory pathogen categories were compared between the NPI and post-NPI periods. RSV detection was first compared between children aged <2 years and those aged ≥2 years. Children were further categorized as 0–<6 months, 6–<12 months, 12–<24 months, and ≥24 months. For each category, RSV positivity was summarized for the NPI and post-NPI periods, and post-NPI vs. NPI risk ratios (RRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs), P values, and FDR-adjusted P values were calculated. ITS and segmented regression models are commonly used to evaluate level and slope changes after public health policy or intervention changes (21–24).For each pathogen, the monthly positivity rate was used as the outcome. The core independent variables included time, intervention status, and time after intervention. Month fixed effects were included to account for seasonality. Models were weighted by the monthly number of testing records. Newey–West robust standard errors were used to account for potential autocorrelation (25). The primary model used Newey–West lag = 1, and lag = 3 was used as a sensitivity analysis.The model was specified as: Yt = β0 + β1 × time + β2 × intervention + β3 × post-intervention time + month fixed effects + εt, where β1 represents the pre-intervention monthly trend, β2 represents the immediate level change after the lifting of NPIs, and β3 represents the post-intervention trend change.2.6.4Multivariable logistic regressionTo evaluate factors associated with pathogen positivity, separate multivariable logistic regression models were fitted for each of the 13 main respiratory pathogen categories. Across 13 pathogen categories and four contextual factors, 52 interaction tests were prespecified. full_text_sections.results: 3Results3.1Study population and baseline characteristicsA total of 20,250 throat-swab testing records were included in the main analysis, covering 60 consecutive months from January 2021 to December 2025, including 6,490 records during the NPI period and 13,760 during the post-NPI period. Monthly testing volume and overall positivity trends are shown in Figure 2. Among the included records, 11,191 were from boys (55.3%) and 9,059 from girls (44.7%). The median age was 2.00 years overall and in both the NPI and post-NPI periods. The overall IQR was 0.75–4.00 years, while the IQRs were 0.67–4.00 years during the NPI period and 0.75–4.00 years during the post-NPI period. The largest age group was 3–<6 years (30.2%), followed by <1 year (29.4%), 1–<3 years (25.3%), and 6–14 years (15.1%). Overall, 16,871 records (83.3%) were collected during school terms and 3,379 (16.7%) during vacation periods. Baseline demographic and temporal characteristics differed between the NPI and post-NPI periods, including sex distribution, age group, season, and school-term status (Table 1).Figure 2Monthly testing volume and overall respiratory pathogen positivity from January 2021 to December 2025. The grey bars show the monthly number of pediatric respiratory pathogen testing records, and the red line shows the overall positivity rate for at least one of the 13 main respiratory pathogen categories. The vertical dashed line indicates the start of the post-NPI period in January 2023. full_text_sections.discussion: 4Discussion4.1Principal findingsThis 5-year hospital-based laboratory surveillance study identified marked changes in pediatric respiratory pathogen detection across the NPI and post-NPI periods, with distinct temporal patterns across pathogens. Overall positivity was higher in the post-NPI period than in the NPI period (75.4% vs. 58.8%), and co-detection was also more frequent (15.2% vs. 6.0%). At the aggregate level, overall positivity showed a significant long-term increasing trend over the 5-year study period, whereas segmented analysis using January 2023 as the interruption point showed no statistically significant immediate level or slope change. At the pathogen-specific level, ITS analyses revealed distinct temporal trajectories across pathogens, with human adenovirus showing a robust immediate decrease and human rhinovirus showing a significant positive trend change and a positive post-NPI slope. Associations with environmental factors and school-calendar status were likewise pathogen-specific, and phase-interaction analyses further showed that selected associations with temperature, relative humidity, and school-term status differed between the NPI and post-NPI periods. Overall, these findings demonstrate a complex temporal profile of pediatric respiratory pathogen detection characterized by a long-term aggregate trend, pathogen-specific changes, and associations with environmental and school-calendar factors.4.2Overall positivity, long-term trend, and co-detection across study periodsCOVID-19-related NPIs substantially altered the circulation of common respiratory pathogens (7–11), and subsequent studies reported renewed circulation and altered epidemiological patterns of multiple respiratory pathogens following relaxation of these measures (12–16). In our study, overall positivity was higher in the post-NPI period than in the NPI period. Further analysis of the overall temporal trend showed that overall positivity increased by an average of 0.49 percentage points per month over the 5-year study period, whereas segmented analysis with January 2023 as the interruption point did not show significant changes in the overall level or trend. These findings place the higher overall positivity observed in the post-NPI period within a broader long-term upward trend and suggest that aggregate measures may not fully capture heterogeneous temporal dynamics across individual pathogens.Co-detection also increased markedly in the post-NPI period, and this increase was supported by both the period comparison and weighted ITS analysis. This pattern may reflect greater temporal overlap in the circulation of multiple respiratory pathogens, thereby increasing the likelihood of detecting more than one pathogen in the same specimen. For hospital-based laboratory surveillance, co-detection patterns provide information beyond single-pathogen positivity and add complexity to etiological attribution and laboratory interpretation. Accordingly, considering both single-pathogen temporal trends and multi-pathogen co-detection patterns may provide a more complete characterization of pediatric respiratory pathogen activity in the post-NPI period.4.3Pathogen-specific reshaping of detection patternsA central finding of this study is that pathogen detection patterns changed heterogeneously after the lifting of NPIs. Although many pathogen categories showed higher detection risks in the post-NPI period, the magnitude, timing, and stability of changes varied across pathogens. This pattern is consistent with reports of asynchronous respiratory virus resurgence and pathogen-specific recovery after relaxation of COVID-19-related restrictions (12, 14, 30). It supports the concept that the post-NPI period may represent pathogen-specific reshaping rather than a simple synchronized return to pre-pandemic seasonality. This distinction is important because aggregate respiratory pathogen positivity may obscure divergent trajectories among individual pathogens.Human rhinovirus showed the most statistically robust trend-related finding in our ITS analysis, with a significant positive trend change after the January 2023 interruption and a positive post-NPI slope. This pattern is consistent with previous pediatric studies showing that rhinovirus activity was less suppressed by NPIs and could remain prominent or increase while several other respiratory viruses showed marked reductions or altered circulation (31–33). The positive association between school-term status and human rhinovirus positivity across age strata is also consistent with evidence that school sessions, holidays, and closures can influence respiratory infection activity in children (20, 34, 35). Thus, human rhinovirus may function as a sensitive indicator of renewed pediatric contact networks in the post-NPI period. Nevertheless, school-term status in this study was defined by calendar timing and should be interpreted as a population-level contextual indicator rather than a direct measure of individual school attendance, classroom exposure, or transmission pathway.Several pathogens, including human metapneumovirus, influenza A H1N1 (2009) virus, human respiratory syncytial virus, human parainfluenza virus, and seasonal human coronaviruses, showed immediate level increases in the primary ITS model. Similar post-restriction shifts in human metapneumovirus, influenza, and other respiratory viruses have been reported after periods of reduced circulation or relaxation of COVID-19 restrictions (13, 36, 37). However, these signals in our study were attenuated after FDR correction, indicating lower statistical robustness under multiple-comparison control. These findings are still informative because they suggest transient post-NPI increases for several pathogens, while also showing that not all apparent rebounds were statistically stable after adjustment for multiple testing. For influenza A H1N1 (2009) virus, the large period-comparison RR and wide confidence interval mainly reflected sparse detections during the NPI period, indicating a marked post-NPI increase with limited precision of the RR estimate.The RSV-focused supplementary analysis further highlights the translational relevance of age-specific surveillance, consistent with previous evidence that RSV contributes substantially to acute lower respiratory infection burden in young children and that RSV activity was altered during and after COVID-19-related restriction periods (2, 10–12). Although the primary age strata were designed to reflect childcare and schooling stages in China, reclassification into RSV prevention-relevant age windows showed that children younger than 2 years accounted for most RSV-positive records and had nearly twice the overall RSV detection risk observed in older children. The highest positivity was observed in the 6–<12-month and 12–<24-month groups, supporting the importance of infant- and toddler-focused RSV prevention and surveillance strategies. The stronger relative post-NPI increase among children aged ≥2 years also suggests broader age redistribution of RSV detection after the lifting of NPIs. Because this study was based on laboratory testing records, these findings should be interpreted as age-specific RSV detection patterns in a laboratory surveillance dataset and may inform future studies that link virological detection with hospitalization and severity outcomes.Human adenovirus showed a contrasting pattern, with both a lower post-NPI detection risk and a robust immediate level decrease in ITS analysis. This divergence from HRV further highlights the pathogen-specific nature of post-NPI changes. This pattern underscores the value of local pathogen-specific laboratory surveillance, because decreases in selected pathogens may be hidden when respiratory pathogen activity is assessed only through aggregate positivity. full_text_sections.conclusion: 5ConclusionOver 5 years of continuous hospital-based laboratory surveillance, pediatric respiratory pathogen detection showed distinct overall and pathogen-specific patterns across the NPI and post-NPI periods, with higher overall positivity and co-detection rates in the post-NPI period. Pathogen-specific interrupted time-series analyses further revealed different temporal trajectories, including an immediate decrease in HADV and a significant positive trend change in HRV with a positive post-NPI slope. Age-stratified analyses and assessments of meteorological and school-calendar factors further showed that associations between pathogen detection, age, and contextual factors were pathogen-specific; phase-interaction analyses additionally indicated that the associations of temperature with HPIV, school-term status with H3, and relative humidity with Ch differed between the NPI and post-NPI periods. Taken together, these findings support continued hospital-based multi-pathogen laboratory surveillance integrating pathogen-specific temporal trends, age stratification, co-detection patterns, and environmental and school-calendar context to facilitate dynamic identification of pediatric respiratory pathogen activity, prioritization of surveillance targets, and pediatric service preparedness.
full_text_sections.other: 1IntroductionAcute respiratory infections remain a major cause of illness among children worldwide and are associated with substantial healthcare use, hospitalization, and public health burden (1). Among specific pediatric pathogens, respiratory syncytial virus, seasonal influenza virus, human metapneumovirus, and human parainfluenza virus contribute substantially to acute lower respiratory infection burden in young children (2–5). Laboratory-based surveillance in China has also shown that pediatric and community respiratory specimens can involve diverse viral and atypical pathogens rather than a single dominant target (6). These patterns vary by age, season, geography, and social contact structure, highlighting the importance of continuous laboratory-based surveillance for understanding temporal changes in pediatric respiratory pathogen activity.During the COVID-19 pandemic, non-pharmaceutical interventions (NPIs), such as mask wearing, school closures, reduced mobility, physical distancing, and enhanced hygiene measures, substantially altered community respiratory virus activity beyond SARS-CoV-2 (7). Observational and pediatric hospital-based studies in China showed broad impacts of NPIs on acute respiratory infections and common childhood respiratory viruses (8, 9). Respiratory syncytial virus-specific studies also reported altered epidemiological and clinical characteristics among hospitalized children during the pandemic period (10). These changes were not uniform across pathogens or regions, suggesting that pathogen biology, population susceptibility, testing behavior, and contact patterns may have interacted to shape observed laboratory detection trends.After the relaxation or lifting of COVID-19-related NPIs, many settings reported renewed activity of pediatric respiratory pathogens, but post-NPI changes have not consistently followed a single synchronized rebound pattern. Studies have described off-season or asynchronous resurgence of influenza viruses, respiratory syncytial virus, human metapneumovirus, and other common respiratory viruses after periods of reduced activity (11–13). Post-NPI resurgence or shifting epidemic features of Mycoplasma pneumoniae have also been reported in China and related pediatric studies (14, 15). The concept of immune debt has further been proposed to help explain heterogeneous pediatric respiratory infection activity after the pandemic (16). These observations suggest that the post-NPI period may be better understood as a phase of pathogen-specific reshaping of respiratory pathogen detection patterns rather than a simple return to pre-pandemic seasonality.In parallel with changes in population contact patterns, environmental and calendar-related factors may provide important context for respiratory pathogen activity. Temperature and meteorological conditions have been associated with viral seasonality and pathogen-specific acute respiratory infection patterns (17, 18). Air pollution has also been linked to respiratory infection susceptibility and pediatric respiratory health (19). School sessions have been associated with seasonal outbreaks of medically attended respiratory infections (20). Nevertheless, few studies have jointly evaluated meteorological conditions, air quality, and school-term status across multiple pediatric respiratory pathogen categories in the post-NPI period.Although evidence on post-NPI respiratory pathogen activity is increasing, the available literature remains constrained by several methodological limitations. Many studies have relied on short observation windows, selected-pathogen analyses, or simple before-and-after comparisons, which are insufficient to separate an abrupt post-policy level change from a sustained change in temporal slope. Continuous multi-year laboratory datasets that span both the NPI and post-NPI periods and simultaneously evaluate multiple pediatric respiratory pathogens remain scarce. Moreover, environmental conditions, air quality, and school-calendar context are rarely assessed within the same pathogen-specific analytical framework. These limitations restrict the ability of surveillance studies to determine whether post-NPI changes represent a uniform rebound or a more complex reshaping of pathogen-specific detection patterns.To address these gaps, we analyzed 20,250 pediatric throat-swab testing records collected over five consecutive years, from January 2021 to December 2025. We compared pathogen detection risks between the NPI and post-NPI periods, evaluated overall long-term and segmented temporal changes, applied pathogen-specific interrupted time-series models, and assessed associations of meteorological factors, air quality, and school-term status with pathogen-specific positivity, including potential variation in these associations across study periods. By integrating a large continuous laboratory dataset with time-series and contextual analyses, this study aimed to characterize pathogen-specific temporal patterns across the NPI and post-NPI periods and their relevance to hospital-based laboratory surveillance. 2.2Study populationEligible testing records were from pediatric or neonatal inpatients aged 0–14 years with a clinician-recorded diagnosis of lower respiratory tract infection on the laboratory test request. These patients underwent routine 13-target multiplex respiratory pathogen testing between January 1, 2021, and December 31, 2025. Testing was ordered by clinicians according to the child's clinical presentation and diagnostic needs. Throat swabs were collected for respiratory pathogen nucleic acid testing. Records were required to contain complete information on sex, age, application date, and pathogen detection results. Outpatient and emergency department records were not included. Throughout the study period, the source wards, age range, eligibility criteria, and specimen type remained consistent.A total of 21,132 original identification records were initially available. After preliminary data cleaning, variable harmonization, and verification of key fields, 20,296 preliminary testing records were retained. To reduce the influence of repeated short-term testing from the same child, 7-day deduplication was performed using medical record numbers. For each child, testing records were ordered chronologically by application time; when multiple respiratory pathogen tests occurred within a 7-day window, only the first record was retained, whereas a test performed more than 7 days after the previously retained record was considered a new testing event. After deduplication, 46 short-term duplicate records were removed, leaving 20,250 testing records for the main analysis, including 6,490 records from the NPI period and 13,760 from the post-NPI period. The final dataset covered 60 consecutive months from January 2021 to December 2025. The overall study design, data-cleaning process, 7-day deduplication procedure, study-period classification, and analytical workflow are summarized in Figure 1.Figure 1Study design, data cleaning, and analytical workflow. The figure shows the data source, exclusion process, 7-day deduplication, study-period classification, and analytical framework. The NPI period was defined as January 2021 to December 2022, and the post-NPI period was defined as January 2023 to December 2025. During 7-day deduplication, only the first testing record from the same child within a 7-day window was retained. title_original: Ecological reshaping of pediatric respiratory pathogen profiles after COVID-19-related non-pharmaceutical interventions were lifted: a 5-year interrupted time-series study

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to investigate how the lifting of non-pharmaceutical interventions (NPIs) related to COVID-19 affected the ecological patterns of pediatric respiratory pathogens, particularly focusing on seasonal influenza viruses.
analysis.study_design_and_population: This 5-year interrupted time-series study analyzed pediatric respiratory pathogen profiles in Nanchong, Sichuan Province, China, from 2018 to 2023. The study population included inpatients and neonates, with data stratified by age groups corresponding to infancy, early childhood, kindergarten age, and school age.
analysis.methods: Respiratory pathogen nucleic acid testing was conducted using a multiplex detection kit based on fluorescence PCR and capillary electrophoresis. The main analysis included 13 respiratory pathogen categories, and results were reported as adjusted odds ratios (aORs) with 95% confidence intervals. Meteorological factors, air quality index, and school-term status were incorporated into multivariable logistic regression models.
analysis.main_results: Pathogen-specific interrupted time-series analysis revealed heterogeneous patterns, with human adenovirus showing a robust immediate level decrease (−13.00 percentage points; 95% CI, −20.13 to −5.87; FDR-adjusted P = 0.005) and human rhinovirus showing a significant positive trend change after the January 2023 interruption (+1.07 percentage points per month; 95% CI, 0.63–1.50; FDR-adjusted P < 0.001). Higher temperature was associated with lower positivity of influenza A H1N1 (2009) virus and influenza B virus, but higher positivity of human parainfluenza virus and human bocavirus.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpreted the findings as indicating distinct and heterogeneous temporal patterns in pediatric respiratory pathogen detection before and after the lifting of NPIs, highlighting the complex interplay between public health measures and pathogen dynamics.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings provide insights into how changes in public health policies can influence the detection rates of respiratory pathogens, which may inform future surveillance and intervention strategies for seasonal influenza viruses in pediatric populations.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study's design was limited to laboratory detection among tested inpatients and neonates, and it did not estimate community incidence or prevalence. The evidence is moderate due to the reliance on observational data and potential confounding factors.

analysis.summary_en: This 5-year interrupted time-series study investigated the impact of lifting non-pharmaceutical interventions (NPIs) related to COVID-19 on pediatric respiratory pathogen profiles, with a focus on seasonal influenza viruses. The study analyzed 13 respiratory pathogen categories using nucleic acid testing, multivariable logistic regression, and interrupted time-series models, incorporating meteorological factors and school-term status. Results showed heterogeneous patterns, with human adenovirus decreasing and human rhinovirus increasing in positivity after NPIs were lifted. Higher temperatures were linked to lower positivity of influenza A H1N1 (2009) and influenza B viruses, but higher positivity of human parainfluenza virus and human bocavirus. The authors interpreted these findings as reflecting distinct temporal patterns in pathogen detection, emphasizing the complex relationship between public health measures and viral dynamics. The study's significance lies in its potential to inform surveillance and intervention strategies for seasonal influenza in children. However, the evidence is moderate due to the study's focus on laboratory detection and the absence of community-level data.

analysis_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 这些发现提供了关于公共卫生政策变化如何影响呼吸道病原体检测率的见解,这可能有助于未来监测和针对季节性流感病毒的儿科人群干预策略的制定。
analysis_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 本研究的设计仅限于对接受检测的住院患者和新生儿的实验室检测,未估计社区发病率或患病率。由于依赖观察性数据和潜在的混杂因素,证据强度中等。

title: Implementation Plasmonic Self-Similar Metasurface for Fast Influenza Virus Detection at Mid-Infra-Red Spectrum with Fano Response

source_records.title: Implementation Plasmonic Self-Similar Metasurface for Fast Influenza Virus Detection at Mid-Infra-Red Spectrum with Fano Response
Implementation Plasmonic Self-Similar Metasurface for Fast Influenza Virus Detection at Mid-Infra-Red Spectrum with Fano Response

priority_tier_reason: 补充性记录、预印本或证据完整度有限
full_text: Abstract Self-similar metasurfaces have been considered as one of the best solutions for manipulate and control the light to enhance the sensing accuracy such as viruses, bacteria and anti-bodies in the optical range. In this paper, a combination of two different size of diamond elements array are used to design a self-similar plasmonic metasurface to achieve the Fano response at mid-infrared spectrum including 1900 and 2100 nm. The structure has asymmetric formation and thus result has dependence to TE and TM mode and this feature is considered for developing the optical switch with ratios of 6.2 and 13.8 for 1900 and 2100 nm respectively. The Coupled Mode Theory (CMT) is employed to describe the interaction between the resonant modes generated within the proposed metasurface absorber. The Fano responses of the proposed metasurface makes it interesting for sensing application and so it is examined as a sensor for Flu virus detecting. The sensitivity and Figure of Merit (FOM) for the proposed optical sensor is obtained 660 to 903 nm/RIU and 25 up to 110 RIU− 1 corresponding with material with refractive index of 1.1 to 1.5. The virus ratio finally is checked with this metasurface which shows a high resolution. full_text_sections.full_text: Abstract Self-similar metasurfaces have been considered as one of the best solutions for manipulate and control the light to enhance the sensing accuracy such as viruses, bacteria and anti-bodies in the optical range. In this paper, a combination of two different size of diamond elements array are used to design a self-similar plasmonic metasurface to achieve the Fano response at mid-infrared spectrum including 1900 and 2100 nm. The structure has asymmetric formation and thus result has dependence to TE and TM mode and this feature is considered for developing the optical switch with ratios of 6.2 and 13.8 for 1900 and 2100 nm respectively. The Coupled Mode Theory (CMT) is employed to describe the interaction between the resonant modes generated within the proposed metasurface absorber. The Fano responses of the proposed metasurface makes it interesting for sensing application and so it is examined as a sensor for Flu virus detecting. The sensitivity and Figure of Merit (FOM) for the proposed optical sensor is obtained 660 to 903 nm/RIU and 25 up to 110 RIU− 1 corresponding with material with refractive index of 1.1 to 1.5. The virus ratio finally is checked with this metasurface which shows a high resolution.
